Fourteen measurements · one shared shape

Flat or globe? Measure it yourself.

Each card below is one thing you can do without buying anything. No explanation here on purpose — the tab behind each card carries the geometry, the sources and the numbers, and every one of them computes both models side by side. One radius, R ≈ 6,371 km, satisfies all of them at once. No flat arrangement satisfies two.

Photograph a distant peak and measure how high it sits above the horizon. Watch a ship leave: the hull goes before the mast, and always in that order. Measure the altitude of Polaris from two cities and subtract. Photograph the star trails for an hour. Note which way they turn. Time a long-haul flight and compare it with the distance your map claims. From a cliff, measure how far below eye level the sea horizon sits. Weigh the same object at the equator and near a pole. Hang a long pendulum and mark where it swings every hour. Take one earthquake and read its arrival times at two distant stations. Let a compass needle tilt freely on a horizontal axis and read the angle. Measure the Sun's angular width in January and again in July. Time how long the sky stays lit after the Sun has gone down. Point at the Sun and read the compass bearing, then look up the place beneath it. Open your phone's GPS status screen and watch satellites rise and set.

And four that answer objections

These four propose no measurement of their own, so they are set apart rather than left out: refraction, which is the standard escape and is modelled everywhere on this page; surveying and levelling, which is what the profession already does about it; the observation guide, which is how to photograph a ridge without fooling yourself; and the celestial theodolite, which is somebody else's experiment examined on its own terms.

Where R/(1 − k) comes from, and why one coefficient has to serve every tab. Two centuries of professional procedure that exist only because flat arithmetic kept missing. How to photograph a ridge against the Sun without fooling yourself — and this page's own attempt. Somebody else's experiment, taken seriously: a clock instead of a theodolite.
The same observer, the same target, one assumption changed. One eye height, one ground distance, one target height, in both. The dashed line is eye level and α is the elevation angle, drawn at the same radius in both panels so the two can be compared by looking.

04

Reverse-engineering the furthest target from two angles

A classic surveyor's trick — the “inaccessible height” — recovers an object's height from two elevation angles taken a known distance apart, without ever reaching it. We use the observer and a second station at the distance of the nearest example object (both close to eye height, which is why the nearest summit being about as high as the observer matters). Then the angles the furthest target actually produces are fed back in, and it is reconstructed two ways.

Tangent: H = b / (cot α_far − cot α_near)
Law of sines: intersect the two real sightlines in the triangle O–N–T
b = baseline (nearest object's distance), α_far and α_near the elevation angles to the furthest summit from the two stations. The tangent method assumes the two “level” lines are parallel — flat‑Earth trigonometry. The law‑of‑sines method solves the real triangle of observer O, near station N and target T, allowing for the fact that “level” tilts by b/R between the stations. On a plane the two are the same formula; on a globe they part ways.

Diagram: what each method assumes

Panels B and C: the same triangle, two reference frames. The three points O, N and T are the same in both; what differs is the direction each angle is measured from.

Does the globe need a different formula? Not a different theorem — only a different reference frame. The sine rule is a statement about triangles, not about flat ground: any three points define a plane, and O, N and T are three points, so a / sin α_far = b / sin(α_near − α_far) is equally valid in panel B and panel C. What curvature changes is where each angle is measured from — the local horizontal at N is rotated from the one at O by the arc b/R, here about 9′ (0.15°).

So the globe procedure is: re-reference the second angle by that rotation, solve the ordinary triangle, then convert the resulting point back to a distance from the Earth's centre. The tangent method cannot do step one at all — parallel levels are baked into cot, so it has nowhere to put the b/R term. That missing rotation is the curvature, and the tables below measure what it costs.

Result 1 — elevation angle of the furthest target

Result 3 — what the flat surveyor actually concludes

This is the decisive number. The frame rotation b/R is not a small refinement here — it is larger than the whole angular difference being measured. Drop it and you don't get a slightly wrong answer; you get an answer that can be falsified by driving to the spot.

The reference rotation compared with the signal it corrects
QuantityValueMeaning

A caveat worth stating. With both stations at the same eye height the two sightlines are nearly parallel, so this particular baseline is a poorly‑conditioned way to pin down a height — small angle errors move the intersection a long way. That is a limitation of the configuration, not of the geometry: the reconstruction above is computed by intersecting the two true rays in the Earth‑centred frame, which is exact. In real surveying the two stations are deliberately placed at clearly different heights, or the baseline is made long relative to the range, precisely to avoid this. The robust result here is the angle comparison in Result 1, which needs no intersection at all.

05

Measuring an angle on a sphere

A common objection: “angles only mean anything on a flat plane — you can't measure elevation on a ball.” But an angle is measured against a reference direction, and every point on a sphere has one: the direction a bubble level settles into. That local horizontal is the tangent at your feet, and it exists everywhere. Below, two protractors sit on a rotating globe — one at the observer, one on the summit — each with 0° along its own tangent. No plane is drawn anywhere.

· drag to turn it yourself
Two instruments, two horizons, one sphere. The blue protractor stands at the observer; its 0° mark lies along the tangent there. The violet protractor stands on the summit with 0° along its tangent. Both are ordinary protractors reading ordinary angles — nothing about the curved ground stops either from working. What the curvature does is tilt the two 0° lines relative to each other, by exactly the central angle between the two locations. The mountain is drawn absurdly large (30% of the planet's radius) so the angles are legible; on the real Earth the same tilt is the tiny b/R term from section 04.

Reciprocal zenith angles — the parameter-free test

Point each protractor at the other station and read the zenith angle — the angle down from straight up, which is just 90° minus the elevation. Do it from both ends at once. The sum of those two readings is the single most decisive number in this whole page, because the flat prediction contains no adjustable quantities at all.

Flat: zA + zB = 180° exactly
Globe: zA + zB = 180° + d/R
If verticals are parallel, the line joining the two stations is a transversal cutting two parallel lines, so the two zenith angles are co‑interior and must sum to 180° — a theorem of plane geometry, independent of the distance, of either height, and of how much taller one station is than the other. On a sphere the two verticals meet at the centre, forming a triangle whose angles sum to 180°; the central angle d/R appears as an excess over 180°. Measure the excess and you have measured the Earth: R = d / (z_A + z_B − 180°).
Reciprocal zenith angles between the observer and the furthest target of the current example
QuantityValueWhat it means

How to read these experiment boxes. An experiment changes one thing and watches what happens to another. The thing you deliberately change is the independent variable (IV). The thing you then measure, and do not control, is the dependent variable (DV). Everything else must be held constant, or you cannot tell what caused what. A model is testable when it predicts a specific DV for each IV — and it is refuted when the measured DV does not match. Both models below make definite predictions, so whichever fails, fails honestly.
Experiment 1 · elevation angles
Two levelled instruments, pointed at each other

Two people stand where they can see each other. Each levels a theodolite with its bubble and measures the zenith angle to the other — the angle down from straight up. Add the two readings together.

Independent variable
What you change: the distance d between the two stations. Do it at 1 km, then 10 km, then 50 km. You pick these — that is what makes it the IV.
Dependent variable
What you measure: the sum of the two zenith angles, z_A + z_B. You do not get to choose this — the instruments tell you.

Hold constant: take both readings at the same moment (so both rays pass through the same air), level both instruments carefully, and use the same instruments at every distance.
Kit: two theodolites or digital levels reading to 1 arcminute or better, two intervisible points, and a map or GPS for d.

Why this one is hard to argue with. Most curvature tests can be met with “your instrument was off” or “that's refraction” or “your height was wrong.” This one cannot be met with a wrong height: the heights cancel. Put a 5 m station and a 3,000 m station 200 km apart and the sum still comes out at 180° + d/R to the last decimal. The flat model does not predict “about 180°” — it predicts 180.000°, always. Any reproducible excess falsifies it, and the size of that excess hands you R.

Refraction, honestly. Bending reduces the excess by roughly the refraction coefficient, so the observed sum is about 180° + (d/R)(1−k). Reading R straight off an uncorrected excess therefore overestimates it by ~15%, exactly as in the dip method. Geodesists have exploited this since the 1800s: because simultaneous reciprocal observations experience nearly the same air, the technique is the standard way to measure k itself — and no value of k brings a curved excess back to zero.

What the demo shows. Rotate it and watch the two 0° tangents: they never become parallel, and their disagreement is the central angle, not an instrument error. This is why a theodolite works perfectly well on a globe — you level it, read an angle against the local horizontal, and get a number. It is also why two such readings taken far apart cannot be combined as if their zeros pointed the same way: that, and only that, is the mistake the flat method makes.

06

Why you subtract the observer's height

A frequent objection: “why (h − e) and not just h? You're smuggling in the globe.” No — this step is derived inside the flat model, using its own assumptions. If the Earth is a plane, then every vertical is parallel to every other vertical and the ground is one straight horizontal line. That is exactly what builds a rectangle:

Only the difference of the two heights ever enters the flat formula. That is why this page asks for heights above mean sea level for both observer and target: not to sneak in a curve, but because any constant added to both cancels out. The globe formula, by contrast, genuinely needs the absolute heights, because R + h and R + e are radii from the centre.

Where tan α = (h − e)/d comes fromTwo lines of right-angle trigonometry, and why the choice of datum drops out of them

Read the pair at the top of this tab again and the flat formula is forced, not chosen. The rectangle's far side is e tall, so the part of the target visible above your eye‑level line is (h − e). That leaves a right triangle with opposite side (h − e) and adjacent side d, giving tan α = (h − e)/d. If you used h alone you would be measuring the angle from the observer's feet, not from their eye.

And the reference level cancels. Heights above mean sea level, above the ellipsoid, above the valley floor — it makes no difference, provided both are measured from the same datum. Add any constant c to both and the formula is untouched: (h + c) − (e + c) = h − e. That is why the page asks for MSL heights for both observer and target: not to sneak in a curve, but because only their difference ever enters the flat calculation. The globe formula, by contrast, genuinely needs the absolute heights, because R + h and R + e are radii from the centre.

07

Angular size: nearly identical, and that's the point

A fair follow‑up: “if the globe changed the geometry, wouldn't mountains look obviously wrong in photos?” No — and the numbers show why. The two models disagree about where a peak sits in your view, but almost not at all about how big it looks.

Flat: β = atan((h−e)/d) + atan(e/d)
Globe: β = elev(top) − elev(base)
Angular size β is the angle between the sightline to the base and the sightline to the summit. On the plane it is just the two right‑triangle angles either side of eye level. On the globe both ends are computed with the arctan2 formula and subtracted — the peak leans away from you by θ = d/R, so it is very slightly foreshortened.

08

How each number is found

What is exact, and what is only drawn. The angle numbers are always computed from the true, un‑exaggerated geometry. The vertical‑exaggeration slider stretches the drawing's vertical axis and nothing else; above 1× the drawn slopes no longer match the printed angles, and a warning on the canvas says so.

Refraction here is a representative average, not a constant. k ≈ 0.13 is typical daytime air. Real refraction varies with the weather and can even go negative over hot ground, which is a mirage — so the table keeps the un‑refracted figure beside the refracted one, and you can read off exactly how much lift k buys.

How each model computes the angleFlat plane, globe, and the refracted globe — the three formulas above, written out in words

Flat plane. The ground is a straight line, so this is plain right‑angle trigonometry. With eye height e, target height h, and horizontal distance d, the elevation is atan( (h − e) / d ). It depends only on that ratio: a target taller than you is always above your eye level, and the angle shrinks slowly as it gets farther away, but never dips below 0°.

Globe. Over distance d the surface curves away from your local horizontal by about d² / 2R. Put the observer's eye at the top of a circle of radius R and the target at arc‑distance d (so the central angle is θ = d/R). Measured against the observer's own eye‑level line, the elevation is atan2( (R+h)·cosθ − (R+e), (R+h)·sinθ ). The curvature term pulls every target down compared with the flat answer; far or short targets fall below eye level entirely (a negative angle), and anything past the horizon distance ≈ √(2Re) has its base hidden by the bulge.

Atmospheric refraction. Air is denser near the ground, so light bends gently downward as it travels, letting you see a little past the geometric horizon and making distant targets sit higher than pure geometry predicts. The standard surveying shortcut is to keep the rays straight but swap in a larger effective radius R_eff = R / (1 − k), where the refraction coefficient k ≈ 0.13 for typical daytime air (k ≈ 0.143 gives the well‑known "7/6 earth" rule). Turning it on here raises every globe angle toward the flat‑plane value and pushes the horizon farther out.

Why the picture looks nearly flat. At true scale the drop is a fraction of a percent of the distance, so both panels look almost identical to the eye — that is honest. The difference lives in the angles, which a surveyor's theodolite reads directly.

Summarises Helbronner's Description géométrique détaillée des Alpes françaises, tome IX (Gauthier-Villars, 1929).

  • [3]Montagne du Cheiron (Wikipédia, FR) — the ridge the original observation was made from, and the source for the observer's height: the summits of the Cheiron are the cime du Cheiron (1,778 m), Jérusalem (1,768 m), the sommet de Viériou, also spelled Viriou (1,395 m), and Coutellade (1,322 m). The same list is published by the Parc naturel régional des Préalpes d'Azur and by Pays de Grasse Tourisme.
  • [4]Castellaras de Thorenc (Wikipédia, FR) — the nearer of the two aligned targets: a rocky pinnacle at 1,400 m at Andon, Alpes-Maritimes, carrying the ruins of a medieval castle, listed as a monument historique on 28 March 1991.
  • [5]The Canigou seen from Notre-Dame de la Garde, Marseille — photographs of the sunset alignment taken from the basilica esplanade at 142 m, together with the argument this page's section 03 formalises: on a plane the visual horizon sits at eye level, so nothing lower than the observer could ever be seen — and things lower than the observer are seen every day.
  • [6]The Bedford Level experiment (Historic UK) — the 1870 three-marker design used as an example here and worked through properly in tab 7: markers at equal height above still water along a 9.7 km straight canal, which is the cleanest classical form of this whole argument.
  • [7]Guinness World Records — longest line of sight on earth photographed — 493.07 km (306.37 mi), Richard Jezik (Slovakia), Giresun, Turkey, 15 December 2024. The citation also records the conditions, which matter more than the distance: months of watching the forecast, a ten-hour hike through snow to the summit, a night at −12 °C with the wind rising to 20–25 m/s, and the frame taken before sunrise. Cited here because the flat-earth argument rests on it — so it is quoted from the certifying body rather than from a repost.
  • [8]Long distance observations (Wikipedia) — the maintained list behind the ceiling table: the 493 km Karagöl → Shkhara shot of 15 December 2024, the 483.5 km Cerro Champaquí → Aconcagua of 13 June 2023, and Marc Bret's 443 km Pic de Finestrelles → Massif des Écrins of 16 July 2016. Useful precisely because it is kept by enthusiasts who would love to list a longer one.
  • [9]Shkhara (Wikipedia) — the target's height, 5,203 m (17,070 ft), on the Georgia–Russia border; the summit sits on the Bezengi Wall, an 11–12 km rampart, which is what makes the “what else should be in the frame” test so sharp.
Further reading
Not cited above, and no claim on this tab rests on it — listed because it is what you would read next, or because it lets you redo the measurement on data this page did not choose.
  • Bowditch, The American Practical Navigator, Vol. 2 (NGA, 2019; PDF hosted by the US Coast Guard) — the standard reference for sightline geometry over a curved sea: visibility of distant objects, dip and refraction corrections, and the tables navigators actually use.
  • Hirt et al. (2010), J. Geophys. Res. — terrestrial refraction coefficient — the k ≈ 0.13 "Gaussian" value used here (Gauss derived it in 1826 from his Hanover survey network), and field measurements showing k varies with weather and can even go negative over hot ground — exactly why this page treats variable-k models as unfalsifiable and keeps k fixed and visible.
  • NGA Maritime Safety Information — the official, free access point for Bowditch and related publications.
  • L. Dettwiller, Phénomènes de réfraction atmosphérique terrestre, C. R. Physique 23 (2022) S1, 103–132 (Académie des sciences) — derives the refraction coefficient from the vertical temperature gradient and gives κ ≈ 0.17 for the US 1976 standard atmosphere at sea level, the value this page assumes for sightlines close to a water surface. Also the reference for what happens when κ goes large or negative (mirages, hillingar).
  • L. Dettwiller, Panorama historique de l'étude de la réfraction astronomique, C. R. Physique 23 (2022) S1, 13–62 — notes the long-run working average of about 0.14 for geodesists, whose observations are typically made from relatively high stations on warm sunny afternoons; used here for the Corsica junction, where no coefficient was published for the observations themselves.
  • IGN — Géoportail and the RGE ALTI elevation model. The French national mapping agency's own coordinates and heights for every summit used on this page. The cases here currently rest on Wikipedia for the observer and target heights; the IGN is the authority those articles are quoting, and it is worth going to it directly. Search "Géoportail" plus the summit name.
  • U.S. Naval Observatory — Astronomical Applications data services. Rise, set and transit times, and altitude/azimuth for any body from any position. If you want to check an elevation angle in this tab against an independent official calculation rather than against this page's own arithmetic, this is where to do it.
  • Marc Bret — Beyond Range. The observer who photographed Pic Gaspard from Pic de Finestrelles in July 2016 at 443 km, then the Pyrenees from the Vosges at 580 km, publishing the predicted panorama beside the photograph each time. First-hand material for the long-distance sightings this tab treats second-hand.
Hidden by the curve · the argument people actually have

How much of it is hidden?

Diagram: the same target, the two models

  • A: the ground is a straight line, so a straight ray always reaches the target's foot
  • B: the ray grazes at d₀, climbs away, and arrives a height H up the wall
  • the same ray through real air: it bends down, grazes further out, arrives lower
One picture, one assumption changed. Everything under the mark in B is behind the planet. The curvature is drawn far larger than life so the two rays separate on screen, and the violet arc's k is exaggerated to 0.35 for legibility; every number printed by the calculator below is computed from true, un-exaggerated geometry.

Angles are the sharper test, but the argument people actually have on the shore of a lake is blunter: can you see the bottom of that far building, or not? The two models answer differently, and not by a few percent. A plane hides nothing, ever — a distant object shrinks until your lens or the haze gives up, but its waterline stays in the geometric line of sight at any distance. A globe puts a bulge in the way, and that bulge covers a definite number of metres that you can write down before you look — and that shrinks in a definite way when you raise the camera.

Horizon: d₀ = R·arccos(R/(R+e)) ≈ √(2Re)
Hidden: H = R·(sec((d−d₀)/R) − 1)
Flat: H = 0
e is your eye height above the water, d the distance to the target, R the Earth's radius. Light leaves your eye, grazes the surface at the horizon distance d₀, and carries on straight; by the time it reaches the target it has climbed H above the water there. Everything below H is behind the bulge. On a plane there is no bulge and no horizon: H = 0 for every e and every d, with no free parameter to tune. That is a sign difference, not a magnitude difference.

Diagram: three quantities that get confused for each other

Three different lengths. The drop (amber) is how far the surface falls away from the tangent line at your feet — d²/2R, the number in every “curvature chart”. The horizon (teal) is where a ray from your eye touches the water; it exists only because your eye is above the surface. The hidden height (red) is measured from the water at the far end up to where that same ray arrives. Only the third one answers “what can't I see?”. They coincide in exactly one case: e = 0, an eye lying on the water, which is also the one case in which you see nothing at all.
The arithmetic trap that ruins most of these arguments — on both sides. The famous “eight inches per mile squared”, d²/2R, is not the hidden height. It is the drop of the surface below the tangent line at your feet, and it assumes your eye is on the water. Standing 2 m up at 14.4 km it predicts 16.3 m hidden; the correct answer is 6.9 m. Use it as a hidden height and you overstate the effect, hand the other side an easy rebuttal, and deserve it. The horizon term d₀ is what carries your own height into the answer, and it is the whole reason a taller observer sees more.

Calculator — what the curve takes away

Type your own numbers, or load one of the documented sightlines. The radius R comes from the Elevation-angles tab, so you can also ask what radius would have hidden what you saw. Refraction is never hidden from you: the geometric and refracted answers are printed side by side, and refraction can only ever uncover more of the target, never less.

Examples

The same case, drawn three ways

Two orthographic cross-sections — the scene seen from the side, from outside — and then the view from the observer's own eye. The flat panel is, admittedly, not very interesting: a straight ground line and a straight sightline that always reaches the foot of the target. That is the flat model's entire content here, and seeing how little there is to it beside the globe panel is worth the space. Everything below is driven by the calculator above, by the Earth radius set in the Elevation-angles tab, and by the refraction controls immediately below, which are that same k slider wired to a second handle.

Each worked example below loads the refraction coefficient appropriate to it, and says where that number comes from. Where the original observers state one, theirs is used; where they do not, the page uses a documented standard and labels it as an assumption — never a value tuned to make the answer come out right. Over water at eye level the standard-atmosphere value is k ≈ 0.17[1]; for geodesists working from high summits on warm afternoons the long-run average is about k ≈ 0.14[2]; the k ≈ 0.13 default elsewhere on this page is Gauss's value from the Hanover survey[3].

The direction is the whole point. Refraction can only ever uncover more of the target, never less, so it cannot rescue a flat prediction that needs the base visible in the first place.

The band is the part that misleads. It does not mean everything below the line is hidden. A target nearer than the horizon drops below that line as soon as you are high up and is drawn on top of the band, because it stands in front of the water and you see all of it — the cable-car case. Only a target beyond the horizon is buried, and there the dashed flat outline carries on down through the band, which is the disagreement. At 1× the side views are true scale; the exaggeration slider draws the planet with radius R/ex and heights ×ex, so curvature, drop and the tilt of verticals stretch together. Every printed angle and distance is computed from the true, un-exaggerated geometry.

Documented sightlines, run through both models

Each row is a real observation someone has published; the two right-hand columns are what each model says should have been invisible
SightlineEye eDistance d Globe hidesPlane hidesWhat was reported

Chicago from across Lake Michigan is the most-cited long-distance claim of all, and it is the easiest to check. The target is a building of published height standing on a lake whose surface is the datum, photographed from a shore with no terrain in between — no crest to identify, no ground profile to model. Four viewpoints are in the list above, from 53 to 93 km. At every one of them the globe hides a definite, predicted fraction of the tower and a plane hides nothing at all, at any distance. The photographs show crowns without bases[12]. The measured column stays empty: how much of the tower was visible is exactly what these pictures rarely state, and it is the one number that would settle each case.

Canigou from Allauch is the same measurement this page is about to attempt, and it has been made since 1808. The peak stands 263 km from Marseille and is seen only when the setting Sun is directly behind it, which happens around 9 February and 1 November — the two dates when the sunset azimuth from Allauch points at the summit[13]. That twice-a-year rhythm is routinely offered as proof that refraction is being invoked selectively. It is the opposite: the dates are fixed by where the Sun sets, not by the air. Standard refraction is there every day; the backlight is not.

And the photograph carries its own verdict. What appears is the top of the mountain and nothing else — the local observers put the cut near 2,450 m of a 2,785 m summit, which needs k ≈ 0.22, strong but ordinary for a warm sea in February. On a plane nothing is hidden at any distance, so the whole 2,785 m would stand against the sky on every clear evening of the year. It does not, and that is the entire content of the case: not that the mountain is visible, but that nine tenths of it are missing.
Not a sketch: the ridge line is swept off a 3-arcsecond elevation model of France, one terrain read, both models. True angular scale on both axes — 2.4′ of azimuth per sample, the same scale vertically — so the solar disc is drawn at the size it subtends. Through a filter everything that is not the Sun is black, sea included, and the black outline is what the globe leaves above the sea at k = 0.13. The blue line is the same terrain with the curvature removed: the massif would stand 31′ above eye level instead of 30′ below it — a gap of 62′, close to two solar diameters. One caveat kept in view: a 90 m model rounds sharp summits, reading Canigou at 2,686 m against its true 2,785, which costs about 1.3′ on the black curve and nothing on the conclusion.

The world record, and the argument built on it

493.07 km, certified — the flat arithmetic conceded first, then answered with numbers

The claim, stated fairly. On 15 December 2024 Richard Jezik photographed Shkhara, on the Georgia–Russia border, from a subpeak near the Karagöl summit above Giresun in Turkey. Guinness World Records certified the line at 493.07 km, the longest ever photographed[4]. The flat-earth argument runs: observer at 3,275 m, summit at 5,203 m, and on a sphere the peak should have been buried about 1,340 m below the observer's line of sight — yet there it is. Their arithmetic is right. Feed those numbers into the calculator above with refraction switched off and it returns 6,553 m hidden, putting the summit 1,350 m — 4,429 ft — under the geometric ray. They did the sum correctly, and the page will not pretend otherwise.

What the sum leaves out is not a rescue, it is the standard correction. Light does not travel in straight lines through 493 km of stratified air, and the amount by which it bends is not a free parameter invented for this photograph: it is tabulated, it is in every nautical almanac, and Helbronner was already correcting for it in 1925 over lines of exactly this length. The honest question is therefore not “is refraction allowed?” but “how much is needed, and is that a normal amount?” Set the calculator to this case and sweep k. The summit reaches the horizon at k = 0.123. The standard-atmosphere value at sea level is 0.17[1], and Gauss's continental working value is 0.13. The record does not need exotic refraction. It needs slightly less than average — and at the standard 0.17 it clears by 491 m, which is 9.4% of the mountain.

And 9.4% is what the photograph shows. This is where the argument turns around, because the flat model does not merely predict that Shkhara is visible. It predicts a great deal more, and all of it is checkable in the same frame. On a plane the summit stands +0.224° above eye level; on a globe it is 1.616° below. That is a gap of 110 arcminutes — three and a half full moons — in the one direction no instrument error can fake. A plane also puts the whole 5,203 m in view: the Bezengi Wall down to its base, the Svaneti valleys, Ushguli, and the Black Sea coast at Batumi, all of it below the summit and all of it in the shot. The record photograph shows none of that. It shows a thin serrated line of summits standing on the horizon with everything beneath them gone.

The record's own difficulty is the evidence. Read the citation: Jezik tracked the weather for months, hiked ten hours through snow to stand on a summit at 3,275 m, waited out a night at −12 °C in a rising gale, and shot before sunrise[4]. Every one of those choices is a curvature correction. On a plane, altitude buys nothing — a plane has no horizon, so the same photograph would be available from the beach at Giresun on any clear day, and the limit would be haze alone. Nobody has ever taken it from the beach. Every entry on the record list, without exception, is from one mountain to another.

Which gives the sphere a hard ceiling — and a way to be killed. Two peaks can see each other only if the sum of their two horizon distances covers the gap between them: d ≤ √(2R′h₁) + √(2R′h₂), with R′ the refracted radius. That expression has no adjustable term once k is fixed at its standard value, and it forbids things. The table below runs it against the record list. Every record ever set falls inside its ceiling; the three current top entries sit at 91–98% of it, pressed right against the limit and never over it. A flat plane has no such quantity, sets no ceiling, and therefore predicts nothing here at all. One photograph past the ceiling — one confirmed shot beyond that sum, between two known summits in ordinary air — refutes this page. A century of people trying very hard to break the record has not produced one.

Every certified long-distance observation, against the maximum the globe allows for that pair of summits

Lake Garda — is there an official measurement?

No survey authority has ever measured it. What exists, and what would settle it

The honest answer: not a published one. No survey authority has ever run a dedicated curvature experiment on Lake Garda, and pretending otherwise would be the kind of thing this page exists to argue against. What is official is the reference surface the lake is administered against: its level is read against a hydrometric zero fixed at 64.027 m above mean sea level, published by the Comunità del Garda[5] and used to run the regulating works at Salionze. “Above sea level” is not a decorative phrase — it means the water is referred to an equipotential surface, a level surface that closes on itself around the planet. Every lake gauge in Italy, and the levelling network that ties them together, is built on that assumption and would drift visibly out of agreement if the reference were a plane.

The lake does, however, have a history here. Italian flat-earth groups have run their own photographic tests on it and published the numbers: Bardolino → the beach at Gardone Riviera at 14.40 km, Desenzano → the harbour at Garda at 17 km, and Desenzano → the shore at Gargnano at 26 km, each reported as “clearly visible”[6]. Their arithmetic is roughly right — the table above shows the globe hiding about 7, 11 and 34 metres on those three lines. What fails is the observation, and it fails on a point of method rather than of politics: recognising a village, a harbour or a hillside says nothing about whether its waterline was in view. Gardone, Garda and Gargnano all rise tens to hundreds of metres behind their quays. A test that cannot distinguish “I can see the town” from “I can see the bottom of the town” does not discriminate between the two models, and both sides should stop citing it.

The nearest thing to a proper measurement on water was made on Rainy Lake, on the Minnesota–Ontario border, in the spring of 2018: seven targets planted on a metre of lake ice out to 9.5 km, every target position fixed by differential GPS to centimetres, and the observer's line of sight compared with both models. The surface came out curved with a radius of about 6,400 km[7]. That is the template Garda deserves, and Garda is a better stage for it: it is longer, warmer, easier to reach, and it is where the argument is actually being had.

The ideal spot on Garda, and how to use it

Malcesine: 25 / 515 / 1,695 m of eye height on one cable-car ticket, aimed 37 km down the lake

Malcesine, and the Monte Baldo cable car. Lake Garda offers something almost no other body of water in Europe does: about 50 km of open water in a straight-ish line from Riva down to Peschiera, with a lift running from the water's edge to 1,760 m standing right on the shore. The three stations of the Funivia Malcesine – Monte Baldo sit at 90 m, 580 m and 1,760 m above sea level[8]; the lake surface is at about 65 m, so in one ticket and one afternoon you can put the same camera at roughly 25 m, 515 m and 1,695 m above the water, aimed at the same target, through the same air. Sirmione is about 37 km down the lake and its Scaligero keep gives you a vertical scale bar you can count storeys on.

What each model has to say before you go. From the Malcesine waterfront at about 2 m the globe hides roughly 80 m of Sirmione at 37 km — the entire castle and a good slice of the hill it stands on. From the lakefront terrace at 25 m, about 29 m. From the mid-station at San Michele, 515 m above the water, nothing at all: the horizon is out past 80 km and the far shore is complete, waterline included. That is the whole experiment. A plane predicts the identical framing at all three heights — the target simply sits lower in the frame and appears no larger — and predicts that the waterline was never missing to begin with, so there is nothing for the climb to restore.

Protocol, so the result means something. Shoot at dawn or in a cold, well-mixed airstream, when the temperature gradient over the water is small and refraction is closest to standard; take every frame the same morning with the same lens; and photograph a target whose waterline you can identify without ambiguity — a moored buoy, an anchored boat, a measured pole, a quay with countable courses of stone — not “a village”. Record the water level from the public gauge, because it moves by more than a metre through the year. Refraction is the only knob either side gets to turn, and it is one-sided: over a lake it lifts the far shore and reduces the hidden height by a fifth or so. No value of it, including the negative values you get over hot ground, brings 80 m of missing castle back to zero.

Corsica from the mainland — the case that was measured officially

Helbronner, 1925: curvature named as the obstacle, four stations above 700 m, ±0.57″ closure

Helbronner's junction, 1925. Corsica sits about 180 km from the Côte d'Azur, and tying it geodetically to the French mainland had been attempted and abandoned since the eighteenth century. Paul Helbronner finally did it in the summers of 1925 and 1926, and the account is explicit about what had defeated everyone before: the obstacle was the curvature of the Earth's surface, which puts a hard ceiling on how far one station can see another[9]. His answer was to climb. All four mainland stations were put above 700 m — Fort du Coudon 702 m, La Sauvette 779 m, Mont Chauve d'Aspremont 840 m, Mont Agel 1,149 m — and all three Corsican ones on summits: Monte Stello 1,307 m, Monte Rotondo 2,622 m, Monte Cinto 2,709 m. On the night of 25–26 August 1925, from the top of Monte Cinto, he held five projector beams at once for eight hours: Stello at 60 km, Mont Agel at 198 km, Mont Chauve at 206 km, La Sauvette at 236 km and the Coudon at 256 km. The adjustment closed to about ±0.6 arcsecond per observed angle.

Now put those two numbers into both models. Helbronner's own computed distance from the Coudon to Monte Cinto is 255,582.75 m[10]. The summit is 2,706 m; the station is 702 m. On a plane, the peak stands 2,004 m above the observer's eye level, at an elevation of +0.449°, and its shoreline and beaches are in plain view beneath it. On a globe, 2,035 m of it is under the bulge, only the top ~670 m shows, and the summit sits −0.700° below eye level — the observer must aim downwards at a mountain two kilometres taller than he is. That is a swing of about 69 arcminutes, more than two full-moon diameters, in the one direction an instrument error cannot fake. Helbronner's whole 1,492-page volume of angles was reduced on the second assumption and closed to arcseconds.

And the amateur version agrees. Photographers on the Riviera routinely catch Monte Cinto from sea level at about 198 km, and the observation is quantitative: from an eye barely 5 m up, geometry alone hides 2,835 m — more than the whole mountain — so the sightings are only possible because refraction lifts it, which is exactly what the observers themselves conclude. Working backwards, the minimum eye height for a purely geometric sighting of Cinto is about 12 m, and for the 2,305 m Cima Statoghia at 194 km about 40 m — the same two figures an independent observer computed from his own photographs[11]. Two people, two methods, one radius. On a plane there is no minimum eye height for anything, because nothing is ever hidden, and the entire Corsican coastline should be photographable from the beach at Nice on any clear day. It never has been.

Experiment 1b · the height sweep
One target, one morning, three camera heights

Pick a target across water whose waterline you can identify — a buoy, an anchored boat, a marked pole, a quay. Photograph it from as close to the water as you can stand. Then raise the camera, without moving sideways, and photograph it again. Then again, higher. Count how much of the base reappears at each step.

Independent variable
What you change: the eye height e. You choose it — a beach, a first-floor window, a hill, a cable car — and you can measure it with a tape or a phone barometer.
Dependent variable
What you measure: the height H of the target that is cut off at the bottom, read against the known scale on the target itself. The target tells you; you do not get to choose it.

Hold constant: the same target, the same distance, the same lens, the same morning, and air as well-mixed as you can get. Zoom is free — magnification cannot restore something that is behind the planet, which is itself a decisive sub-test.
Kit: a camera with a long lens, a tripod, a target with a countable vertical scale, and a map or GPS for d.

Why zoom is the cleanest sub-test. The commonest rescue for a vanished hull is “it is just too small to resolve — zoom in and it comes back”. It is a testable claim, and it is testable in the same photograph. Something lost to angular size returns smoothly under magnification, top and bottom together. Something behind the bulge does not: the top sharpens, the bottom stays amputated at the same waterline mark however much focal length you throw at it, and the cut is horizontal and clean rather than fading. Take one frame at 24 mm and one at 600 mm from the same tripod and the two explanations separate without any arithmetic at all.

What would refute the globe here. A target of known height, at a measured distance, photographed from a measured eye height, with its waterline visible when the table above says H metres of it should be missing — reproducibly, in still cold air, at several distances, with the missing height staying at zero as d grows. That result would kill the sphere on this page's own terms. The symmetric case is just as clear: if the hidden height grows as R(sec((d−d₀)/R) − 1) and shrinks as you climb exactly as tabulated, then the flat model is finished, and the one number you had to fit — R — comes out the same 6,371 km that every other panel keeps returning.

Refraction · where R/(1−k) comes from

Light bends. Here is exactly how much — and why that does not rescue a flat Earth

Same planet, four atmospheres. One observer, four horizontal rays differing only in k, each labelled with its own. Curvature is exaggerated; the factor is printed on the figure and the ratios between the arcs are exact.

Every other tab on this page carries a refraction switch. Turn it on and the globe stops using its real radius R = 6,371 km and starts using an effective radius R/(1−k). That single substitution is the most suspected line on the whole page, so this tab does nothing but justify it: Snell's law first, then the geometry, then the weather that fixes k, then the measurements that pin it down.

And then the part nobody expects — the same formula that lets refraction help the globe puts a hard ceiling on what refraction is allowed to do, and that ceiling is exactly where the flat model would have to live.

1/ρ = −(cos β / n) · dn/dh
k ≡ R/ρ
Reff = R / (1 − k)
Three steps, and only the middle one is a definition. A vertical gradient of refractive index bends a ray into a circle of radius ρ; the refraction coefficient k is nothing but the ratio of the ray's curvature to the Earth's; and because only the difference of two curvatures can ever be observed, a curved ray over a sphere of radius R behaves exactly like a straight ray over a sphere of radius R/(1−k). Everything below is the proof, the numbers, and the limits.

What refraction actually is — and which way it bends

The refractive index of a medium is n = c/v: the speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in that medium. Denser air is slower air, so denser air has a larger n. At sea level, air has n − 1 ≈ 2.77 × 10⁻⁴ — light is slowed by about three parts in ten thousand. At the top of the troposphere that number has fallen by roughly three quarters. The atmosphere is therefore a stack of transparent layers whose n decreases upward, and a ray crossing it obeys Snell's law at every level: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with θ measured from the vertical.

The cleanest way to see which way it bends is to stop thinking about rays and think about the wavefront — a marching band advancing in line abreast. If the left half of the line steps onto mud while the right half stays on tarmac, the left half falls behind and the whole line pivots toward the mud. A wavefront does the same: the part of it that is in the slower, denser medium lags, so the front swings toward the dense side, and the ray, which is always perpendicular to the front, turns with it.

That is the whole mechanism, and it is why the popular one-liner "light bends toward the denser medium" is nearly right but worth stating precisely:

The exact statement. A ray's centre of curvature lies on the denser side. In the Earth's atmosphere, denser means lower, so a near-horizontal ray is concave downward — it bends around the planet rather than away from it.
Note what this does not say: it does not say the ray moves downward. Over a long sightline the ray actually rides above the straight chord joining its two endpoints, bulging up into the thin, fast air like a lifeguard who runs further along the beach to shorten the swim. Both descriptions are the same curve. The first is local (which way does it turn?), the second is global (where does the path go?), and confusing them is the single commonest error in amateur refraction arguments — on both sides.
Snell's law, layer by layer. Refractive index increases downward. A ray launched slightly upward is bent a little more horizontal at each interface it crosses going up, until it levels off and comes back down. Short ticks are the wavefront, always perpendicular to the ray. The dashed line is the straight chord: the real path lies above it. Index steps are hugely exaggerated so the kinks are visible; in real air there are no steps at all, only a smooth gradient, and the polyline becomes a circular arc.
Two circles, one subtraction. The planet is one circle; under a uniform gradient the light path is another, of radius ρ = R/k — about 7.7 times larger at k = 0.13. Measured down from the observer's horizontal, the ground falls away by d²/2R and the ray only by d²/2ρ. What an observer can ever see is the gap between them. Curvature is exaggerated (factor printed on the figure), but the ratio ρ/R is exact.

The atmosphere is a measured stack, not a free parameter

Air's refractivity for visible light follows a formula fixed in the laboratory: n − 1 ≈ 78.8 × 10⁻⁶ · P/T, with pressure P in hectopascals and temperature T in kelvin. Put in P = 1013 hPa and T = 288 K and you get the 2.77 × 10⁻⁴ quoted above. Nothing here is adjustable — it is a property of nitrogen and oxygen.

To find how n changes with height, differentiate that expression and feed in the one other thing the atmosphere is obliged to do — support its own weight. Hydrostatic balance says dP/dh = −ρair g, which for an ideal gas becomes dP/dh = −(g/Rd)·(P/T) = −0.0342 · P/T hPa per metre. Combining the two:

dn/dh = −78.8 × 10⁻⁶ · (P/T²) · ( 0.0342 + dT/dh )
P in hPa, T in K, dT/dh in K per metre. This is the entire physical input to everything that follows. Under a standard atmosphere at sea level (P = 1013 hPa, T = 288 K, dT/dh = −0.0065 K/m) it evaluates to −2.66 × 10⁻⁸ per metre: the index of air drops by about 27 parts per billion for every metre you climb. That is a fantastically small number, and it is enough to bend a sightline visibly over 50 km.

Snell's law on a round planet: the ray is an arc of a circle

Applying Snell's law across a stack of curved layers gives a conserved quantity, first written down by Pierre Bouguer in 1729 and known ever since as the refractive invariant: n · r · sin z = constant along a ray, where r is distance from the Earth's centre and z is the ray's local zenith angle.[1] It is the optical twin of angular momentum, and it falls straight out of Fermat's principle in a spherically symmetric medium.[8] Differentiating it along the path gives the curvature of the ray itself:

1/ρ = −(cos β / n) · dn/dh   →   1/ρ ≈ |dn/dh| for a near-horizontal ray
β is the ray's elevation above the local horizontal, so cos β ≈ 1 for the long, nearly level sightlines this page argues about, and n ≈ 1 always. A ray aimed steeply upward bends far less — which is why the Sun's refraction is 34′ at the horizon and essentially zero at the zenith. With the standard gradient above, ρ = 1/(2.66 × 10⁻⁸) ≈ 37,500 km; at the page's default k = 0.13 it is ≈ 49,000 km.
Yes — under uniform refraction the ray really is a circle, and your two-circle picture is the right one. Look at the formula: if dn/dh is constant over the slab of air the ray occupies, then 1/ρ is constant, and a curve of constant curvature is a circular arc. So the geometry reduces to exactly two circles — the Earth of radius R, and the light path of radius ρ, sharing a common vertical at the observer and slowly separating.
Three honest caveats. First, dn/dh is not truly constant: it falls off with height, so the arc is only locally circular, and a ray that climbs several kilometres straightens out as it goes. Second, cos β means a steep ray curves less than a flat one, so "one ρ" is only well defined for a family of near-horizontal rays. Third, the approximation needs h ≪ 8 km (the scale height of the atmosphere), which every terrestrial sightline satisfies. Within those limits the circular-arc model is the standard working tool of geodesy, not a simplification invented for this page.[3]

Subtracting one curvature from the other: R/(1−k), derived

Now the step everything else on this page depends on. Define the refraction coefficient as the ratio of the two curvatures: k ≡ R/ρ — how much of the Earth's curvature the light path already imitates. Stand an observer on the sphere and drop a horizontal tangent line from the eye. Over a horizontal distance d:

ground below tangent:  xE = R(sec(d/R) − 1) ≈ d²/2R
ray below tangent:  xL ≈ d²/2ρ = k·d²/2R
ray above ground:  xE − xL = (1 − k)·d²/2R = d² / 2Reff
One line of algebra, and Reff = R/(1−k) drops out. The point is not the algebra but what it means: no observation can separate "the ground curved away from me" from "my line of sight curved down with it". Only the difference of the two curvatures is ever visible. So you may legitimately subtract 1/ρ from both, which straightens the ray and leaves a sphere of curvature (1−k)/R. Curved ray over a real Earth ⇔ straight ray over a bigger fictitious Earth. Exactly equivalent, to second order in d/R.
Why a curved ray over R is exactly a straight ray over R/(1−k)Snell gives the ray its own curvature; one subtraction gives the equivalence; and the last two lines price what the subtraction throws away
(1) n cos β = const
(2) dβ/ds = (cos β / n)(dn/dh)
(3) 1/ρ = −(cos β / n)(dn/dh)
(4) y_ground = −x²/2R
(5) y_ray = βx − x²/2ρ
(6) H(x) = y_ray − y_ground = βx + (x²/2R)(1 − k)
(7) H(x) = βx + x²/2R_eff
(8) 1/R_eff = (1 − k)/R ⟹ R_eff = R/(1 − k)
(9) R(sec(d/R) − 1) = d²/2R + 5d⁴/24R³ + …
(10) residue = (5d⁴/24R³)·3k(1 − k)
Line (1) is Snell's law in an atmosphere stratified into level layers, with β the ray's elevation above the local horizontal: it is conserved along the whole ray. Differentiate (1) with respect to arc length s, using dh/ds = sin β; the sin β cancels from both sides and (2) is what is left. The ray turns at exactly that rate, so its curvature is (3) — which is the first line of the formula block near the top of this tab, now derived rather than quoted. Nothing has been assumed but Snell's law and layers that are level. Now put x along the tangent plane at the observer and y upward. To second order the ground falls away as (4), and a ray leaving at elevation β with the constant curvature (3) follows (5). The ray's height above the ground is the difference of the two, which is (6), where k ≡ R/ρ. A straight ray over a sphere of radius R_eff would instead give (7). Compare (6) with (7): they agree at every distance x and for every launch angle β if and only if (8). That is the equivalence — not an analogy but an identity between two parabolas, and it is why every other tab on this page may swap R for R_eff and otherwise pretend light travels in straight lines. What that second order costs is line (9): both (4) and (5) are truncated circles, and keeping the next term on both sides leaves the residue (10). Over d = 100 km at k = 0.13 that residue is 2.7 cm, against a ray-above-ground of 683 m — four parts in 100,000, and roughly a thousand times smaller than the ±0.03 that k itself is known to. That is the caveat stated below this section, with a size on it.
Unbend the light
Watch the gap, not the arcs. Press play and the whole scene is bent by one common amount until the light comes out straight — subtracting 1/ρ from the ray and from the ground at the same time, which is the only move the derivation above makes. The ray unrolls from a 49,000 km arc into a line; the planet swells from 6,371 km to 7,323 km. And the orange bar, the amount of the far pole that sits below the line of sight, does not move by a single pixel, because it is set by the difference of the two curvatures and that difference is what the subtraction leaves alone.
Everything an observer could measure lives in that bar. Curvature is exaggerated so that any of this is visible at all — the factor is printed on the figure, and every ratio between the drawn arcs is exact.

This is why k, and not ρ, is the number quoted everywhere: it is dimensionless and it is already the answer. k = 0.13 gives Reff = 1.149 R, the value Gauss used for continental sightlines. k = 0.143 gives exactly 7/6 R — the classic surveyor's rule of thumb. Radio engineers, whose wavelengths bend rather more, use k = 0.25 and call it the "4/3 Earth". And k = 0.17 is the standard atmosphere at sea level, which the hidden-height tab uses when it concedes the world-record sighting.[3]

What each k costs you — computed live from the formulas above, R = 6,371 km, eye height 2 m
Refraction coefficient kRay radius ρ = R/kρ / R Reff / RHorizon from 2 mHidden at 20 km

A caveat this page owes you. The other tabs feed Reff into the exact secant formulas rather than into the parabolic approximation the derivation above used. Strictly, the equivalence is only second-order in d/R, so the two disagree slightly at very long range. The disagreement is several orders of magnitude smaller than the uncertainty in k itself, which is why every geodesy textbook does the same thing — but it is an approximation, and it should be named rather than buried.

What sets k? Weather, and nothing else

Multiply the gradient formula by R and you get the working expression every surveyor knows, usually attributed through Gauss to the modern form given in Torge's Geodesy:[3]

k = 503 · (P / T²) · ( 0.0342 + dT/dh )
P in hPa, T in K, dT/dh in K per metre. Read what it says. Pressure and temperature move k by a few per cent — a mountain top has thinner air and refracts less. But the bracket is the whole story, and only one term in it can change: the temperature gradient. Everything interesting about refraction, including its sign, is decided by how fast the air cools as you climb.

The number 0.0342 K per metre in that bracket has a name and a meaning. It is the autoconvective lapse rate, 3.42 °C per 100 m: the rate of cooling at which the fall of pressure and the fall of temperature exactly cancel, so the density of the air is the same at every height.[6] An atmosphere cooling at precisely that rate is optically homogeneous, and light crosses it in perfectly straight lines: k = 0.

Cool more slowly than that — which is what real air normally does — and density falls with height, so rays bend down and k is positive. Cool faster, as air does in the first metre above sun-baked asphalt, and density increases upward: rays bend up, k goes negative, and you get the puddle mirage on the road ahead.

The same formula across real conditions (P = 1013 hPa, T = 288 K) — k is computed, not chosen
ConditiondT/dhk Ray curvature vs Earth'sWhat you see

k is measured, not assumed — and here is the instrument

The charge that refraction is a fudge factor would be fair if k could only ever be inferred from the answer you wanted. It cannot. Surveyors have measured it directly for two centuries with simultaneous reciprocal zenith angles: two instruments, one at each end of a line of known length s, each measuring the angle down from its own local vertical to the other, at the same instant so both see the same air.

zA + zB = 180° + γ(1 − k),   γ = s/R   →   k = 1 − (zA + zB − 180°) / γ
γ is the angle the line subtends at the Earth's centre — 16.19′ over 30 km. With no refraction the two zenith angles would sum to 180° + γ; refraction bends both rays down, subtracting kγ. The two station heights cancel out entirely: they never appear. Simultaneity matters because k swings through the day, and it is what makes the two rays share one atmosphere.[7]
(a) z_A = ζ_A − δ_A,  z_B = ζ_B − δ_B
(b) z_A + z_B = 180° + γ − (δ_A + δ_B)
(c) z_A − z_B = ζ_A − ζ_B − (δ_A − δ_B)
What reciprocal observation actually cancels — and it is not what most people remember. Write each reading as the straight-line zenith angle ζ minus the refraction angle δ that lifts the far station, line (a). Add the two, line (b): the geometry contributes 180° + γ and the two refraction terms add, giving 180° + γ(1 − k) with δ_A = δ_B = kγ/2. Subtract them, line (c): the two refraction terms cancel, and so does the curvature, leaving nothing but the height difference between the stations — which is why reciprocal trigonometric levelling is famous for being refraction-free, and it genuinely is.
Simultaneity is what earns both results, for one reason: it makes δ_A equal δ_B. So the difference gives you a height with no k in it, and the sum gives you curvature and refraction together, with the heights gone. This tab uses the sum, on purpose: it is the combination where the nuisance parameter cancels and the two things being argued about survive — and k is separable there because it multiplies γ rather than hiding inside it.

Run over test networks with lines from 4 to 23 km, this method returns a mean k of about 0.10 in daylight rising to 0.34 at night, when the ground has cooled and inversions form.[5] A 2010 study at ETH Zurich parked two pairs of total stations over grass and logged k continuously at minute-scale resolution, watching it oscillate with the surface heat flux exactly as the temperature-gradient formula predicts.[4] k is not a knob. It is a weather observation, and it behaves like one.

The circularity objection, taken seriously. A sharp reader will notice that γ = s/R uses the very radius the exercise is supposed to be testing, so measuring k this way assumes a globe. That is true, and it matters — which is why the page does not rest on it.
Two replies. First, R is over-determined elsewhere on this page by methods that do not use k at all: great-circle distances flown daily, the magnetic dip law, the analemma, four-satellite GPS closure. Second and more useful, the qualitative result needs no R whatsoever: on a plane, reciprocal zenith angles must sum to 180° or less — exactly 180° for straight light, and less than 180° for the downward-bending light that normal air produces. Surveyors measure sums that exceed 180°, everywhere, by an amount that grows in proportion to distance. No value of k on a plane can produce that sign.

The six refraction arguments, answered with numbers

These are the objections as they are actually made, not softened versions of them. Each one deserves a quantity in reply rather than a rebuke.

1. "Refraction was invented to save the globe."

Bouguer published the invariant in 1729 and used it to predict the raising of the horizon before anyone was arguing about the shape of the Earth.[8] Refraction tables were in nautical almanacs a century before that argument existed, and Helbronner was applying them to 250 km sightlines across the Mediterranean in 1925. If it had been invented to rescue anything, it would have been tuned to fit; instead the Guinness-record sighting in the hidden-height tab clears the horizon at k = 0.123, below the standard-atmosphere value. A rescue device that asks for less than average is not a rescue device.

2. "If light bends, it can bend enough to hide things on a flat Earth."

This one fails on sign, not on magnitude. To hide a distant object below your sightline on a plane, the ray must curve upward, away from the ground — and that requires n to increase with height, i.e. air that gets denser as you climb. The formula above says exactly what that costs: the temperature must fall faster than 3.42 °C per 100 m, sustained over the entire height band the ray occupies. That gradient exists in the first metre or two over hot asphalt and desert sand, where it produces inferior mirages — shimmering, inverted, obviously distorted images — and it cannot exist over a kilometre of height because the air column would be top-heavy and would immediately overturn. Refraction of that sign is not a hiding mechanism, it is a visible and violently unstable one.

3. "k is a free parameter, so the model can fit anything."

It is one number, not a function; it is bounded by measurable weather; and this page deliberately refuses to tune it. Look at the maintainer's rule in the source of this file: k is never adjusted per example to make a number come out, examples that quote a k carry its provenance, and there is exactly one k in the whole page, shared between the elevation and hidden-height tabs, so it cannot be quietly forked into two. Above all, every refracted figure on this page is printed beside its unrefracted twin. You can see, in every row, that refraction shrinks the effect and never reverses it.

4. "Then strong enough refraction could explain flat-Earth observations anyway."

This is the most interesting objection, because the algebra answers it exactly rather than approximately. Set k = 1 in Reff = R/(1−k) and the effective radius becomes infinite. That is not an analogy:

k = 1 is the flat model. A flat Earth is precisely what a globe looks like when light curves exactly as much as the ground does. So "refraction explains the flat observations" is not a rival theory at all — it is the assertion that k = 1 always, everywhere, in every wind and season, over ocean and desert and ice alike. And the price is on the table: k = 1 requires the air to warm with height at +0.129 K per metre — 12.9 °C for every 100 m of climb — held over the whole depth of the sightline. Real inversions reach that only in layers a few tens of metres thick over cold water or polar ice, and when they do they do not quietly flatten the world. They duct: the ray is trapped and bounced, and you get Fata Morganas, stacked and inverted images, and the Novaya Zemlya effect in which a slot-shaped Sun appears days before it should.[2][9] These events are famous because they are rare and grotesque. Meanwhile weather balloons from more than 800 stations report the actual temperature profile twice a day, every day, and have done since 1905.[11] Nowhere in that archive is a permanent global +12.9 °C per 100 m.
5. "Refraction lifts distant objects, so it explains the sightings anyway."

It lifts them, but by a bounded amount, and the page's sharpest cases are chosen so that the bound is visible. Take the Viériou photograph from the elevation tab: a plane puts the far summit 8.5′ above the near one, straight-ray spherical geometry puts it 2.9′ below, and refraction at k = 0.13 recovers 1.5′ of that, landing at 1.4′ below. Refraction moved the globe's answer toward the plane's — and then stopped. To close the remaining 9.9′ you would need k = 1, which by the previous paragraph is the flat model and carries the +12.9 °C/100 m bill. The photograph, meanwhile, settles it with no instrument at all: the far summit is below.

6. "Refraction varies, so no prediction is possible."

It varies within bounds that are themselves measured, and — decisively — it varies in ways that do not mimic curvature. Real k swings between roughly 0.1 and 0.35 with the hour and the surface; the globe's curvature term does not swing at all. So the two are separable by anyone patient enough to repeat a sighting. Refraction changes with the weather; curvature changes with distance squared, everywhere, every day, in the same direction. That is what the ceiling table in the hidden-height tab is testing, and every certified long-distance record sits inside it.

The four things refraction cannot do

It cannot give a plane a horizon. Refraction corrects the difference between two curvatures, and a plane has none of its own to correct. Bend the light down over an infinite plane and the sightline meets the ground eventually — but the ground it meets is at your own feet's level, so nothing is ever hidden behind a bulge, because there is no bulge. Worse for the flat model, ordinary downward-bending light on a plane pushes distant objects up, not down. It is the wrong sign for every observation it is invoked to explain.

It cannot reverse the dip of the horizon. Rise, and a spherical sea horizon drops below eye level by an angle that refraction reduces from √(2e/R) to √(2e/Reff) — about 12% less at k = 0.13. It shrinks the dip; it cannot make it negative, and it cannot make it zero, which is the flat prediction at every altitude forever. Airline pilots and sextant users correct for dip on every observation.[10]

It cannot vary correctly by accident. To reproduce a single constant R across the whole of geodesy, the flat model's refraction would have to depend on distance as d², on nothing else, identically in every azimuth, in every climate, at every hour, for two centuries of surveys. A quantity that is forced to imitate d²/2R exactly is d²/2R.

It cannot survive reciprocal observation. This is the cleanest test on the page because the station heights cancel and nothing is left to argue about. On a plane the two zenith angles must sum to at most 180°. On a sphere they sum to 180° + γ(1−k), which for a 30 km line is 180° + 14.1′ at k = 0.13. That is a sign difference, not a magnitude difference, and no positive k can rescue it.

Experiment 1c · refraction
Measure k yourself, and let it convict the model of your choice

Put a total station or theodolite at each end of a line several kilometres long, ideally with a clear reciprocal view. At an agreed instant, each observer measures the zenith angle to the other instrument's centre. Swap the numbers. You now have everything: the sum tells you which geometry you live on, and its excess over 180° tells you the refraction coefficient of the air you measured in.

Independent variable
What you change: the line — its length s, and the time of day you observe it. Try noon and again an hour after sunset.
Dependent variable
What you measure: the two zenith angles zA and zB, from which the sum and hence k follow with no further assumptions.

Hold constant: simultaneity above all — both angles at the same instant, or the two rays are not in the same atmosphere. Also instrument height above ground, since the gradient is steepest near the surface.
Kit: two instruments reading to a few arcseconds, and a known distance. This is standard second-order survey practice, not laboratory work.
The tell: the plane's ceiling is 180.000°, with refraction only able to push the sum lower. Any repeatable sum above 180° is fatal to it.

The through-line. Every tab on this page offers refraction as a toggle and prints both answers, because the honest position is not "refraction is negligible" — it is not — but "refraction is measured, bounded, and of known sign". The elevation and hidden-height tabs share one k with this one. The surveying tab shows the reciprocal-angle correction being applied in the field. And the horizon-dip tab shows the 12% that k shaves off the dip without ever touching its sign. One radius, one refraction coefficient, and the two are told apart by the fact that only one of them cares what the weather is doing.

Which is why a beam skimming water is the worst possible probe of k. Everything above prices k from a temperature gradient, and the gradient over water on a warm afternoon is both the steepest and the least stable anywhere in the lower atmosphere: cold water chills the air touching it, the profile inverts, and k over that surface routinely runs several times the standard 0.13 and can pass 1. Recall what k = 1 means here — light bending exactly as fast as the ground falls away, which is a globe wearing a plane's appearance. A laser aimed level from a metre or two above a lake samples precisely that layer, and because the beam widens as it goes, its lower edge samples it even when the centre does not. Such a test is a measurement of the duct, reported as a measurement of the shape[12].

Sight reduction · the 1′ = 1 nm rule

Why celestial navigation only closes on a globe

One rate, or a rate that keeps changing. On the globe the zenith distance to a star equals the central angle θ = d/R, so sailing 60 nm toward the ground position changes the altitude by exactly 1°, anywhere. On a plane a body at finite height gives altitude = atan(H/x): equal steps in distance give unequal steps in angle. Distances are schematic; the star is at infinity.

A sextant sight measures one thing: the altitude of a body — its angle above the sea horizon. Everything else in navigation is built on how that altitude changes as you move over the surface. That rate is the whole game, and only one shape of Earth produces the rate ships actually measure.

applies to every figure in this tab
a = d × k  ⇔  d = a / k  ⇔  d = a × R  (a in radians)
a = change in a body's altitude  ·  d = distance moved over the ground toward or away from its sub‑point  ·  k = the rate linking them. The last two forms can both be true only if k = 1 / R — the signature of a sphere of radius R.

Point a body straight up and you are standing on its geographic position (GP) — the spot where it sits at the zenith. Because the stars are so far away, their light arrives parallel across the whole Earth, so a body's zenith distance (90° − altitude) equals your angular distance from its GP. Move toward the GP and the altitude climbs; move away and it falls. On a sphere the arc you walk and the angle you turn are locked together by arc = R × angle — that is d = a × R — so k = 1/R is identical everywhere, in every direction, for every body.

The measured constant. Navigators find that 1 arcminute of altitude change = 1 nautical mile of travel toward the GP — which is how the nautical mile was defined. Feed that into d = a/k: with k = 1′/nm, R = 1/k = 3438 nm ≈ 6371 km. The radius drops out of star sights alone, and it matches the Earth's independently‑known size. It is the same R that curves the terrestrial sightlines over in the Simulator tab.

See it in 3D: four sights, one fix · click & drag to orbit

Each star stands above its ground position (GP); the observer measures its altitude and computes a distance d = a/k, which draws a circle of position on the surface around that GP. We give the flat model every advantage: its star height H is calibrated so that sight ① works perfectly. Then watch the other three.

Globe. With k = 1/R, all four circles d = a/k pass through the observer — one point satisfies every sight simultaneously. This is a celestial fix, performed at sea every day.
Flat plane. Stars at height H over the same GPs. Even with H tuned so circle ① hits the observer exactly, circles ②–④ fall short (red gaps) — because atan(r/H) isn't proportional to r. No single H fixes all four; on a plane the sights contradict each other.

The four sights: measured altitude → d = a/k, versus what the flat model's circles actually do

Experiment 2 · celestial navigation
Drive north and watch Polaris climb

Measure the altitude of Polaris (or any star) above the horizon. Drive a known distance due north along a straight road. Measure it again. The star has climbed — the question is by how much.

Independent variable
What you change: the distance d you travel due north. You choose it — 100 km, 300 km, 500 km.
Dependent variable
What you measure: the change in the star's altitude, in degrees. The sky decides this, not you.

Hold constant: travel due north (not diagonally), measure the same star, take both readings at the same sidereal time or use Polaris (which barely moves), and keep the same instrument.
Kit: a sextant or a phone clinometer app, a car odometer, and a clear northern sky.
The tell: the globe says the rate is the same everywhere. The flat model says it depends on where you started — change the starting latitude below and watch its prediction wander.

Verdict rule, symmetric. The globe fails if Polaris measures at an altitude that is not the latitude, or if the rate along a long north–south baseline is not one degree per 111 km. The flat model fails if that rate comes out constant over thousands of kilometres, because on an azimuthal-equidistant disc it has to change with distance from the centre. A sextant to ±10′ is ample; over 1,000 km even ±0.5° separates them.

Why the plane fails, in one line. On a flat plane a body at finite height can never reach the horizon (atan(H/x) stays positive), so the Sun would never set; different bodies would need different heights H and return contradictory fixes; and k would change with where you stand. The globe uses a single radius R and one k = 1/R for the Sun, the Moon and every star at once — and from that same geometry it predicts sunset, the “Polaris altitude equals your latitude” rule, and the southern stars a disk cannot show.

The through‑line. The two tabs are the same geometry seen twice. The curvature term d² / 2R that lowers a distant tower's elevation angle in the Simulator is produced by the very same R that makes k = 1/R here. Flatten the Earth and you break both at once — and no single flat layout reproduces the terrestrial dips and the constant one‑arcminute‑per‑mile star rate that ships have logged for three centuries.

Sources and further reading for this tab

Everything this tab computes is the working method described there.
