  • U.S. Naval Observatory — Celestial Navigation Data for Assumed Position and Time. Fill in a position and a time and it returns Greenwich hour angle, declination, computed altitude and computed azimuth for every body above your horizon, plus the altitude corrections. This is the single most useful link on this tab: the stars drawn here are synthetic, chosen for legibility, but this service will give you real ones, from the organisation that publishes the almanac, and you can run the whole argument again on numbers this page had no hand in.
  • The Nautical Almanac (U.S. Naval Almanac Office with HM Nautical Almanac Office). Published every year for over 150 years, tabulating hour angle and declination hourly to 0.1 arcminute. Every line of it is computed on a rotating sphere.
  • Sight Reduction Tables for Air Navigation (Pub. 249 / AP 3270), and Pub. 229 for marine use. Prepared jointly by the U.S. Naval Observatory and the UK Hydrographic Office. These tables cannot be generated by any other geometry: they are spherical trigonometry, printed by two governments, for operational use.
  • USNO — Celestial Navigation Algorithms. The modern least-squares formulation, which solves for course and speed as well as position. Useful here because it shows the sphere is not a legacy assumption kept for tradition: it is still the model when the method is rebuilt from scratch.
  • T. H. Sumner, A New and Accurate Method of Finding a Ship's Position at Sea (Boston, 1843). The origin of the line of position. Sumner found it by accident in December 1837 approaching the Irish coast in bad weather: working three different assumed latitudes, he noticed the three results fell on one straight line, and that line ran through Small's Light. Digitised and out of copyright; search the title.
  • Marcq de Blond de Saint-Hilaire, « Calcul du point observé », Revue Maritime et Coloniale (1875). The intercept method — the procedure this tab models — in the original French.
  • IMO, International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers (STCW), tables A-II/1 and A-II/2. Celestial navigation is a competence required by international treaty of officers in charge of a navigational watch. Whatever else it is, it is not a belief anyone is free to hold or not hold.
Star trails · the one thing a rotation cannot fake

Two people watch the same sky turn opposite ways.

Point a camera at the sky for an hour and the stars draw arcs. From Europe they turn counter-clockwise about a point in the north; from Chile they turn clockwise about a point in the south. That difference is not a matter of degree. It is a sign, and a sign is the hardest thing in this whole page for a model to get wrong quietly.

The result, and it is about the flat model alone. The apparent sense of a rigid rotation is the sign of ω · û, where û is the direction you are looking. Reversing it means crossing the surface ω · û = 0; nothing else does it — not distance, not size, not speed. On a plane, everyone shares the same up. The dome turns about a vertical, so ω points up for every observer at once, and the fixed point sits at altitude atan(h/r), which is above the horizon everywhere on the disc whatever h is. So ω · û > 0 everywhere, and the sense is the same everywhere. The flat model does not get the sense wrong: it cannot produce a reversal at all, and no setting helps it.

Where the numbers come from, before any of them is used. The stars are the Yale Bright Star Catalogue, J2000, as published[1], checked line by line against Hipparcos: the largest disagreement is 2.4″, except α Centauri at 21″, which is its proper motion between the two catalogue epochs[2]. Precession to the date is applied — 0.36° by 2026, the same order as the precision claimed here — so Polaris sits 0.625° from the pole rather than the 0.736° of J2000. Proper motion is not applied; it is an order of magnitude below anything asserted. The twelve cities are Natural Earth, public domain[3], the same dataset as the coastlines elsewhere on this page.

sense = sign(ω · û)
ω is the rotation vector — along the axis, by the right hand. û is the direction you are looking. The sense you see is the sign of their dot product, so reversing it means crossing the plane ω · û = 0 and nothing else does: not distance, not size, not speed. On a plane, ω points up for every observer at once and the fixed point is always above the horizon, so the sign never changes anywhere on the disc.

1 · The fixed point, place by place

Nothing is fitted here. The globe puts the fixed point at the altitude of the pole — that is the celestial-navigation result, and it is argued there rather than again here[6]. The flat model puts it at atan(h/r), where r is the distance to the centre of the azimuthal-equidistant map. Read the table for what it is worth in both directions: at northern mid-latitudes the two models agree to about two degrees, and that half of the case is stated here rather than buried.

a = arctan(h / d)
d = √(r² + ρ² − 2rρ cos θ)
The flat model, edge-on and from above. h = height of the dome, r = your distance to the centre of the azimuthal-equidistant map, ρ = the radius of the circle the star's ground point travels, θ = how far round that circle it has got. a is what you would measure with a clinometer. Note that a is positive for every r, every ρ and every θ: on this model nothing ever sets.
The flat dome is swept, never fitted. The break between the two models is not in the altitude — it is in the azimuth and in the sense, and both of them flip south of the equator without any value of h being involved.
sin a = sin δ sin φ + cos δ cos φ cos H
The spherical triangle the globe uses everywhere on this page. Z = your zenith, P = the celestial pole, ★ = the star. Its sides are 90° − φ, 90° − δ and 90° − a; the angle at P is the hour angle H, which advances at 15.041° per hour and is the only thing that changes during a night. Latitude and declination are fixed, so the whole trail follows from one turning angle.

2 · The shape of a trail

A trail is a circle on the sky if and only if the observer stands on the axis of the circle the star describes. On the disc that happens at the centre and nowhere else. Everywhere else the observer sees an oblique cone over a circle, and its angular radius from the fixed point varies by a factor of two around one turn.

p = 90° − |δ|
a_up = φ + p, a_low = φ − p
½(a_up + a_low) = φ
Looking due north along the meridian. The pole P sits at the latitude φ, and a circumpolar star crosses the meridian twice a day, at p above P and p below it. Their mean is therefore the latitude and their half-difference is p — for any star and any latitude, with nothing fitted. Two altitudes read off a clinometer are the whole measurement.
On a globe the two culminations sit at φ + p and φ − p exactly, so their mean is the latitude and their half-difference is p, for any star and any latitude. Two altitudes read off a clinometer settle it: no camera, no lens correction, no calibration.
The rule only holds while the star stays between the pole and the zenith. In general the two culminations sum to 2·min(φ, δ): once δ < φ the star passes the zenith, comes down the other side of the meridian, and the mean gives δ instead of φ. The star chosen above is therefore one with δ ≥ |φ|, and with the largest trail radius available rather than the brightest — a trail 0.6° across is nearly symmetric in both models, and a test that cannot separate them is not a test.

3 · The dilemma that consumes the dome height

The flat model has one free parameter here, and it has to serve two masters. Bring the dome closer and the fixed point sits at the right altitude while the trails deform; push it away and the trails become circular while the fixed point climbs to everyone's zenith. The two requirements are tens of degrees apart and no intermediate value satisfies both.

Dome heights are swept, as the azimuth tab already sweeps its lamp. Note that the star dome is not that lamp: flat cosmology puts the firmament above the Sun, so two heights are legitimate — but a page that argues there is only one refraction coefficient owes the reader that sentence.

4 · What a photograph can and cannot settle

The expected objection is that trails photograph as ovals. They do — in both models — and the figure below is the answer rather than a warning. The dashed curve is the image of a mathematically perfect circle about the fixed point, seen through the same lens from the same framing. On a globe the trail lies on it. On the disc it hugs it on one side and falls away on the other.

    The focal length deforms nothing. Changing f multiplies the image by a constant — that is a zoom, and it only sets the field of view. What changes shapes is the projection law and the residual distortion, which is why the list offers one focal length per law. All eight are radial maps: each moves a point along the ray joining it to the centre of the image and never touches its polar angle, so none of them can make a symmetric thing asymmetric or the reverse. The barrel coefficients are typical of their class of lens, not the measurement of a particular model, and no number on this page depends on them.

    5 · The rhythm along the trail

    Cut the exposure into equal intervals — an intervalometer, or a card held over the lens — and the trail becomes dashes. On a globe each dash sweeps exactly the same angle about the fixed point: 15.041° per hour[4], for any star, at any latitude, with no free parameter anywhere. On the disc the star comes closer and goes away again, and the dashes stretch and bunch.

    Δψ = 15.041°/h × Δt
    ψ is the position angle about the fixed point F — where the star sits round the circle, not how far from it. On a globe it advances at a constant rate, so equal exposures give equal dashes, for every star and every latitude. The measurement is an angle about the centre of the image, which is why no radial lens distortion can touch it.
      One place, one night, one photograph. This is the only test on the tab that needs neither travel nor anyone else's data. It is also immune to the lens: aimed at the fixed point, that point becomes the centre of the image, and any radial distortion preserves angles about the centre exactly. Measure with a protractor on a print. The test is strong at middle and southern latitudes, weak near the pole where the trail radius collapses, and unavailable at the equator where no trail closes.

      6 · Always up, seasonal, never seen

      On a globe a constellation falls into one of three classes and its declination decides, compared with 90° − |φ|. On the flat disc there is one class: the altitude is atan(h/d), positive everywhere and always, so everything is always up, everywhere.

        Seasonality on its own proves nothing — a dome turning at the sidereal rate reproduces the four-minute daily drift without effort, and saying so costs nothing. What can be checked is which constellations never set and which never rise, and from what latitude. The dates below are there to make the observation practicable, not to make an argument: they put a constellation on the meridian at a civil hour.
        Positions are those of the group of stars named in the catalogue below, not the centre of the IAU boundary. The difference is a few degrees and changes none of the three classes unless a constellation sits on a limit, in which case the limit is printed and the reader can see it.

        Experiment 2b · photograph the axis

        Independent variable: the place — the hemisphere first, the latitude second. Dependent: (a) the sense of rotation, one bit; (b) the two culmination altitudes of one circumpolar star. Held constant: the same lens, the aim on the fixed point, a fixed foreground for the horizon, a stated exposure. Kit: a phone on a wall and thirty minutes of stacking. For (b) a clinometer is enough — no camera at all. Every altitude printed on this tab can be checked against the USNO service[5] before you go outside.

        Verdict rule, announced in advance and symmetric. The globe fails if a southern observer photographs arcs centred on Polaris, if the sense is the same in both hemispheres, or if the mean of the two culminations does not return the latitude. The flat model fails if the sense reverses between hemispheres, or if that mean does return the latitude instead of missing it by several degrees.

        Deliberately left out: differential refraction and extinction near the horizon, which are modelled nowhere else on this page and which the culmination test does not need; aberration, stellar parallax and proper motion, all below anything claimed here; and trail photometry, which is real and predicted differently by the two models but cannot be measured without calibration.

        These are the intermediate quantities the tables above are built from, printed rather than hidden. Feed the same instant to the USNO service[5] and you should get the same altitudes to the second decimal; if not, one of the two accounts is wrong, and the numbers here are enough to find out which.

        Map ≠ territory · the azimuthal equidistant trap

        Two equal segments — until you flatten the Earth

        The same two points, three geometries. Schematics of the algebra, not scale drawings: no distance in them is to scale, and none is used for any number on this page.

        Take a diagonal segment in the northern hemisphere — one that cuts across parallels and meridians — and its exact mirror image across the equator. On the globe the two are identical in length by symmetry. Now flatten the Earth, keep the coordinates, and measure with a ruler: the mirror twins stop agreeing, and how they disagree depends on which flat map you chose. Two pairs are shown, in different directions and regions.

        Globe: great‑circle arc
        Cartesian map: straight line in (λ, φ)
        Polar map (AE): straight chord on the disk
        One pair of endpoints, three rulers — each model measured its own way: the sphere's shortest path on the globe, and honest straight ruler lines on both flat maps. Only the globe's answer matches odometers, flight times, and surveyed distances; the polar disk is the azimuthal equidistant projection of the globe, centred on the north pole.

        The three rulers, written out

        Each model is asked the same question — how far apart are these two coordinate pairs? — and each answers in its own geometry. These are the three formulas the page actually evaluates for the table above, with nothing hidden inside a function name.

        cos σ = sin φ₁ sin φ₂ + cos φ₁ cos φ₂ cos Δλ
        d = R σ
        The spherical law of cosines, the oldest formula on this page.[1] σ is the angle the two points subtend at the Earth's centre, so the distance is nothing but R times an angle. The code evaluates the equivalent dot product of two unit vectors. For legs of a few kilometres the arccosine is ill-conditioned and the haversine form is the right one to use;[4] at the thousands of kilometres compared here it makes no visible difference.
        x = R λ,   y = R φ
        d = R √(Δφ² + Δλ²)
        The plate carrée, or equidistant cylindrical projection: latitude and longitude read straight off as y and x.[3] Pythagoras then prices every degree of longitude at its equatorial length wherever you happen to be, inflating the answer by roughly 1/cos φ. It stays symmetric across the equator, which is exactly why this map hides the asymmetry while still disagreeing with every odometer.
        r = R (π/2 − φ),   θ = λ
        d = √(r₁² + r₂² − 2 r₁ r₂ cos Δλ)
        The azimuthal equidistant projection centred on the north pole, with a straight ruler line laid across it.[3] This is the flat-earth disk, and not by our choice of words: the Boston Public Library catalogues Gleason's 1892 original as the globe flattened into a circular plane, and his own patent claim is filed on a projection.[5] Distances on it are true along the radii — any line through the pole — and along nothing else.

        Why the mirror test works, and where the disk's error comes from

        globe: cos σ(−φ₁, −φ₂, Δλ) = cos σ(φ₁, φ₂, Δλ)
        disk: r(−φ) = R (π/2 + φ) ≠ r(φ)
        This is the whole tab in two lines. Flip both latitudes and the spherical formula is unchanged: sin(−φ) appears twice so the two minus signs cancel, and cos(−φ) = cos φ. Mirror-image segments are therefore exactly equal on a globe — not approximately, exactly, and for every value of R. The disk's radius is simply not an even function of latitude, so its answer has to change. No choice of disk size, scale or centring repairs that, because the disagreement is about shape, not size.
        along a parallel  ·  globe: d = R cos φ Δλ
        disk: d = R (π/2 − φ) Δλ
        ratio = (π/2 − φ) / cos φ
        Take the simplest leg there is, due east along a parallel, and both models close into elementary form. R divides out of the ratio, which makes this a radius-free test like the magnetism tab: it constrains the shape alone, whatever the size. The ratio equals 1 only at the pole and rises without bound going south — 1.11 at 45° N, 1.57 at the equator, 3.33 at 45° S, 17.1 at 80° S.
        The stretch factor, plotted. The curve is the ratio above; the teal line at ×1 is what vehicles actually log. The disk never reads short, and never reads true except at the pole. At ±45° the two halves of a mirror pair differ by a factor of three, which is the discrepancy the experiment below asks you to go and settle.
        One honesty note about that last pair. A leg flown due east along a parallel is a rhumb line, not the shortest path: between 45° N 0° and 45° N 60° E the parallel measures 4,718 km and the great circle 4,605 km, 2.4% shorter. That approximation is real, and it is not what is being tested — both models are asked for the same parallel-following leg, so the ratio between them is unaffected. The table at the top of this tab avoids the issue entirely by giving the globe its true great-circle answer and the flat maps their own straight ruler lines, and it reaches the same verdict.

        Two legs the globe calls equal — and each flat map breaks a different one

        The mirror pairs above leave the cartesian map a way out: its grid is symmetric across the equator, so it keeps mirror twins equal and only inflates them both. This pair closes that door. Two legs, each exactly 60° of arc, chosen so the sphere makes them identical to the kilometre. Neither flat map can hold them equal, and — this is the part worth sitting with — they fail in opposite directions.

        polar leg:   60°N 0° → 60°N 180°
        equator leg:   0° 30°W → 0° 30°E
        σ = 60° for both  ⇒  d = 6,672 km
        Both equalities are exact, not fitted. For the polar leg, cos σ = sin²60° + cos²60°·cos 180° = 0.75 − 0.25 = 0.5, so σ = 60°: the great circle runs straight over the pole, 30° down each side. For the equator leg cos σ = cos 60° directly. Same central angle, therefore the same distance, and R does not need to be known for the two to be equal — only for the 6,672 km. Any route planner returns both numbers.[2]
        The same pair under three rulers. Panel A shows each leg on the great circle that carries it, seen face-on: two identical 60° arcs, which is the whole point — the sphere has no way to distinguish them. Panels B and C are drawn to scale within themselves, so the lengths you see are the lengths each model claims; there is no exaggeration factor anywhere in this figure, and none is needed.
        Equal on the globe by construction; each flat map preserves one leg exactly and breaks the other
        Segment (endpoints)Globe great‑circleFlat cartesian rulerFlat polar (AE) ruler
        polar  60°N 0° → 60°N 180°6,672 km20,015 km (+200%)6,672 km (0%)
        equator  0° 30°W → 0° 30°E6,672 km6,672 km (0%)10,007 km (+50%)
        Verdict rule, stated in advance. Go and measure both legs — flight time × ground speed, a GPS track, or published great-circle tables. If they come out equal, the sphere survives and both flat maps are refuted, each by a different leg. If the polar leg really is three times the equator leg, the cartesian map survives and the sphere is refuted. If the equator leg really is one and a half times the polar one, the polar disk survives instead. The three models make three different predictions here, so this single measurement can eliminate at least two of them — and note that no flat map can be rescued by rescaling, since each is already exactly right on one of the two legs.

        See it in 3D · click & drag to orbit

        Globe. Pair A (blue / orange) and pair B (teal / violet): each southern segment is the mirror of its northern twin, so within each pair the great‑circle lengths are exactly equal. The arcs look curved because on a sphere the shortest path is an arc.
        Same endpoints, three rulers — flat maps measured with straight lines, as a ruler would
        Segment (endpoints)Globe great‑circleFlat cartesian rulerFlat polar (AE) ruler
        Experiment 3 · distances
        The same east–west trip, north and south

        Pick an east–west leg spanning a fixed number of degrees of longitude, and measure how long it really is. Then do the mirror-image leg in the other hemisphere. Book the flights, or read the published great-circle distances and flight times.

        Independent variable
        What you change: the latitude of the leg — try +45°, then −45°. You choose which parallel to travel along.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the ground distance actually covered — odometer, GPS track, or flight time × cruising speed.

        Hold constant: the same span of longitude Δλ for both legs, and the same way of measuring (don't compare an odometer with a flight time).
        Kit: no instruments at all — airline timetables and a great-circle calculator will do. This is the one experiment you can run from a chair.
        The tell: the globe says the two mirror legs are equal. The flat disc says the southern one is several times longer.

        The confusion, named. The flat‑earth disk (the “Gleason map”) is the azimuthal equidistant projection of the globe. It preserves distances only along straight lines through the pole; every east–west distance is stretched by (90°−φ)/cos φ — a factor of 1.11 at 45° N but 3.33 at 45° S. Treating that projection as the territory forces the southern hemisphere to be three times wider than it measures. Real ships and aircraft cross it anyway: Sydney–Santiago is ~11,400 km and is flown non‑stop in ~12½ hours; on the disk it would be ~25,000 km, longer than any airliner's range.

        Why the cartesian ruler also fails. Reading latitude/longitude as x‑y coordinates (a plate‑carrée grid) at least keeps north and south symmetric — but it prices every east–west degree at its equatorial length, inflating both segments by 1/cos φ (+41% at 45°). It hides the asymmetry while still disagreeing with every odometer. Coordinates are addresses on a sphere, not distances; the only ruler that returns what vehicles actually log is R·cos φ·Δλ — spherical geometry.

        The through‑line. This is the third appearance of the same R: it curves the sightlines in the Simulator, sets k = 1/R in Celestial navigation, and here converts coordinate differences into the distances the world actually measures. One sphere explains all three; each flat model must fail at least one.

        • [2]Great Circle Mapper — segment C is a real scheduled route, Santiago de Chile → Sydney, flown daily in about 12–13 hours; its northern mirror is the identical pair of coordinates reflected across the equator. Any route planner will return the same great-circle length for both, which is the point: the polar disc returns nearly twice as much for the southern one.

        Not cited above, and no claim on this tab rests on it — listed because it is what you would read next, or because it lets you redo the measurement on data this page did not choose.
        • NGA Office of Geomatics — Department of Defense World Geodetic System 1984 (NGA.STND.0036, v1.0.0, 2014) — where the reference figures used throughout this page are actually defined, rather than merely quoted: semi-major axis a = 6,378,137 m exactly, flattening 1/f = 298.257223563, arithmetic mean radius R1 = 6,371.0088 km. The standard states that it supplements IERS Technical Note 36, IERS Conventions (2010), which is the civilian side of the same constants. Two defence and scientific standards agreeing on one figure is a stronger check than any single agency; and any flight-booking site's city-pair distances give the same geodesics an independent everyday test.

This page deliberately works on a sphere; Vincenty is how you check what that simplification costs, which for the legs here is a few kilometres in eleven thousand.

A commercial timetable is a harder thing to wave away than a great-circle calculator: an airline that has mis-stated a flight time by four hours is an airline that has run out of fuel.
        Dip of the horizon · the navigator's daily correction

        The horizon drops as you rise — by a measured amount

        Where the sea horizon sits, relative to eye level. Same eye height in both. On a plane the sea runs out to meet eye level and there is no angle to measure; on a globe the horizon is the tangent from the eye, an angle δ below level. Curvature is exaggerated.

        Climb, and the sea horizon sinks below your eye level. Every sextant sight is corrected for it before anything else. The globe predicts exactly how much; a flat plane predicts exactly zero, at every height, forever. Drag the observer up and down and compare.

        Dip = arccos( R / (R+h) )  ≈  1.76′ × √h
        Horizon = √(2Rh + h²)  ≈  3.86 km × √h
        h in metres. The bold constants are the refracted values printed in every nautical almanac and dip table (geometric: 1.93′√h and 3.57 km·√h). On a flat plane both formulas collapse: dip = 0 at every height, and the ground never reaches a horizon at all.
        What each model predicts at the current eye height
        ModelDip below eye levelDistance to horizonSharp edge?

        Solve the triangle: the flat model contradicts itself

        Suppose the flat model is granted the measured dip angle δ — the one a dip meter actually reads. On a flat plane the eye, the point straight below it, and the point where the sightline meets the ground form a right triangle: height h, horizontal run d, right angle at the foot. That triangle is solvable, and it fixes where the ground must be:

        tan δ = h / d  ⇒  d = h / tan δ
        Feed the measured dip into flat geometry and it says the sightline strikes the ground at distance d. But δ ≈ √(2h/R), so d ≈ h/√(2h/R) = √(hR/2) = ½·√(2Rh) — exactly half the measured horizon distance, at every height. And on a plane nothing ends there: the ground simply continues, seen at ever‑smaller angles.
        Grant the measured dip, then solve the flat triangle — and compare with the horizon that can actually be ranged
        Eye heightMeasured dip δFlat: d = h / tan δMeasured horizonRatio
        Three statements, no consistent flat answer. (1) The dip is real and measured — so the flat triangle puts the ground at h/tan δ. (2) The horizon is real and ranged — radar, known landmarks and ship disappearance all put it twice as far. (3) On a plane the surface has no edge at either distance. The globe satisfies all three at once with a single number: the tangent point of a sphere of radius R sits at √(2Rh), and the angle to it is the dip. The factor of 2 isn't a fudge — it's the signature of a tangent line on a circle versus a chord to a plane.

        The surface you never drew

        Here is the same measurement with no ground drawn at all. Every line is one sightline to the horizon, taken from a real vantage point on the same vertical — a beach, a ship's bridge, a lighthouse, a cliff, a summit, an airliner — each tipped below horizontal by its own measured dip δ(h). Nothing else is plotted: no circle, no arc, no Earth. Yet the lines cannot enter a certain region, and that forbidden region has a shape. The dip angles alone carve the planet out of the negative space. Click any sightline to see which altitude it came from.

        This is what a mathematician calls an envelope: a family of straight lines whose boundary traces a curve that none of them crosses. Because a tangent to a circle touches at one point and lies outside it everywhere else, the sightlines can only be tangents of one specific circle — the one whose radius satisfies cos δ = R/(R+h) at every height simultaneously. A flat plane produces no envelope at all: with δ = 0 at all heights, every line is horizontal, they never fan, and the empty region is an unbounded half‑plane with no curve anywhere in it.

        Measuring the Earth from one dip angle

        Turn the formula around. If you can measure your height h and the dip δ, you can solve for R — no satellites, no travel, no second observer:

        cos δ = R/(R+h)  ⇒  R = h·cos δ / (1 − cos δ)  ≈  2h / δ²
        δ in radians for the approximation. One hill, one angle, one number — and it must come out the same from a sea cliff, a mountain, or an aircraft window. That consistency is the test; a single value would prove nothing on its own.
        Solving for R from the current height, and what refraction does to the answer
        Dip usedValue at current hR = h·cos δ/(1−cos δ)Compared with 6,371 km

        Who did it first: al‑Bīrūnī, around 1018An astrolabe, a hill in the Salt Range, and an answer within a fraction of a percent — partly by luck, since he had no way to correct for refraction
        Who did it first: al‑Bīrūnī, around 1018. The Persian scholar Abū Rayḥān al‑Bīrūnī carried out exactly this measurement from a hill at Nandana, in the Salt Range of what is now Pakistan. He first obtained the hill's height by triangulating it from the plain below, then used an astrolabe to measure the dip of the horizon — reporting roughly 34 arcminutes — and applied the same relation R = h·cos δ/(1 − cos δ). Depending on which cubit he used, his answer corresponds to an Earth radius of about 6,300–6,340 km, within a fraction of a percent of the modern 6,371 km. Eratosthenes had measured the Earth some 1,250 years earlier, but by a completely different route — comparing midday shadow angles at two latitudes — so the dip method is credited to al‑Bīrūnī. His accuracy involved some luck: as the table above shows, refraction biases this method by more than 10%, and he had no way to correct for it.
        Experiment 4 · horizon dip
        Climb, and measure how far the sea horizon falls

        Stand at the shore with a levelled instrument and measure the angle between true horizontal and the sea horizon. Then climb — a cliff path, a tall building, a hill — and measure again from a known height.

        Independent variable
        What you change: your eye height h above sea level. You choose it by where you stand: 2 m, then 50 m, then 300 m. Set it with the height control at the top of this tab.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the dip angle — how far the horizon sits below level. The world decides this.

        Hold constant: the same instrument, an open sea horizon (no distant land), calm conditions, and level the bubble each time. Take readings on the same day if you can, so the air is similar.
        Kit: a theodolite, a dip meter, or a sextant with an artificial horizon — anything that reads arcminutes. A phone clinometer is too coarse below about 50 m, but works from a high cliff.
        The tell: the flat model does not predict "a small number" — it predicts zero, at every height, because an infinite plane has no tangent point and its surface reaches level only at infinity.

        Below eye level and still in the sky — the band the Sun has to cross

        Everything above treats the dip as a correction. Turn it round and it becomes something you can watch. If the horizon sits δ below your eye level, then there is a strip of sky, δ tall, that is below the level line and above the horizon at the same time. Anything in that strip — the Sun, the Moon, a planet, a distant aircraft — is seen whole, against sky, with nothing in front of it, while a bubble level says it is beneath you. From a mountain or an airliner the strip is several Sun‑widths tall and it takes the Sun a quarter of an hour to cross it.

        On a flat plane that strip cannot exist, and not by a little. The ground's depression angle is atan(h/x), which shrinks toward zero as the ground recedes: eye level is the vanishing line, and the surface fills every direction below it out to the limit of visibility. An object seen below your own eye level would have to be seen through the ground. The flat model does not predict a thin strip, or a strip that needs good conditions. It predicts a strip of width zero, at every height, which is rule 4 again: an absence against a presence.

        Whole Sun below level and clear of the horizon  ⇔  δ(h) > 32′
        window = δ − 32′
        time = (δ − 32′) / (15.04°/h × cos φ)
        The Sun spans about 32′[4], so its whole disc is under your eye level once its centre is 16′ below, and it is still wholly clear of the horizon until its centre reaches 16′ above the horizon line. Subtract: the window opens at a dip of one Sun‑width, which is an eye height of about 330 m. The rate is the equinox rate at latitude φ; away from the equinox it is slower still, which only lengthens the window.
        The band below eye level, at documented heights, and how long the Sun spends inside it
        Eye heightDip δBand, in Sun‑widthsWhole disc below level and clearTime to cross, φ = 45°Flat plane

        This is not the Sun setting, and that is the whole point. Occultation is a separate event that happens later, when the disc finally reaches the horizon line. The claim here is about the interval before it: the Sun entire, nothing covering any part of it, sky visible underneath it, and a levelled instrument reading it as below the horizontal. You can photograph the state directly — one frame containing the Sun, the sea horizon under it, and a plumb line or a levelled bar in the same field of view. There is no version of a flat plane in which that frame exists.
        Three things that can spoil it, stated in advance. First, the level has to be a real level: in an aircraft the apparent vertical follows the resultant of gravity and acceleration, so a bank or a climb tilts it — take the reading in steady cruise, and prefer the angle from the Sun to the horizon, which no instrument error can manufacture. Second, refraction lifts objects near the horizon by roughly 34′[1] and shrinks the dip by about 8%[2]; both are already in the numbers above, and both work against the effect rather than creating it. Third, over land the horizon is terrain, not the geometric horizon, so this is a sea‑horizon measurement. None of the three turns a zero into 3°.
        Experiment 4b · the doubled sunset
        Watch the same sunset twice, and get the radius of the Earth out of a stopwatch

        Sit at the water's edge facing west and watch the Sun's last edge disappear. Then stand up — or run up a dune, or take a lift, or take off — and it comes back. The delay is not an illusion and it is not small: it is δ(h₂) − δ(h₁) divided by the rate at which the Sun sinks. Rawlins proposed this in 1979[3] as a way to measure the planet with a wristwatch and a metre stick, and Minnaert did the six‑metre version by running up a dyke.[2]

        Independent variable
        What you change: your eye height, between the first sunset and the second. Sitting to standing is half a metre; a stairwell is ten; an aircraft is eleven thousand.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the delay in seconds between the two disappearances — one number, from a stopwatch.

        Hold constant: the same limb of the Sun (upper edge is easiest), an open sea horizon, and the same weather minute to minute. Do it at the equinoxes if you can, when the Sun descends most steeply and the arithmetic is simplest.
        Kit: a stopwatch, a tape measure for the two eye heights, and something to know your latitude. Never look at the Sun except at the last moment when it is dimmed at the horizon.
        The tell: on a plane, raising your eye changes nothing about when a distant object disappears behind a vanishing line that is always at eye level — the predicted delay is 0 s. Every observed delay is positive, and it scales as √h₂ − √h₁.

        Verdict rule, symmetric. The globe fails if the dip does not grow as the square root of your height, or if the doubled sunset gives a repeatable zero delay from a height difference where seconds are predicted. The flat model fails on any non-zero dip at all, at any height: on a plane the horizon stays exactly at eye level. A stopwatch to ±1 s and a height to ±1 m are enough.

        It is measured, not inferred. A dip meter (or a theodolite levelled with a bubble, or a sextant's artificial horizon) reads the angle between the true horizontal and the sea horizon directly. From a 10 m bridge it is about 5.6′ (0.093°); from a 100 m cliff about 17.6′ (0.293°); from an airliner at 10 km about 3.0°. Those numbers are tabulated, reproducible with hardware costing a few hundred euros, and they track √h exactly as arccos(R/(R+h)) requires. A plane predicts 0.0′ = 0.000° at every one of those heights.

        Why a plane has no horizon at all. On an infinite plane the ground's depression angle below eye level is atan(h/x), which shrinks toward zero as x grows but never reaches it. The surface would fade into haze at a distance set by air clarity — blurry, weather‑dependent, and different for every camera. What is actually seen is a sharp, hard edge at a definite distance that sharpens with better optics, sits lower the higher you climb, and hides ships hull‑first. The right panel shows the flat model's depression at the same distance where the globe places its horizon: a number that is not zero, but is far too small and in the wrong place.

        Refraction, again. Air bends light downward, pushing the horizon farther away and reducing the dip by roughly 8%. That is why the almanac constant is 1.76′√h rather than the geometric 1.93′√h. Toggle it above: it changes the numbers by a few percent, never the sign, and never rescues zero.

        The through‑line. Same R again — the dip is simply the elevation angle of the tangent sightline, the limiting case of the Simulator's geometry when the target's height goes to zero. It is the horizon whose dip the perspective panel already draws, and the same R that fixes k = 1/R and converts Δλ into kilometres.

        Sources for this tab

        • [2]Andrew T. Young, Dip of the Horizon (San Diego State University) — the derivation of the dip and of the R/(1 − k) substitution, the sensitivity of the dip to the temperature difference between eye and horizon, and the historical accounts of the doubled sunset: Minnaert running up a six-metre dyke for twenty more seconds of green flash, and Captain Havinga seeing it earlier from the lower bridge than his officer on the upper.
        • [3]D. Rawlins, "Doubling your sunsets or how anyone can measure the earth's size with wristwatch and meter stick", American Journal of Physics 47(2), 126–128 (1979). Left unlinked on purpose: the journal text is paywalled and the copies that circulate are scans of uncertain provenance. The method is described in full in [6].
        • [4]NASA NSSDCA, Sun Fact Sheet — the Sun's apparent angular diameter, 31.6′ to 32.7′ over the year, which sets the 32′ used throughout this section.
        Further reading
        Not cited above, and no claim on this tab rests on it — listed because it is what you would read next, or because it lets you redo the measurement on data this page did not choose.
        • Sparavigna (2013), "The Science of al-Biruni" (arXiv) — al-Bīrūnī's height-plus-dip measurement at the Fort of Nandana and the resulting Earth radius, within about 2% of the modern reference value.
        • MacTutor History of Mathematics: al-Biruni — biography and his geodesic work in context.
        • Hirt et al. (2010), J. Geophys. Res. — terrestrial refraction coefficient — why refraction biases the one-hill method by ~10% and why k is weather-dependent, as the table above shows.
        • Bowditch, The American Practical Navigator, Vol. 2 — dip tables — the published dip and horizon-distance tables against which every entry in the vantage-point list above can be checked. The heights themselves are the operators' own published figures (basilica esplanade 142 m, Eiffel Tower top platform 276 m, Burj Khalifa SKY 555 m); the summits are from the sources in tab 1.
        • Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Almanac, 3rd edition (2013), chapter 7 — the conventions behind the dip and refraction corrections that the almanacs tabulate.
        • Jamil Ali (trans.), The Determination of the Coordinates of Positions for the Correction of Distances between Cities (American University of Beirut, 1967). The standard English translation of al-Bīrūnī's Taḥdīd, in which the mountain-dip method is set out by the man who used it around 1018. The sources above discuss it; this is the text itself.
        Gravity and level · what a bubble is really finding

        A spirit level does not find a plane — and a gravimeter in a lift measures the radius of the Earth

        Where "down" points, in each model. On the globe every vertical is a radius, so no two are parallel. On an infinite slab — the flat model at its strongest for this measurement — every vertical is perpendicular and every bubble is centred. Directions are exact; the bobs' heights are schematic.

        “Water always finds its level” is the oldest argument there is, and it is true. It is also empty until someone says what level means. Level is not a geometrical idea: it is whatever a plumb line and a bubble say it is, and both of them are instruments that measure gravity.[1] So the question is not whether water is level — it is — but what shape a surface has when it is everywhere perpendicular to the local vertical. That is a question with an answer you can measure, in three separate ways, without ever looking at the horizon.

        What both models agree on, stated first. Still water sits perpendicular to gravity. A bubble level shows no slope on it. A plumb line hangs at right angles to it. None of that is in dispute here, and nothing on this page contradicts it. The disagreement is about three measurable consequences: whether the local vertical points the same way in two places, whether gravity gets weaker as you climb, and whether it has the same strength at every latitude. A flat world and a round one give different answers to all three, and the instruments are cheap.

        01 · Down is a direction, and it is not the same direction twice

        Hang a plumb bob in Marseille and another in Lille and ask the only question that matters: are the two strings parallel? On a plane they must be — “down” is one fixed direction for the whole world, so every vertical is a copy of every other. On a sphere they cannot be: each one points at the centre, so two of them separated by d along the ground make an angle d/R between them, which is 1° for every 111.2 km you travel. Both statements are testable, because the direction of a plumb line can be compared with the stars, and that comparison is exactly what astronomic latitude is.

        Angle between two verticals  =  d / R
        1° per 111.2 km
        flat plane: 0.000°, always
        This is Eratosthenes' measurement stated in modern words. He compared two shadows, which is the same as comparing two verticals against the same distant light. Every ship's noon sight, every star transit recorded by a zenith telescope, and every levelling network re-measures it.
        Angle between two plumb lines, as a function of how far apart they hang
        Separation along the groundGlobe, R = 6,371 kmFlat: infinite planeFlat: disc, from its centreMeasured (1° per 111.2 km)

        The last column is not a model output: it is the measured rate at which astronomic latitude changes with northward travel, which is how every degree of every meridian arc has been surveyed since Picard in 1670. The fourth column is computed below, by integrating the gravity of the disc itself.

        02 · Give the flat model the best gravity it can have

        A flat earth is not obliged to have no gravity. Take the strongest version available and it is a good one: an infinite uniform slab of matter. By Gauss's law the field above such a slab is 2πGσ — perpendicular to the surface, and exactly the same everywhere on it, forever. Water is level, plumb lines are parallel, nothing tilts. That model passes section 01 outright, and this page will not pretend otherwise. What it cannot do is survive being weighed.

        Infinite slab:  g = 2πGσ  ⇒  σ = —
        at Earth's mean density that is — of matter under every square metre, and no edge
        σ is mass per square metre of surface. The number is forced: to feel 9.81 m/s² you need that much matter under every square metre, spread out to infinity in every direction. Give the slab an edge and the argument collapses — the missing matter beyond the rim stops pulling sideways, and everything near the rim tilts.

        So take the map the flat model actually publishes: a disc with the north pole at the centre and the rim 20,000 km out, the same disc the magnetism tab uses. Give it Earth's own mean density and make it thick enough to produce 9.81 m/s² at the pole. Now integrate its gravity at points across its face. The vertical component stays near 9.8 — but a horizontal component appears and grows with distance from the centre, because there is more disc on one side of you than the other. The local vertical tilts inward, and so does every level surface.

        The disc weighed against itself: tilt of the local vertical, computed by integrating the disc's own gravity
        Place on the flat mapDistance from the centreTilt of the verticalSlope water would run downObserved slope

        The flat model cannot have it both ways. To keep water level everywhere it needs a field perpendicular to the disc everywhere, which requires the disc to be infinite — no rim, no ice wall, no edge, and infinite mass. To keep its own map it needs a rim at 20,000 km, and then the field tilts by the amounts in the table above: about 7° at the latitude of Paris and 26° at the latitude of Sydney. A 7° slope is a 12% grade. Rivers would all run north, seas would pile against the pole, and a bubble level would be visibly off in every building in Europe. Nobody measures that, on either side of the argument.

        03 · Gravity weakens as you climb — and the rate is the radius

        Here is the measurement that separates the two models with no map, no horizon and no sightline. Above a sphere, g falls off as 1/(R+h)². Above an infinite slab it does not fall off at all: Gauss's law makes the field of an infinite plane independent of height, exactly, at every altitude. So one model predicts a definite gradient and the other predicts zero. This is a rule‑4 test: not a small difference, a presence against an absence.

        dg/dh = −2g/R = —  ⇒  R = 2g / |dg/dh| = —
        Read it right to left and it stops being a correction and becomes an instrument. Every gravity survey on Earth applies the free‑air correction, 0.3086 mGal per metre of elevation[2], before anything else — and that constant, inverted, hands back the radius of the planet to a fraction of a percent. Geophysicists are not measuring the Earth's size when they apply it; they are using it, every day, and it works.
        How much gravity you lose by climbing, and whether an instrument can see it
        Height above the surfaceGlobe: change in gInfinite plane: change in gTimes the noise of a field gravimeter

        A relative gravimeter reads to about 0.01 mGal in the field and a laboratory absolute meter to a few microgal, so the difference between the pavement and the first floor of a building is already dozens of times the noise. The effect has been mapped up a real hillside with a portable atom interferometer[4], and airborne surveys apply it routinely at 11 km[3].

        04 · Richer's clock, 1672: g is not the same at every latitude

        Jean Richer took a pendulum clock to Cayenne, 5° from the equator, and found it running 2 min 28 s per day slow[5] against the stars, having kept perfect time in Paris. A pendulum's period depends only on its length and on g, so the clock was a gravimeter: gravity is weaker near the equator. Newton and Huygens both seized on it, for different reasons, and the modern reference formula[3] reproduces it. An infinite slab predicts one value of g everywhere; a disc accelerating upward predicts one value of g everywhere; a rotating sphere predicts a systematic sin²φ pattern of about half a percent, pole to equator.

        Standard gravity by latitude, and what a pendulum clock does about it
        Latitudeg, international formulaDifference from the poleClock rate vs ParisAny flat model

        The limit of a sphere, admitted. Rotation alone accounts for about two thirds of the pole‑to‑equator difference: ω²R at the equator is 0.0339 m/s² against a measured 0.0519[3]. The missing third comes from the equatorial bulge, which this page does not model — everywhere else the sphere is good enough, and here it is not. That residual is not an embarrassment, it is Newton's prediction: a rotating self‑gravitating fluid must flatten, by roughly 1 part in 300, and the Lapland and Peru arc expeditions of the 1730s went out to measure precisely that. A flat model has no residual to explain because it predicts no variation at all.

        05 · Mass attracts mass, and you can watch a mountain prove it

        In 1774 Nevil Maskelyne parked two observatories on the north and south flanks of Schiehallion and measured the vertical against the stars from each. The plumb lines leaned toward the mountain, by a total of 11.6″[6]. That single number does three jobs at once. It shows gravity is not a fixed downward direction but an attraction toward matter. It gave Charles Hutton the Earth's mean density, about 4.5 times water, later refined to 5.51[8]. And it is why the flat model's field has to be produced by something: a field that simply points down, with no matter making it, is not a physical theory, and the moment matter makes it, a disc's rim starts pulling sideways[7].

        Cavendish closed the loop in 1798[9] by measuring the attraction between lead balls in a room, which fixes G. With G in hand, g and R give the mass of the planet directly:, and a mean density of — twice the density of surface rock. Something denser is inside. The seismology tab finds that same something independently, from the shadow zone of P waves, and puts its boundary at 2,891 km. Two completely unrelated measurements, one object.

        06 · “Things fall because of density, not gravity”

        This is the usual alternative and it deserves a straight answer. Buoyancy is real and it is Archimedes' law: the upward force on a body in a fluid is ρfluid V g. The g is inside the formula. Density decides which way a thing moves through a fluid; it cannot supply the field that defines “down”, and it says nothing at all in a vacuum, where a feather and a hammer fall together. The serious flat proposal is the other one — the disc accelerating upward at 9.8 m/s² — and it is a real theory, so it can be priced.

        Three flat proposals against three measurements. A cross is a prediction the measurement contradicts
        ModelVertical tilts with position?g falls with height?g varies with latitude?
        Where the accelerating disc dies. Constant proper acceleration reproduces free fall perfectly — that is Einstein's equivalence principle and it is not a joke. But an accelerating floor accelerates all of itself equally: the same 9.8 m/s² at the pole and at the rim, in the cellar and at the top of the Burj Khalifa. It therefore predicts a free‑air gradient of exactly zero and a latitude variation of exactly zero, and both are measured, daily, by people whose surveys would not close if they ignored them. It also has to explain why the whole disc has been accelerating for the age of the universe without arriving anywhere.
        Experiment 1f · gravity and level
        Weigh the same object in two cities, or time a pendulum in both

        Every flat model on the table predicts that g is one number, the same everywhere. The globe predicts a specific difference between any two latitudes, set by rotation and the bulge. Two ways to see it: a pendulum, whose period goes as 1/√g, or a good spring‑type balance carrying a heavy mass. Pick your two places, and the calculator tells you in advance how big the effect is and whether your kit can resolve it.

        Independent variable
        What you change: the latitude at which you make the measurement. Nothing else — same instrument, same mass, same pendulum, carried between the two places.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the period of the pendulum, or the reading of the balance. Both are proxies for g and the world decides them.

        Hold constant: the pendulum's length and bob (temperature changes the rod — that is exactly what spoiled 15% of Richer's number), the swing amplitude below about 5°, and the same instrument at both ends. Keep both stations at similar altitude, or correct for it with the free‑air gradient from section 03.
        Kit: a two‑metre pendulum and a phone timing several hundred swings; or a 10 kg mass and a balance reading to 0.1 g. Note that most digital kitchen scales are load cells factory‑calibrated to one assumed g, which is fine — they will still show the change, since they are really reading force.
        The tell: the flat prediction is not “a small difference”. It is zero, at every latitude, for every version of the model, because a uniform slab and a uniformly accelerating floor are both uniform by construction.

        Verdict rule, symmetric. The globe fails if g at the equator and near a pole agree to better than a few parts in ten thousand, or if the variation with latitude is not sin²φ. The flat model fails on any latitude dependence of the observed size and sign, for which a plane gives no reason. A pendulum timed over a thousand swings reaches one part in 10⁴, which is the size of the effect.

        The through‑line. “Level” is the hinge this whole page turns on. The horizon‑dip tab measures how far the horizon sits below level; the surveying tab shows the curvature correction that a levelled sightline needs; the hidden‑height tab counts what a level surface hides. All three assume that level means perpendicular to gravity — and this tab is where that assumption is cashed out and measured. The same R comes back a fourth way here, out of a gravimeter, with no light involved at all.

Any library edition gives the torsion‑balance apparatus and the density figure of 5.48 times water.
        Foucault · the sine that gives away the sphere

        A weight on a wire measures the angle between your floor and the axis of the world

        Only the part of Ω square to your floor can turn a swing plane. All of it at every station on a spinning disc; none at the equator on a globe, reversed past it. Dashed: below the floor. The disc is lent a daily spin here — the flat model as usually held has none, and predicts no precession anywhere.

        In February 1851 Léon Foucault hung a 67 m wire from the dome of the Panthéon, tied a 28 kg brass bob to the end, burned the cord holding it aside, and let Paris watch its own floor turn. The demonstration is famous for proving that the Earth rotates. That is the smaller half of what it does.

        The plane of swing turns at 15.041°/h × sin(latitude) — and that sine is not about rotation at all. It is a statement about the angle between the local vertical and the axis of spin, measured separately at every latitude, and it is the sharpest shape test on this page that needs no distant object, no clear air and no horizon.

        ω = Ω sin φ
        T = 23h56m04s / sin φ
        Ω = 15.041 °/h
        Ω is one turn per sidereal day — relative to the stars, not the Sun. φ is your latitude, signed: positive north, negative south. Read the formula as a prediction machine rather than a result. It says the swing plane turns clockwise in the northern hemisphere, anticlockwise in the southern, and not at all on the equator. A flat Earth spinning once a day predicts the same rate everywhere with the same sense; a flat Earth that does not spin predicts zero everywhere. All three are testable in an afternoon with a stairwell.

        What a pendulum on a turning floor actually does

        A pendulum hung so that its pivot cannot transmit twist has nothing to tell it which way to swing. Once it is moving in a plane, the only forces on it are gravity, which acts along the wire and in the plane, and the wire's tension, likewise. Nothing pushes it sideways. In an inertial frame the plane therefore stays put — and the floor, the building and the city underneath rotate past it. What the visitor sees as the pendulum turning is the room turning.

        Foucault said exactly this in four pages to the Académie des sciences on 3 February 1851, presented by Arago. His point was not the physics, which was old, but that the effect could be seen: the swing plane, he wrote, moves gradually from east to west, giving a perceptible sign of the diurnal motion of the terrestrial globe.[1] He had already built a 2 m version in his cellar in January and an 11 m one at the Paris Observatory in February; the Panthéon wire was the third and the one that made the newspapers.

        Concede this immediately. A single Foucault pendulum, observed at one place, does not prove the Earth is a sphere. It proves that the frame you are standing in is rotating — nothing more. A flat disc spinning once a day would also make a pendulum precess. Anyone who tells you one pendulum settles the shape of the world is overselling, and the overselling is what gives the objection its bite. The shape argument lives entirely in the sine: in how the rate changes when you carry the pendulum somewhere else. That is what the rest of this tab is about.
        Draw it in
        Latitude
        • floor frame: the room is held still and the swing plane creeps round it — what a visitor sees
        • swing frame: the plane is held still and the floor turns underneath — what is physically happening
        The same motion, drawn twice. Looking straight down at the floor. Nothing about the pendulum changes between the two buttons; only the choice of what to nail to the screen. Set the latitude to 0° and both pictures go inert, because sin 0 = 0. One honest caveat on the naming: at the pole the swing frame really is the frame of the stars, but at any other latitude it is the frame the plane is parallel-transported in. Swing rate and time are both scaled, the factors are printed on the figure, and the angle the plane sweeps is real.

        Where the sine comes from

        The Earth turns about a single axis, at a single rate. Stand anywhere on it and that rotation vector Ω can be split into two pieces relative to your local vertical: a component along the vertical, of size Ω sin φ, and a component along the local horizontal pointing north, of size Ω cos φ. Only the vertical component can turn a horizontal swing plane. The horizontal component tries to tip the plane out of horizontal, and gravity and the wire will not let it — to first order it does nothing at all.[2]

        Ωvertical = Ω sin φ
        Ωhorizontal = Ω cos φ
        At the pole the axis is the local vertical: sin φ = 1, and the floor turns a full circle under the pendulum in one sidereal day. At the equator the axis is horizontal: sin φ = 0, and the swing plane does not turn even though the Earth is rotating as fast there as anywhere — faster, in fact, measured in kilometres per hour. In between you get the sine, and its sign flips when you cross the equator because the local vertical flips relative to the axis.
        One rotation vector, three floors. Ω is the same arrow everywhere — same direction, same length, parallel to the axis. What changes from place to place is your floor. Near the pole the arrow is almost straight up out of the floor and nearly all of it counts; near the equator it lies almost flat in the floor and almost none of it does. The vertical piece, drawn in teal, is Ω sin φ, and it is the whole of the precession rate.
        What you actually watch. The bob's track over six hours at the latitude of Paris, drawn in the frame of the floor. The swing plane creeps round at 11.3° per hour, so the star pattern closes up after about 32 hours. The narrow ellipse is exaggerated here to make successive swings distinguishable; in a well-started pendulum it is the thing you spend all your effort making smaller, for reasons three sections below.

        Why the sine is a statement about a sphere, not about spinning

        Here is the part that turns a rotation demo into a geometry measurement. Forget forces and watch the swing direction as a little arrow lying flat on the ground, carried once around a circle of latitude as the day passes. The arrow is never twisted about the vertical — there is nothing to twist it. In differential geometry that is exactly the definition of parallel transport, and the striking fact about parallel transport on a curved surface is that an arrow carried around a closed loop comes back rotated.

        The amount it comes back rotated is the solid angle enclosed by the loop. For a circle of latitude φ on a sphere that solid angle is 2π(1 − sin φ), so after one full day the arrow has slipped by 2π sin φ relative to the ground — which is the Foucault rate, obtained with no dynamics whatsoever.[3] It is the same mathematical creature as Berry's phase in quantum mechanics, and the pendulum is its oldest instrument.[5]

        The sentence that matters. Parallel transport around a closed loop only produces a mismatch if the surface is curved; on a flat surface the arrow always comes home pointing exactly where it started. So the Foucault mismatch is not merely evidence of rotation — it is a direct measurement of the Gaussian curvature enclosed by the pendulum's daily path. As one review of the geometry puts it, while the conventional reading is that the pendulum shows the Earth rotates, the geometric reading is that it shows the Earth is a sphere.[4] Another derives the same result as a special case of Gauss–Bonnet, and notes that the pendulum shows not only that the planet turns but that it is curved.[3] This is not a rhetorical flourish added for this page; it is why the result appears in differential-geometry lectures at all.

        There is a homelier way to say it. A pendulum measures the angle between your floor and the axis of the world. Carry it around and you are mapping the direction of the local vertical over the whole surface. If the verticals all point the same way, the surface is flat and every pendulum agrees. If the verticals fan out as sin φ, the surface is a sphere and every pendulum disagrees with its neighbour by precisely the amount the sphere requires. Two centuries of pendulums have disagreed in exactly that pattern.

        Three models, three different predictions

        The flat model is not one claim but two, and both are on the table in flat-earth discussion, so both get a column. Either the Earth does not rotate — in which case a free pendulum has no reason to precess anywhere — or it is a disc spinning once a day about the pole at its centre. On such a disc the local vertical is parallel to the spin axis at every single point, so sin φ is effectively 1 everywhere: every pendulum, from the middle to the rim, precesses at the full 15.041°/h, all turning the same way.

        Predicted precession of the swing plane — every number computed from the three models, none fitted
        LatitudeGlobe: Ω sin φGlobe: full turn Flat, not rotatingFlat disc, 1 turn/day
        Three predictions, and the data picks one. A pendulum at Paris precesses at all, which finishes the non-rotating flat model on its first afternoon. The pendulum run at the geographic South Pole in 2001 precessed the other way round from every northern installation — which finishes the spinning-disc model, because a disc turning one way cannot make a swing plane turn the other way anywhere on it. The disc also owes an explanation for the equator, where the globe says the rate must fall to exactly zero. Note the shape of the argument: this is a sign and zero-crossing test, not a comparison of two numbers that happen to differ a little. There is no parameter anyone can adjust to move a zero crossing to the equator and a sign reversal south of it, other than being on a sphere.
        The whole argument in one curve. Precession rate against latitude for the three models. The globe's sine crosses zero at the equator and changes sign; the spinning disc is a horizontal line at the full rotation rate; the stationary flat Earth is the axis itself. Dots mark installations whose latitude is listed in the table below. Any single pendulum sits on one dot and cannot distinguish the models on its own — the argument is the shape of the curve those dots lie on.

        Installations, and what they were measured to do

        Below are five installations at widely separated latitudes, with the rate the globe model predicts from the latitude alone. Two of them carry a measured value from a published account. The most useful of those is the one taken as close to a pole as anyone has managed: in the winter of 2001 four researchers hung a 33 m wire with a 25 kg bob down a six-storey stairwell of the station then under construction at the geographic South Pole, at −68 °C, and marked the apex of the swing on the floor every twenty minutes for a day.

        Documented Foucault installations — predicted rate computed from latitude, measured values as published
        SiteLatitudeWire Predicted ratePredicted full turnMeasured

        They found the plane turning 5° every twenty minutes, giving a full turn in 24 hours ± 50 minutes against a prediction of 23 h 56 m, and — the detail that matters more than the number — turning reversed with respect to every northern installation — exactly the sign change the sine demands once φ goes negative.[6] They also got a bonus: timing the swing gave g = 9.85 ± 0.03 m/s², which is the polar value, and which nobody was trying to fit.

        The experiment is genuinely hard, and pretending otherwise helps nobody

        A real pendulum has a systematic error that can swamp the effect, and it is worth knowing about before someone presents it to you as a scandal. If the bob traces even a very thin ellipse rather than a straight line, the ellipse itself precesses, for reasons that have nothing to do with the Earth. George Airy worked out the rate in 1851, and it is proportional to the area of the ellipse:

        ωAiry = (3/8) · (a·b / L²) · √(g/L)
        a and b are the semi-axes of the ellipse, L the wire length. The precession runs in whichever direction the bob is going round its ellipse. Put in the Panthéon's numbers — L = 67 m, a 3 m swing, and an ellipse just 1 cm wide — and you get 0.198°/h, about 1.7% of Foucault's 11.3. Now shorten the wire to 5 m with a 0.5 m swing and the same 1 cm of ellipse: 21.7°/h, roughly twice the real signal and pointing wherever your release happened to point. The rate falls off as L−5/2. That, and not showmanship, is why Foucault wanted 67 metres of it.[7]

        This is why the ritual matters: the bob is drawn aside with a thread, allowed to settle completely, and the thread is burned rather than cut, so that no sideways impulse is given at release. Museums that must run unattended for years add a Charron ring — a small ring below the pivot that the wire brushes near the end of each swing, bleeding away the elliptical component while leaving the planar one alone. Both are corrections for a known, calculable, signed error. Neither is a thumb on the scale, and the reason lies in the last line of this section.

        The error has a tell, and it is a good one. The Airy precession follows the direction the bob circulates its ellipse — start it the other way round and it reverses. The Coriolis precession does not care how you released it: at a given latitude it is the same rate in the same direction every time, forever. So the two are separable by anyone with an afternoon and no equipment: release the bob a dozen times with deliberately opposite ellipses and average. Whatever survives the averaging is the Earth. This is the standard control, and a modern study measuring both effects together on a 4.8 m pendulum finds exactly the interplay the formulas predict, right down to amplitudes at which the two cancel and the precession stops.[7]

        Six objections, answered with numbers

        1. "It only shows rotation, so it says nothing about shape."

        Correct for one pendulum, and this tab conceded it in the first callout. Wrong for two. The rate depends on latitude as sin φ, which is the projection of a fixed axis onto a local vertical that changes direction from place to place — and a vertical that changes direction from place to place is what a curved surface is. On a flat surface, however it moves, every local vertical is parallel to every other, so every pendulum must run at the same rate. They do not.

        2. "Museum pendulums are driven by an electromagnet, so the museum sets the rate."

        The drive is a ring or coil mounted on the vertical axis, directly under the pivot point, and it is axially symmetric: it pulls the bob along the line it is already travelling, replacing energy lost to air, and by symmetry it exerts no torque about the vertical. It cannot set a direction it does not know. And the claim is testable rather than arguable: if drives set the rate, driven pendulums would show a rate characteristic of their drives rather than of their latitudes. Instead they show sin φ. Foucault's own pendulum had no drive at all, and neither did the South Pole one — it was restarted by hand every couple of hours as the swing died.[6]

        3. "Even Airy called it a fraud."

        He did, in private correspondence, before attending a single demonstration — and his stated objection was that starting a pendulum swinging in a true plane is extremely difficult. On that narrow point he was right, which is the whole of the previous section. What he was wrong about is whether the difficulty is insuperable, and that was settled by burning threads, Charron rings, longer wires and averaging over opposite releases. An 1851 objection to experimental technique is not an outstanding objection to a result reproduced for 175 years on every continent including Antarctica.

        4. "The South Pole team kept adjusting until they got the answer they wanted."

        They did rebuild the apparatus twice, and they say so themselves, in print, in the same account that reports the result — which is already a strange way to run a fraud.[6] Look at what the two failures were. First, they hung the bob with its long axis vertical, and air resistance on it spun the whole pendulum; second, they got a rate twice the expected one. Both are recognised apparatus faults with recognised fixes, and both were diagnosed before the final run rather than explained afterwards. Set against that: the same apparatus returned g = 9.85 ± 0.03 m/s², a quantity nobody was steering, and it landed on the polar value. Debugging an instrument until it stops lying is what experimental work consists of; the question to ask is whether the diagnosis was independent of the wanted answer, and here it demonstrably was.

        5. "Coriolis is a fictitious force, so it cannot do anything."

        "Fictitious" is a technical term meaning "an artefact of describing motion in an accelerating frame", not "imaginary". The pendulum is the instrument that detects that your frame is accelerating. Complaining that the force is fictitious is complaining that the experiment worked. In the frame of the stars there is no Coriolis force and no puzzle: the plane sits still and the building turns.

        6. "Air currents, building sway, a twisting wire."

        All real, all present, and none of them latitude-aware. A draught in Chicago does not know it should produce 10.02°/h while an identical draught in Melbourne produces −9.22°/h and one in Quito produces zero. Systematic errors that happen to reproduce sin φ across a hundred independent buildings, built by people who never met, are not systematic errors. They are the signal.

        Experiment 1d · Foucault pendulum
        Find a stairwell, and measure the angle between your floor and the axis of the world

        This is the rare shape test you can run indoors, alone, at night, with hardware from a builders' merchant. Hang the heaviest compact mass you can from the longest wire your building allows, on a pivot that cannot transmit twist. Draw the bob aside with a thread, wait until it is dead still, burn the thread. Mark the apex of the swing on the floor every twenty minutes. The calculator below tells you before you start whether your stairwell is tall enough for the answer to mean anything.

        Independent variable
        What you change: your latitude — ideally by persuading someone at a very different one to repeat it. A second site is what converts a rotation demo into a shape measurement.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the angle the swing plane turns in a measured time, and its sense. The sense alone already separates the three models if you can get south of the equator.

        Hold constant: the release procedure, above all. Same thread, same starting point, same settling time — and then deliberately vary it, releasing with opposite ellipses on alternate runs so the Airy term averages out.
        Kit: wire, a compact heavy bob, a swivel-free suspension, chalk, a watch. No optics, no electronics, nothing to calibrate.
        The tell: a rate that varies with latitude as a sine, crossing zero at the equator and reversing south of it. A flat disc gives one rate everywhere; a stationary flat Earth gives none.

        Verdict rule, symmetric. The globe fails if the precession rate is not 15.041 sin φ degrees per hour, or if it does not reverse when the pendulum crosses the equator. The flat model fails on any reversal between hemispheres, and on any latitude dependence at all. Ten metres of wire, one hour and a chalk mark: the rate is about 11°/h at 45°.

        A caveat this page owes you. The sin φ law is first-order. A full treatment carries small corrections — the pendulum's own amplitude, the fact that the precession is not perfectly uniform through a single swing, the ellipticity of the Earth changing the direction of the local vertical by up to about 11′ between geodetic and geocentric latitude, and, at the level of parts in 109, frame dragging. None of them approaches the size of the effect being argued about here: the difference between the globe and the spinning-disc prediction at Paris is 3.7°/h, roughly a quarter of the whole rotation rate, while every correction just listed is smaller than the width of a chalk mark.

        The through-line. Every other tab on this page tests the shape of the Earth by looking at something far away — a mountain, a horizon, a star, a satellite — and therefore has to argue about the air in between. This one does not. There is no sightline, no refraction, no atmosphere in the argument at all; the instrument is a weight on a string in a stairwell, and the quantity it reports is the orientation of your own floor. That is why it belongs beside the optical tabs rather than among them: it is the same conclusion reached with none of the same assumptions.
