        Magnetism & the compass · the needle is a 3-D instrument

        The needle doesn't just point north — it tilts

        How far the needle turns over, along the same 20,000 km. On the globe the turn completes — nose down, level, nose up. On flat ①, with the buried magnet’s depth already set in the flat model’s own favour, it stalls short: nothing on the disc gets past about 35° up. Red end is north-seeking.

        A compass needle is a freely-pivoting magnet: it settles along the local magnetic field vector, in three dimensions. The familiar hiking compass hides this by clamping the needle to a horizontal card; free the other axis and the needle dips — down in the northern hemisphere, level at the magnetic equator, up in the southern hemisphere. That tilt pattern is measured daily, and the two shapes below predict very different versions of it. Drag either scene to orbit it.

        tan I = 2·tan λ
        B = B₀·√(1 + 3·sin²λ)
        B₀ ≈ 30 μT
        The centred-dipole field of a sphere. I = inclination (dip, + downward), λ = magnetic latitude. Two clean consequences: the dip changes sign at the magnetic equator, and the total field at the poles is exactly twice the equatorial value — 30 → 60 μT, never more, never less. Real Earth adds an ~10° tilt of the magnetic axis and non-dipole wrinkles of ±20% or so; neither ever flips the hemisphere pattern.
        Globe — central dipole
        • each needle lies along the local field; its red end is the north-seeking one
        • the violet needle is yours — move the λ slider
        • red dashed: the magnetic equator
        • grey dashed: the spin axis, which the magnetic axis misses by about 10°
        One magnet, in the middle of a sphere. Field lines leave near the south magnetic pole, arc over, and re-enter near the north one. Notice how fast the needle steepens: the factor 2 in tan I = 2 tan λ puts the dip past 45° only 27° from the magnetic equator, so the field is near-parallel to the ground in that narrow band only — Paris already tilts 64°. True scale.

        That 10° offset is why a compass needs a declination correction at all, and why the correction is different in every place and drifts from decade to decade.

        Flat disc — magnet under the centre
        What each model predicts for your compass at the slider's latitude / map position
        ModelDip IHorizontal pull HTotal field BNorth end points…

        The dip profile: one curve, ten cities, no free parameters left

        Both flat layouts have been tuned in their own favour: the magnet depth (①) and the ring strength (②) are chosen so that their dip-zero circle lands exactly on the observed magnetic equator, ~10,000 km from the pole, and their field strength is normalised to 30 μT there. That spends every adjustable quantity each model has. Everything else on the curve is now a forced prediction.

        Inclination vs distance from the north magnetic pole. Teal band: the globe dipole — the width is the ±10° axis tilt, mapped through tan I = 2 tan λ; a few extra degrees of non-dipole scatter are expected and stated below. Amber: flat ① (solid) and flat ② (dashed), after tuning. Dots: measured values. The measured points ride the teal band all the way to −90° and never come near either amber curve past the calibration circle.
        Dip angle I, measured (IGRF, rounded) vs each model's forced prediction
        Placeλ (magnetic)Measured IGlobeFlat ①Flat ②
        Total field strength |B| in μT — a smartphone can read this column
        PlaceMeasured BGlobeFlat ①Flat ②

        Where both flat layouts break, in plain words. ① A magnet under the centre does produce a dip-zero circle — but beyond it the field dies as 1/r³ and the dip goes shallow, not steep: at Melbourne's position the needle should pull ~5× weaker than it measurably does and dip only −19° instead of the measured −69°, and no point on the entire disc can dip past −35° — yet Dunedin measures −72° and one Antarctic point −90°.
        ② The rim-ring version, and what it trades. Feeding the field back in through a rim ring only trades failures: the far south goes nearly level (Melbourne −13°, Cape Town −12°, against measured −69° and −66°), the dip then snaps to −90° along the entire ice wall — one continuous magnetic pole encircling the world — and the strong centre pole the ring must balance makes the Arctic read over 400 μT where instruments find 57.
        And where the one real pole is. Measurement instead finds exactly one point with I = −90°, off the coast of Adélie Land, Antarctica — claimed overland by David, Mawson and Mackay in 1909 — modern reassessment puts their flag within ~130 km of the wandering pole — and pinned down repeatedly since, most precisely by Barton in 2000, within ~2 km. A point is not a ring, and a working Australian compass is not a spinning one.

        Why the needle aligns — and how the dip is actually read

        τ = m × B  ⇒  needle rests along B
        hiking compass reads only H = B·cos I
        A needle with magnetic moment m feels a torque m×B that is zero only when it lies along the field, north-seeking end pointing the way B points. A baseplate compass pivots about a vertical axis only, so it can respond to nothing but the horizontal component H — the dip is still there, expressed as the needle's urge to drag its nose down. That is why manufacturers balance needles differently per hemisphere (counterweighting the south end in the north, and vice versa) and why "global needle" compasses exist at all: an engineering industry quietly built around the very tilt the flat models cannot produce.
        A dip circle (Robert Norman's instrument, 1581): a needle balanced on a horizontal axle at the centre of a vertical graduated circle, the whole thing free to turn about a vertical stand. Shown reading I = +64° — roughly Paris.
        Reading it properly (the null trick):
        1. Level the base with the bubble — everything is referenced to true horizontal.
        2. Turn about the vertical axis until the needle stands exactly vertical. In that orientation the needle's plane is perpendicular to the magnetic meridian: only the vertical part of B can act on it. No reading is taken — this is a null alignment, insensitive to scale errors.
        3. Rotate exactly 90°. The circle now lies in the magnetic meridian; the needle swings freely under the full field and settles along B. Read I off the circle.
        4. Cancel instrument error: read both needle ends, reverse the circle face east↔west, re-magnetise the needle reversed, and average — the classical four-fold reversal that removes pivot friction and balance bias.
        Before that instrument, dip was a nuisance: compass makers were already gluing tiny counterweights to needles in the 1500s to keep them level. Norman asked why the needle wanted to tilt — and measured it.
        The tabletop version: Gilbert’s terrella, 1600A lodestone machined into a small sphere reproduced the whole dip-against-latitude pattern — and you can repeat it tonight with a sphere magnet and a button compass, then try to match it with any magnet under a flat plate
        William Gilbert machined a lodestone into a small sphere — a terrella, "little Earth" — and walked a short compass needle across its surface. The needle stood upright at two opposite points, lay flat along the mid-circle between them, and tilted by the dipole rule everywhere else: the exact dip-vs-latitude pattern navigators were reporting. His conclusion opens the modern subject: the Earth itself is a great magnet. You can repeat this tonight with a sphere magnet and a cheap button compass — then try to reproduce the same needle behaviour with any magnet arrangement under a flat plate. The sphere takes one magnet; the plate has no arrangement that works, because the failure is in the shape, not the magnet.
        Experiment 5 · the field in your pocket
        Read inclination and field strength wherever you are — the sensor is already in your phone

        Every smartphone carries a 3-axis magnetometer. A free sensor app reports the total field |B| in μT directly; add a level surface (or the phone's accelerometer, which sensor apps use automatically) and it reports the inclination I too. A ~15€ dip needle, or a magnetised sewing needle floated on a cork disc and then re-balanced on a horizontal pin, does the same with no electronics.

        Independent variable
        What you change: your position — magnetic latitude λ, or on the flat map, distance r from the centre. Travel, or recruit friends and relatives by latitude; the further apart, the sharper the test. Set it with the λ slider above.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: two numbers per location — the dip I (sign included!) and the total field |B| in μT. The world decides both.

        Hold constant: measure outdoors away from cars, rebar and speakers (steel shifts readings by tens of μT up close — walk 20 m and it stops changing); same app; average a few readings.
        The tells, stated in advance: the globe says I flips sign at one specific circle and marches to −90° at a single southern point, while |B| stays inside roughly 22–67 μT worldwide, poleward-heavy by about a factor 2. Flat ① says southern |B| collapses several-fold and compasses lose all direction near the rim; flat ② says the whole rim reads I = −90°. Any Australian phone refutes both before lunch.

        Verdict rule, symmetric. The globe fails if the dip angle does not follow tan I = 2 tan λ, or if the field at the pole is not twice the field at the equator. The flat model fails if the dipole law holds across latitudes at all — this is the one test on the page that constrains the shape without using a radius. A dip needle to ±1° suffices: the law predicts 63.4° at 45°.

        The escape hatches, pre-empted. Crustal rocks bend the local field (ore bodies, volcanic terrain) and the whole pattern drifts by ~0.1°/yr — both real, both mapped, and both small: a few degrees and ±20% in |B|, the largest being the South Atlantic weak patch (São Paulo's low 23 μT above). None of it ever flips the sign of I across a hemisphere, moves the dip-zero line to a different circle, or makes a compass fail in Patagonia. Corrections shrink residuals; they never rescue a wrong shape.

        One honest subtlety. The table's λ is dipole-frame magnetic latitude (approximate), not geographic latitude — the axis tilt makes them differ by up to ~10°. Also, the point where a dip needle reads exactly ±90° (the dip pole) sits a few degrees from the ideal dipole axis because of the non-dipole part; that is why the South-magnetic-pole row shows the dipole predicting −81° where the measured value is by definition −90°. A 9° residual against a 60–90° signal, with the correct sign everywhere, versus flat errors of 30–70° with impossible geometry — that is the comparison.

        The through-line. The other four tabs share one radius R. This tab needs no radius at all: tan I = 2 tan λ and the pole/equator factor of exactly 2 are properties of a dipole centred in a sphere, whatever its size. The compass tests the shape alone — and it is the oldest instrument on this page, telling the same story since sailors first noticed their needles leaning in the 1500s.

        Sources and further reading for this tab
        Nothing on this tab carries an inline [n] marker yet: these are the works it was built from, listed in full rather than pinned to individual sentences.
        • NOAA NCEI — International Geomagnetic Reference Field (IGRF) — the standard model behind the "measured" columns; NOAA's geomagnetic models & calculators let you compute I and |B| for your own coordinates and check every number in the tables.
        • British Geological Survey — Magnetic Poles — dip poles vs geomagnetic (dipole) poles, why they differ and move, and the dipole axis tilt of about 10°; the BGS education pages also cover smartphone magnetometers, the sensor Experiment 5 relies on.
        • Suunto — Understanding balancing zones — the manufacturer's own explanation of hemisphere-balanced needles and the global needle: the compass industry engineering built around the dip.
        • William Gilbert, De Magnete (1600), full English translation at Project Gutenberg — the terrella experiments and the conclusion that the Earth itself is a great magnet.
        • Australian Antarctic Program and National Museum of Australia — the 1909 David–Mawson–Mackay journey toward the South Magnetic Pole, the modern reassessment of how close they came, and Barton's 2000 fix within ~2 km of the drifting pole.
        • ESA Swarm and NASA SVS — the South Atlantic weak patch: the largest non-dipole anomaly, flagged with * in the tables above.
        • INTERMAGNET, with data served through the BGS data portal. Around 150 magnetic observatories worldwide, publishing definitive one-minute and one-second data, free to download. This is the check this tab most needs and has been missing. Everything in the tables above is read off a model; here are the measurements the models are fitted to. Take the observatories' latitudes, take their inclinations, plot one against the other, and see whether tan I = 2 tan λ falls out of data that nobody assembled to make this argument.
        • NOAA NCEI / BGS — World Magnetic Model. The operational model rather than the research one: the WMM is what runs in the compass app on your phone and in aviation and defence navigation systems, and it is rebuilt every five years because the field moves. A model that had the shape of the Earth wrong would be noticed by its users within weeks.
        • Robert Norman, The Newe Attractive (London, 1581). The discovery of magnetic dip, by a London compass-maker who found that a needle he had balanced perfectly before magnetising it would afterwards tip downward, and had to trim it to make it lie level again. Nineteen years before Gilbert, and the more concrete of the two: it starts from a workshop annoyance.
        • Edmond Halley, A New and Correct Chart Shewing the Variations of the Compass (1701). The first isogonic chart, drawn from measurements Halley made himself on two Atlantic voyages. The field's structure has been mapped continuously for over three centuries.
        • ESA — VirES for Swarm. Interactive access to the Swarm satellite magnetic measurements. The same verification as INTERMAGNET, from orbit instead of the ground, and again free.
        The Sun · distance, motion & the analemma

        How far is the Sun? Ask a moon of Jupiter

        Globe. Both panels are what a level camera aimed at the year's mean Sun would frame. The 8 is one rigid curve on the celestial sphere, the same for every observer at every hour, so its drawn shape never changes — slide φ and it only turns with you.
        Flat disc, steel-manned. The Sun circles above the disc at exactly the height that makes the equinox noon altitude correct for your latitude — the model is given its best free parameter, not a straw one.

        Move to mid-latitudes and it breaks. Solstice altitudes miss by 10–16° at φ = 45–60°, and — unlike the globe's rigid celestial curve — the flat 8's very shape morphs as you travel, from 65°×16° at the equator down to 29°×11° by φ = 60°. Slide φ and watch it deform: no analemma photograph has ever shown that.

        And the Sun's altitude never reaches zero. On a flat disc the horizon can never cut the 8 — no sunset at any latitude, and no polar night at any pole, where six months of measured darkness are the plainest fact of Arctic life. The Sun can only shrink into the distance; it measurably does not.

        The Sun's distance was pinned down by several completely independent routes — triangulating a planet from two points on Earth, timing Venus crossing the Sun's face from opposite hemispheres, and, most elegantly, using light itself as a ruler. Then, once a year of noon Suns is photographed from one spot, the sky draws a figure-8 — the analemma — whose exact shape is a fingerprint of the geometry producing it.

        A brief history of the distance (simplified)

        Each method independent of the last · values rounded
        WhenWho / methodResult (million km)
        ~270 BCAristarchus — angle Sun–Earth–Moon at half moon; right idea, the angle (89.85°) was too fine for naked eyes~8 (20× too small)
        1672Cassini & Richer — Mars triangulated simultaneously from Paris and Cayenne, 7,000 km apart~140
        1761 / 1769Transits of Venus — Halley's 1716 plan; worldwide expeditions incl. Cook at Tahiti; Encke's combined solution~153 (2.5% high)
        1849–62Fizeau & Foucault measure c on the ground — combined with Io's eclipse delays (below), light itself becomes the ruler~148–154
        1961+Radar echoes off Venus + Kepler's third law149.598
        2012IAU Resolution B2 — the au fixed by definition 149.597 870 700 exactly[4]

        The routes share no assumptions: parallax needs only a baseline on Earth and simultaneous angles; the transit method needs timing; the light-time method needs a stopwatch and a terrestrial measurement of c. They agree to a fraction of a percent. One number, many roads.

        Rømer's clock, run in reverse

        In 1676 at the Paris Observatory, Ole Rømer noticed that the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io — a natural clock ticking every 42.5 h — ran late when Earth was far from Jupiter and early when near, and he predicted the 9 November eclipse would arrive 10 minutes behind Cassini's tables[1]. It did. Light, he concluded, takes time to travel: about 22 minutes (his estimate) across Earth's orbit. Huygens turned that into the first speed of light.

        Now run it backwards. By 1849 Fizeau had measured c on the ground — a toothed wheel and a mirror 8.6 km apart in Paris, no astronomy involved — and Foucault refined it to ~298,000 km/s[2]. Feed that c into Io's timings: the eclipse delay swings by ≈16.6 minutes between Jupiter's opposition and conjunction, and the only distance that swing can correspond to is the diameter of Earth's orbit: 2 AU = c × ~998 s ⇒ 1 AU ≈ 149.6 million km. Note what is not assumed: Jupiter's distance comes free from its 11.86-year period via Kepler's third law, which needs only angles; the relative map of the solar system was already known — Io's lag simply sets its absolute scale[3].

        Δt = D / c  ⇒  2 au = c · Δtmax ≈ 299,792 km/s × 998 s  ⇒  1 au ≈ 1.496×10⁸ km
        The flat model has no account of this at all: a lamp a few thousand kilometres up gives Earth–Sun and Earth–Jupiter distance variations of a few thousand km — light-time wobbles of hundredths of a second, not sixteen minutes ticked out by a moon on schedule.
        Left: top view, to scale in AU — Earth laps Jupiter every 399 days. Right: the light-travel time from Jupiter, day by day: a smooth ~16.6-minute swing that Io's eclipse clock writes into every observing logbook. The dot is today's geometry. (Circular, coplanar orbits are assumed here; the real eccentricities shift the swing by a few percent and nothing about the 16-minute scale.)

        The analemma: a year of noon Suns, one exposure

        Photograph the Sun at the same clock time every few days for a year and it traces a lopsided figure-8: east–west spread from the equation of time (orbital eccentricity + axial tilt, ±16 minutes), north–south from the declination swing (±23.44°). Both models below are driven by the same equation-of-time and declination inputs — what differs is the geometry turning them into a sky position. The flat sun's height is tuned in its favour so the equinox noon altitude at your latitude is exact.

        Noon Sun at your latitude — measured (any almanac / NOAA calculator)[6] vs the two geometries
        DateMeasured noon altitudeGlobeFlat (tuned)Flat error

        Two more measured properties the flat sun cannot survive. (1) Angular size. The real Sun's disc varies only ±1.7% over a year (perihelion in January — measured with any solar filter or pinhole), exactly matching a mildly elliptical orbit. A local sun a few thousand km up must swell and shrink by a factor of ~2–3 between noon and night, every single day (computed for your latitude in the table note above); it does not. (2) Sunset. The Sun crosses the horizon at a sharp, predictable time and is cut by the horizon bottom first, at full angular size. A receding lamp would dwindle to a dot near the horizon and never touch it. The analemma, the constancy of the disc, and sunset are three views of the same geometry — and each is a backyard measurement.

        The daily motion: one sky-clock, many observers

        What is actually measured, every day, everywhere: the Sun crosses the sky at a constant angular speed — 15.0°/h at the equinox, the equal spacing of the discs in any solar time-lapse, the reason sundial hour lines are evenly cut (corrected only by the ±16-min equation of time) — and at constant angular size. On the flat disc, a sun circling the pole at a uniform rate cannot produce either: it is close to you at your noon and far at your midnight, so its apparent speed across your sky must surge and slacken, and its disc must swell and shrink. The two panels are driven by the φ slider above; the equinox is used throughout.

        measured: dψ/dt ≈ 15°/h, constant
        flat, uniform spin: varying
        flat, tuned for you: wrong for everyone else
        The flat model's only escape is to make the sun itself accelerate and decelerate along its track so that your sky-rate comes out constant. But the sun is one object, shared in real time: the speed schedule that flattens your curve is simultaneously measured by an observer at another latitude — and for them it is worse than the uniform case. There is no schedule that works for two observers at once; the globe needs none, because a rotating sphere gives every observer the same 15°/h for free.
        One equinox day, whole-sky chart (zenith at centre, horizon = outer circle, dots every hour). The globe's path is one arc of a perfect circle about the celestial pole — the same circle long-exposure sun- and star-trail photographs show — entering and leaving at the horizon with its hourly dots evenly spaced. The flat sun traces a lopsided loop whose shape changes with your latitude, with dots crowded on the far side and stretched on the near side — and the loop never touches the horizon.
        Apparent angular speed through the day. Teal: measured (and the globe's prediction) — flat at 15°/h. Amber solid: the flat sun at uniform spin, as seen from your latitude. Amber dashed: what an observer at 10°S measures at the same moments if the sun's track speed is re-tuned to flatten your curve — the acceleration that fixes your sky breaks theirs. One sun cannot keep two skies uniform; a rotating Earth keeps them all uniform at once.

        The sundial: a stick aimed at the axis

        Humanity's oldest clock is the hardware version of the last section. A sundial keeps time all year only if its shadow-caster — the gnomon — is set parallel to Earth's rotation axis, pointing at the celestial pole. Then the sun simply revolves around the stick at 15°/h, whatever the season, and the hour lines can be engraved once and trusted forever. The price of that trick is written on every dial ever made: the gnomon must lean above the ground by exactly your latitude — vertical at the pole, flat on the ground at the equator, 51.5° in London — which is why antique dials are cut for a stated latitude and mis-read when moved. Below, one distant sun held fixed at the left while the planet turns beneath it: drag to orbit, pause the day with the button.

        gnomon tilt = φ
        horizontal-plate hour lines: tan θ = sin φ · tan H[5]
        shadow rate about the gnomon: 15°/h
        All three follow from one fact: an axis-parallel stick sees the sun circle it uniformly. The flat model has no counterpart — under a nearby circling sun, no fixed stick orientation gives season-proof hour lines, the required "tilt" would not follow the simple tilt-equals-latitude law that dials from Egypt to China to Peru all obey, and a dial carried across the disc could not be corrected by latitude alone. Every garden sundial is a standing measurement of the axis it points at.
        • dashed extensions: every gnomon is parallel to every other and to the axis
        • the violet gnomon is yours
        • the grey dashed ring is the terminator — dials on the night side cast no shadow
        • the row below is each dial face from above, north up, with its own latitude's hour lines
        Five dials, one sun. Seen from the side the gnomons lean at 65°, 35°, 0° and 30° south, each equal to its own latitude. The hour fans below all differ — splayed wide at 65°, tighter at 35°, running anticlockwise on the southern dial, and a horizontal dial fails outright at the equator, where the equatorial master dial takes over. Yet every shadow lands on the same hour, matching the readout on the globe, computed from one and the same shadow function: the agreement is geometry, not styling.

        Watch the planet carry the dials through the fixed sunlight. The shadows sweep together, in lock-step, at 15°/h about every gnomon at once; dials crossing the terminator light up — sunrise, on camera — while the far side goes dark. That planet-wide synchrony is what makes "solar time ± longitude" work, and it is exactly what the flat model's surging, latitude-dependent shadow speeds cannot produce.

        Experiment 6 · the Sun with a pinhole
        Measure the Sun's angular size and noon altitude — cardboard, tape measure, stick

        A pinhole in foil projects a solar image whose diameter is the projection distance ÷ 107.5 — that ratio is the angular size (32′). A vertical stick's shadow at solar noon gives the altitude: alt = atan(stick ÷ shadow). Repeat at different hours and dates.

        Independent variable
        What you change: the time of day and the date — morning vs noon vs just before sunset; equinox vs solstices. Set latitude above to see the predictions for your home.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the Sun's angular diameter and its noon altitude. The sky decides both.

        Hold constant: the same pinhole and screen distance; never look at the Sun directly — project onto paper. The tells, stated in advance: a distant sun keeps the same 32′ disc from sunrise to sunset (±0.005%, far below your pinhole's precision) and its noon altitude follows the almanac column above; a nearby sun must change apparent size by whole factors through the day and can never reach the horizon at all.

        Experiment 6b · who has daylight right now
        Poll one instant across the world — no instrument at all, and the December version cannot be argued with

        This is the cheapest experiment on the page: it needs no equipment, no clear sky and no patience. Pick one instant in UTC. Ask people in half a dozen widely separated places whether the Sun is above their horizon at that instant — a message each, or six public webcams, or six live-streamed city squares. Write down six yes/no answers against one clock reading. Both models predict that set of answers in advance, and they do not predict the same one.

        Independent variable
        What you change: the set of longitudes and latitudes you poll, and the date. Spread the places as widely as you can in longitude; then repeat near a solstice, when the two models diverge most.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: a single bit per location — Sun up, or Sun down — all read at one agreed UTC minute. Not a length, not an angle, not a brightness. Nothing to calibrate and nothing to fudge.

        Hold constant: the instant. Agree a UTC minute in writing beforehand and have everyone answer for that minute, not "when they get round to it"; an hour of drift is 15° of longitude and will smear the boundary you are trying to find. Take the Sun's centre on the horizon as the criterion, and ignore mountains — a valley floor loses several minutes.

        Kit: none. A group chat, or the webcam pages that Antarctic stations, harbours and ski resorts publish for free. This is the one experiment on this page that a reader with no money, no sky and no daylight can run tonight.

        The tells, stated in advance. On a sphere the lit region is exactly half the surface at every instant, and its boundary is a great circle, so your yes/no answers must sort cleanly on either side of one such line and no other. On the standard flat map — a disc with the north pole at its centre — the lit region is a spot cast by a Sun circling above the tropics, so it must be a compact patch, and places on opposite sides of the disc cannot both be lit.

        Then the December version, which is the one that ends it. Between late October and mid-February the Sun never sets anywhere inside the Antarctic Circle. On a globe that region is a cap around one pole. On the flat map it is the entire rim of the disc — so the flat model must light the whole circumference at once, all 360° of it, while leaving the middle of the disc in darkness. There is no position for a spotlight that does that. Ask two Antarctic stations on opposite sides of the continent — say a Ross Sea station and one on the Atlantic side, some 150° of longitude apart[7] — on any January midnight, and the answers decide between the two geometries without a single number being measured.

        The verdict rule, symmetric. The globe fails if your polled answers cannot be separated by any great circle — if two places 180° apart in longitude are both in daylight at the same instant while a place between them is dark, or if any Antarctic station reports a genuine night in January. The flat model fails if the lit set is consistently a hemisphere rather than a patch, and if stations spread right around the Antarctic coast all report continuous daylight at once. Both statements are checkable tonight, and only one of them survives.

        Sources for this tab
        • [1]Paris Observatory — how Rømer and Cassini's Io program revealed the finite speed of light in 1676, and an American Journal of Physics analysis of Rømer's method.
        • [2]University of Virginia lecture, "The Speed of Light" — Rømer's 10-minutes-late prediction of 9 Nov 1676, then Fizeau's toothed wheel (1849) and Foucault's rotating mirror: the terrestrial c this tab feeds back into Io.
        • [3]Royal Society — "Captain Cook and the transit of Venus of 1769": why one absolute distance calibrates the whole solar system whose relative map Kepler had already fixed from angles alone; plus Royal Observatory Greenwich on the transit expeditions and Sky & Telescope's history (Encke's 2.5%-high solution).
        • [4]IAU — the astronomical unit, defined since 2012 as exactly 149,597,870,700 m; background at the JPL Solar System Dynamics FAQ and Paris Observatory.
        • [5]British Sundial Society — How Sundials Work — why the gnomon must parallel the Earth's axis, how the equatorial dial's 15° hour lines become the splayed lines of horizontal dials, and how hour-line angles change with latitude: the dial-maker's craft is applied globe geometry.
        • [6]NOAA Solar Calculator — check every noon altitude, declination and equation-of-time value in this tab for your own coordinates; the calculation details page documents the formulas this tab implements.
        • [7]British Antarctic Survey, Australian Antarctic Program and the United States Antarctic Program — station positions, and the live webcams and daily reports from which the daylight answers in Experiment 6b can be read directly rather than taken on anyone's word. The stations sit at very different longitudes, which is the whole point of asking them at the same instant.
        Further reading
        Not cited above, and no claim on this tab rests on it — listed because it is what you would read next, or because it lets you redo the measurement on data this page did not choose.
        • « Démonstration touchant le mouvement de la lumière trouvé par M. Rœmer », Journal des Sçavans, 7 December 1676, pp. 233–236 — digitised by the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Four pages, in the original French, reporting Rømer's argument to the Académie: the eclipses of Io run late when Earth is receding and early when it is approaching, therefore light takes time. It is the first measurement of a solar-system distance scale that did not depend on the parallax expeditions, and you can read the original rather than an account of it.
        • Edmond Halley, "Methodus singularis quâ Solis Parallaxis sive distantia à Terra…", Philosophical Transactions 29 (1716), 454–464. The proposal that sent the transit expeditions out: observe the transit of Venus from widely separated latitudes, time the contacts, and the difference gives the solar parallax. Halley knew he would be dead before the 1761 transit and wrote it for whoever came after.
        • IMCCE (Observatoire de Paris) and NASA JPL Horizons. Two independent ephemeris services, one French, one American. Any number in this tab can be regenerated in either, from institutions with no stake in this page's argument.
        Dawn & twilight · the light that arrives before the Sun does

        The sky is lit for an hour before sunrise — and on a plane there is nothing above you for the Sun to light

        • left: a cross-section through the observer and the Sun, at true scale
        • the last ray to graze the ground at the terminator, passing overhead at height h
        • everything under that ray is in the planet's own shadow
        • right: the same three ceilings on a plain height axis in kilometres
        Why there is light overhead and none underfoot. Drawn at true scale with no exaggeration at all — none is needed, and the thinness of the lit shell is itself the finding. Note what the picture does not contain: any assumption about how bright the scattering is. The claim is only that a boundary exists and that its height is set by R.

        Long before the Sun clears the horizon the sky is already bright, and long after it has gone the sky stays bright a while longer. That is not the question this tab asks. The question is sharper and much harder for a flat model to answer: why is it bright up there while it is dark down here?

        A lit sky over an unlit ground is an asymmetry, and an asymmetry needs an edge. An edge needs a shadow. A shadow needs a body big enough and round enough to cast one. On a plane the Sun is above the plane at every hour of the day and night, so there is nothing anywhere that can be in shade while the air above it is in sunlight.

        h = R(sec θ − 1) ≈ Rθ²/2
        θ = the Sun's depression below the horizon
        When the Sun is θ below your horizon, the last ray that grazes the Earth's surface passes over your head at a height h. Below h you are in the planet's shadow; above h the air is still in full sunlight and scatters some of it down to you. That single line is the whole of twilight, and it contains R — so twilight is a measurement of the radius, not merely a consequence of it. Put θ = 6°, 12° and 18° into it and out come 35 km, 142 km and 328 km, which is the table further down.

        Three twilights, and why they stop where they stop

        The three stages are defined by the Sun's geometric depression and by nothing else: civil twilight runs from sunset to 6° below, nautical from 6° to 12°, astronomical from 12° to 18°.[1]

        The names record what a person could still do. Through civil twilight you can carry on outdoors without a lamp and the horizon stays crisp. Through nautical twilight the sea horizon is still visible while the brighter stars are out, which is exactly the window in which a sextant sight works and is why sailors named it. By the end of astronomical twilight the sky no longer adds measurable light to a telescope's field.

        Those are human conventions, chosen for human tasks. What is not a convention is the height each one corresponds to. The formula above turns each threshold into a height above your head, and the answers land on the structure of the atmosphere without having been aimed at it. The table computes them; nothing in it is typed in by hand.

        Each twilight threshold, turned into the height of the shadow's ceiling over the observer — computed from h = R(sec θ − 1) with R = 6,371 km
        Stage ends atSun's depression θShadow ceiling h h as a fraction of RWhat is still in sunlight up there
        How much of that is an argument, and how much is a coincidence. Be careful here, because the temptation is to claim more than the geometry gives. The 6/12/18 thresholds were fixed by what people can do, not derived from air density, so the correspondence in the last column is a consistency check, not a derivation. What the geometry does give, with no wiggle room, is the mapping itself: an 18° Sun puts the shadow ceiling at 328 km and a 6° Sun puts it at 35 km, and those follow from R alone. The interesting part is that the point where a human stops being able to see the sky glow lands where the air runs out — and that the same R which fixes the horizon in the dip tab, the star altitudes in the navigation tab and the arrival times in the seismology tab also fixes this.

        What the inverse-square law actually predicts on a plane

        Now the flat model, taken seriously and given its best case. Put a Sun at height H above an infinite plane, let it be as small and as close as you like, and let its light fall off as the inverse square of distance — which is the correct law for a compact source and is the law flat-earth accounts appeal to when they explain sunset as the Sun becoming distant and dim. An observer at ground distance d from the point directly under it is at slant range r = √(H² + d²), and the light lands on the ground obliquely, at an angle whose cosine is H/r.

        E(d) = I·H / (H² + d²)^{3/2}
        ϑ(d) = D / √(H² + d²)
        E is the illuminance on level ground — the quantity a light meter pointed at the sky measures, and the quantity the published twilight measurements report. ϑ is the Sun's apparent diameter, with D its real diameter. Both are elementary and both hold on a plane for any H, any D and any brightness I.

        Divide each by its value at noon, when the observer stands directly under the Sun, and something useful happens: every free parameter cancels. H disappears. D disappears. The Sun's brightness disappears. What is left is a relation between two things you can measure with a phone.

        E(d)/E(0) = (H/r)³ = (ϑ(d)/ϑ(0))³
        On a plane, the ground can only get dark to the exact extent that the Sun gets small. Dim it by a thousand and it must have shrunk tenfold. That is not a claim about any particular flat map, or any particular Sun height, or any particular disc diameter — it is inverse-square geometry with the nuisance parameters divided out, in the same way the reciprocal zenith angles in the elevation tab cancel the two station heights. If you prefer the illuminance measured face-on to the rays rather than on level ground, drop the obliquity factor and the exponent becomes 2 instead of 3. It changes none of what follows.

        So the flat model owes two numbers that must agree, and both have been measured to death. The measured day-to-night ratio of downwelling light is about one hundred million: a recent open-data study spanned it with two spectrometers precisely because no single instrument covers a factor of 108.[2] Full sun is of order 100,000 lux; a clear moonless night sky is of order 0.001 lux.[2][10]

        And the Sun's apparent diameter runs between 31.6′ and 32.7′ over a whole year, a 3% swing caused by the Earth's orbital eccentricity, and is constant to far better than a percent across any one day.[7]

        The flat model's own arithmetic, with the Sun at three heights that have been proposed — all computed, none fitted
        Sun height HDistance d at "midnight"Predicted brightness drop Predicted disc shrinks toMeasured dropShort by a factor of
        The steel-man, and why it eats itself. H is the flat model's free parameter, so tune it in the flat model's favour: pick whatever H makes the night as dark as the night actually is. The answer is H ≈ 43 km on a 20,000 km disc — the Sun would have to be lower than a weather balloon's ceiling. But the relation above is a package deal. Buying a factor of 108 in brightness means buying a factor of 464 in apparent size, so that Sun would cross the sky shrinking from 32′ at noon to 4″ at midnight, from a disc to a star. Nobody has ever recorded that, and a mobile phone with a solar filter rules it out in an afternoon.
        Tune it back the other way, and it eats itself. Push H back up to keep the disc the right size and the night gets bright again: at the usual 5,000 km the model's midnight is one seventieth of noon, about the difference between direct sun and a dull overcast afternoon, not the difference between noon and starlight. There is no H that does both jobs, because the exponent linking them is fixed by geometry.
        • the inverse-square prediction for three Sun heights, out to the rim of the usual flat map
        • the measured night level, eight decades down[2]
        Eight orders of magnitude, and where the flat curves stop. The vertical axis is the light on level ground relative to noon, on a log scale, so each gridline is a factor of ten; the horizontal axis is ground distance.

        The gap is not a discrepancy that better numbers might close. The flat curves flatten out because a source at finite height never gets far away compared with itself, while the measurement falls off a cliff. On a globe there is no curve to draw at all past the terminator — the direct beam is geometrically zero there, and every photon that reaches you has been scattered down out of the sunlit shell above.

        The two models side by side, in motion

        Everything above compares one place at one moment. This panel puts the whole planet under both models at the same instant, because the disagreement is not really about how bright the sky is — it is about the shape of the lit region, and shape is the thing you can check without owning a light meter. On the left, a globe shaded by the Sun's altitude, with the three twilight thresholds drawn as the small circles they actually are. On the right, the same instant on the standard flat map, in two versions.

        The second of those versions is the one that matters, and it is worth being clear about why it is not a straw man. Suppose everything is conceded: forget the inverse square, forget the Sun's height, and assume only that brightness on a plane is some decreasing function of your distance from the point beneath the Sun. We never need to know what that function is. Because it decreases, its contours are circles centred on the subsolar point — for every such function, without exception.

        So a flat Earth is committed to a circular day–night boundary whatever its photometry turns out to be, and the single remaining number, the radius, is then tuned in the flat model's favour: each ring is pinned so that the plane is exactly right at 45° N at that instant. It touches the truth at one latitude, by construction, and misses everywhere else. The dashed teal curve is where sunset is really happening, which is not a claim of this page but the content of the sunrise and sunset tables printed for every city on Earth.

        Moment
        • the real day–night edge at that moment, from published rise and set tables
        • its ticks point into the night side
        • that morning's sunrise at 45° N, where the flat model is made correct
        • that evening's sunset at 45° N, the second calibration point
        One instant, two geometries. The teal curve is not this page's assertion: it is the published rise and set tables, drawn as a line. One calibration pins both amber dots and every ring passes through them, so the plane is exact there by construction — the comparison is everywhere else. The globe's zone boundaries are computed, not traced; its daylight ramp is Lambert's cosine, but the ramp through twilight is interpolated, and schematic, because this page owns no scattering model.

        Watch the ticks reverse. In July the day–night curve hugs the lit region and they face outwards; in December it closes around the pole and they face in, because in December the pole is the part in darkness. That reversal is not a drawing choice — it is what a tilted planet does.

        The two halves do not animate alike, and it is worth knowing which. On the globe the viewpoint is fixed relative to the Sun, so the terminator holds still and the coastlines slide through it. On the flat map the coastlines are held still, in the orientation flat maps are always drawn in, and the lit patch sweeps across them instead. Both show the same rotation; they differ only in what they nail down. The right-hand panel offers two shadings: 1/r² shades the plane by E/E₀ = (H/r)³ with the Sun 5,000 km up, and Fitted instead draws the circular contours that any decreasing law is forced to produce.

        Switch the right-hand panel to 1/r² and an obvious question arises: if the plane never goes dark on this map, then where does it go dark? The formula answers it. Solving E(d)/E(0) = 10−8 for the distance, with the Sun 5,000 km up, puts real night 2,320,800 km from the point beneath it — a hundred and sixteen times the radius of the whole flat map, and six times the distance to the Moon.

        Even a mere thousandfold dimming, which is still a bright overcast afternoon rather than night, does not arrive until 49,700 km, two and a half times the rim. Lowering the Sun does not rescue this: at 1,000 km, about the lowest anyone has proposed, night still needs 464,000 km, twenty-three times the map. The plane is simply too small for its own light to fall off across it, and that is not a defect of one flat map but of the inverse-square law applied to a source hanging a few thousand kilometres above a surface you can walk on.

        The day almost nobody is in the dark. Set the panel to 8 July, 11:15 UTC and look at where the night is. Combining their solar data with a gridded population dataset, timeanddate found that at that moment it is night for just under 80 million people — so roughly 99% of humanity is receiving some sunlight at once, about 83% in full daylight and 16% somewhere in twilight.[11]
        What that number does and does not say. They are careful, and so is this page: around 3% of that total, some 257 million people, are in astronomical twilight, which is not distinguishable from night by eye, so the honest figure for perceptible light is nearer 96%.[11] It is also not unique to one date — it holds on about sixty days around the June solstice, with the daily peak falling between 11:00 and 11:03 UTC.[12] This page ships no population grid and does not recompute those percentages; it quotes them, and they are checkable against the sources.

        Why is that an argument rather than a curiosity? Because the number is a census of who is standing inside the shadow, and the shadow's shape is precisely what the two models disagree about.

        It comes out that high because the middle of the night, on that date at that hour, sits in the emptiest part of the Pacific, while the tilt keeps the whole northern half of the planet — where most of humanity lives — in daylight at the same time. That is not a coincidence anybody arranged; it falls out of a tilted sphere turning once a day, and you can watch it fall out by pressing play.

        Then switch the right-hand panel between its two versions and ask which landmasses each one puts in the dark. They are not the same landmasses, and only one of the two answers agrees with the sunrise and sunset times published for those cities on that date.

        The duration of twilight is the test with no radius in it

        Everything so far has used R. This section does not, and that makes it the counterpart on this tab of the magnetism tab's dip law: a constraint on shape that survives any rescaling. Twilight lasts as long as the Sun takes to travel from the horizon down to 18° below it, and how long that takes depends on the angle at which the Sun's daily circle meets your horizon. At the equator it comes down almost vertically and the whole business is over in a little over an hour. At 50° north it slants, and in June it slants so much that the Sun never gets 18° down at all.

        cos H = (sin h − sin φ sin δ) / (cos φ cos δ)
        h_min = |φ + δ| − 90°
        The first line is the hour angle at which the Sun stands at altitude h, for latitude φ and declination δ; the duration of a stage is the difference of two hour angles divided by 15.041° per hour. The second line is the Sun's altitude at local midnight, and it is the one that decides everything: if h_min never reaches −18°, there is no astronomical night at that place on that date, however long you wait. Notice that neither line contains R, or any distance at all, and an independent implementation of the same formulae is published by a different institution in a different country's service.[9] These are statements about a sphere's shape and its tilt, and they would read the same for a planet twice the size.

        Set h_min = −18° and the condition falls out: astronomical night disappears above latitude 90° − 18° − δ. At the June solstice, with δ = 23.44°, that is 48.6°. Nautical night goes at 54.6° and civil night — the genuine white nights — at 60.6°. Those are three sharp latitudes, predicted from the obliquity of the ecliptic and nothing else, and every one of them can be checked by looking up a published almanac[8] or by going outside in June.

        Paris sits at 48.86°, a fifth of a degree past the first threshold, which is why Paris has no astronomical night for about two months either side of midsummer and Nice, 5° further south, has one every night of the year.

        Length of each twilight stage, computed from latitude and declination alone — sunrise taken at the standard −0°50′ for the centre of the disc
        PlaceLatitudeDate CivilNauticalAstronomicalSun's altitude at midnight
        • three solid curves: minutes from sunset to the end of civil, nautical and astronomical twilight
        • a vertical dashed line in each curve's colour: the latitude past which that stage never ends
        • the same journey to −18° at the equinox, which never blows up
        • each place sits on the deepest stage it still completes; a hollow ring completes none
        Twilight length against latitude, and the three places it becomes infinite. All three curves are at midsummer — June in the north, December in the south — so the axis is latitude without a sign and Ushuaia is plotted at its own midsummer rather than pretended to be northern. The three latitudes are 48.6° for astronomical, 54.6° for nautical, 60.6° for civil.

        A flat model has no counterpart for any of this. Its Sun is above the plane at every instant, it never crosses a horizon, and nothing in an inverse-square falloff produces a latitude past which a stage takes infinitely long in June and eighty minutes in December.

        This is a sign test, not a near miss. The page prefers these wherever it can get them, for the reason set out in the elevation tab: a disagreement of a few percent can always be blamed on the instrument, but a question with a yes and a no cannot. Does astronomical night occur at your latitude in the third week of June? At 48° the answer is yes and at 49° it is no, and the almanac agreed with the calculation for a century before anyone thought to argue about it. The flat model does not give a different answer here. It gives no answer, because it has no quantity whose sign could flip.

        The Earth's shadow is an object, and you can photograph it

        On a clear evening, turn your back on the sunset and look east about ten minutes after the Sun has gone. There is a dark blue-grey band lying along the horizon, with a soft pink band above it, and the boundary between them is straight enough to measure and slightly curved if you take in enough sky. The pink is sunlight reddened by its long passage through the lower atmosphere and back-scattered towards you — it has been called the Belt of Venus for a long time. The dark band under it is the Earth's own shadow, projected onto the air, seen edge-on.[6]

        It behaves exactly as a shadow should. It appears opposite the Sun, centred on the antisolar point to within the accuracy anyone can hold a camera. Its top rises as the Sun sinks, at the Sun's own rate, so that its elevation above the eastern horizon tracks the Sun's depression below the western one. It is wider than the Sun because the Sun is not a point. And it fades out as it climbs, for the plainest of reasons: it is being projected onto air that is thinning as it goes up, so by the time the shadow's edge is 20° high there is nothing left up there to catch it.

        The eastern sky at three moments after sunset. The dark segment is the geometric shadow of the Earth, drawn at the elevation the Sun's depression puts it, with the reddened band immediately above it. This is a schematic: the colours are indicative and the fading is drawn, not computed from a scattering model. What is computed is the height of the boundary in each frame, and that is the whole falsifiable content — an edge exists, it sits opposite the Sun, and its elevation equals the Sun's depression. The flat model predicts no edge at all in the eastern sky, because there is no body between the observer and the Sun to cast one and the Sun is never below the plane.

        Four objections, and what each one costs

        Refraction is real and this page models it everywhere, so before the objections, here is its size: at the horizon it lifts an object by about 34′, a little over half a degree, and that is the reason sunrise is reckoned with the Sun's centre at −0°50′ rather than at zero.

        1. "It is just perspective — the Sun goes too far away to see."

        Perspective moves things towards a vanishing point; it does not switch them off, and it certainly does not switch off the ground while leaving the sky lit. If the Sun were merely far, its light would still be falling on your street at the same fraction of noon as on the air 200 km above your street, because both are essentially the same distance from it. The asymmetry is the whole phenomenon and perspective has nothing to say about it. Perspective also cannot make an edge: the shadow in the eastern sky has a boundary you can put a protractor on.

        2. "The Sun is a spotlight and its beam has a limited reach."

        This is the stronger version, and it is worth taking seriously because it does at least produce a boundary. But it produces the wrong one. A spotlight on a plane illuminates a circle, and the edge of that circle is at a fixed distance from the sub-solar point, so the time your location spends in the fade is set by how fast that edge sweeps past — which is nearly the same everywhere and in every season. The measured twilight lasts 68 minutes at the equator, 107 minutes at Paris in March and never ends at Paris in June. A beam of fixed reach cannot do that. It also cannot put the fade boundary in the sky opposite the Sun rather than in the direction the beam is going.

        3. "Refraction explains it."

        Its size is priced above: about 34′ at the horizon, against the 1,080′ that twilight runs to — thirty times larger, and refraction shrinks rapidly as you move away from the horizon. There is also no free parameter left to spend: the refraction tab prices the flat limit k = 1 at a sustained inversion of +12.9 °C per 100 m, and radiosondes have been failing to find one since 1905.

        4. "The air simply gets dimmer as the light travels further through it."

        Extinction along a long slant path is real too, and it is why the setting Sun is red and dim enough to look at. But extinction is a smooth, monotonic, exponential attenuation with air mass. It gives no threshold, no edge, and no dependence on the direction you look — whereas the observed twilight sky is bright in the west and dark in the east by an amount that tracks a single angle. And extinction cannot produce the latitude thresholds of the previous section, because the air mass along the path is a function of the Sun's altitude, and the whole point of that section is that the Sun's altitude at midnight is fixed by φ and δ in a way no atmospheric effect can touch.

        Experiment 1f · dawn and twilight
        Time first light against the clock, twice a year, from your own doorstep

        This one costs nothing and needs no instrument beyond a phone and a clear horizon. Pick a spot with an open view east, go out well before sunrise on a clear morning near an equinox, and write down the clock time at which you can first make out the horizon line and the time the Sun's upper edge appears. Then do it again within a few days of the June solstice from the same spot. The interval is civil dawn, and the calculator below predicts both lengths from your latitude and the date alone, with no fitting and no free parameter. If you are north of about 48.6°, the more dramatic version is available to you: on the June nights the sky never goes properly dark at all, and the almanac will print a dash where the end of astronomical twilight should be.

        Independent variable
        What you change: the date, and therefore the Sun's declination. Two dates two months apart are enough at mid-latitudes; equinox against solstice is the sharpest pair. Changing your latitude instead works just as well if you are travelling.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the number of minutes between first light and sunrise. A clock and your own eyes. No angles, no instruments, no trust in anyone else's data.

        Hold constant: the site, the direction you face, and the criterion you use for "first light" — pick one and stick to it, because the criterion is worth several minutes and the effect you are after is tens of minutes. Clear sky both times; cloud on one morning and not the other ruins the comparison.
        Kit: a phone. If you want the version with a number in it rather than a judgement call, point the phone's camera east on a tripod, shoot at fixed exposure every thirty seconds, and read the frame brightness afterwards — the curve is the twilight curve and its knee is unmistakable.
        The tell: at 45° north the interval grows by roughly a quarter between March and June; at the equator it barely moves at all; north of 48.6° astronomical night vanishes outright in June. A flat Sun that dims by distance has no mechanism that makes the fade take longer in one month than another at the same place.

        How high the shadow stands — and why it climbs faster than the Sun sinks

        The table above gives the shadow's ceiling over your head, in kilometres. What you actually look at in the east is an angle, and the two are not the same number. Getting from one to the other takes no new physics, only the same formula applied twice. A patch of air lying angular distance ψ from you towards the antisolar point has the Sun that much further below its own horizon, at depression θ + ψ, so it is lit only if it clears its own ceiling: R(sec(θ + ψ) − 1). Follow a line of sight leaving your eye at altitude a, ask where along it that condition is first met, and the trigonometry collapses to one line.

        Sunlit at distance s along a sight line at altitude a, when the Sun is θ below the horizon: s · sin(a − θ) > R (1 − cos θ). Two consequences arrive with no free parameter whatever. First, if a ≤ θ the left-hand side is never positive, however far you look — so the top of the shadow always stands higher than the antisolar point, at every depression, above any atmosphere, on any sphere. It cannot be at or below it. Second, the whole sky goes shadowed once the ceiling rises past the layer that does the scattering, that is at cos θz = 1 / (1 + H/R) — which is the ceiling formula read backwards.

        Only one quantity there has to be supplied from outside: H, the effective top of the scattering layer, which is not a sharp surface — air density falls off smoothly, so the shadow's edge is a gradient rather than a line. Rather than pick a value, the table prints three and lets you see how little the interesting behaviour depends on the choice. What does not depend on it at all is the shape: the shadow rises faster than the Sun sinks, the ratio grows without bound, and the sky is fully shadowed at a depression of a very few degrees.

        Altitude of the top of the dark segment in the east, computed from s · sin(a − θ) = R(1 − cos θ) with R = 6,371 km — three values of the scattering-layer top H, none of them fitted to anything
        Sun's depression θ H = 10 km H = 15 km H = 20 km Rise ratio at H = 15 km
        Depression at which the shadow reaches the zenith and the dark segment covers the sky: . Note what that means for an observer: the angle is the same everywhere on Earth, in every season — but the clock time it takes to get there is not, and runs from about thirteen minutes near the equator to three quarters of an hour at high latitude in spring.
        Experiment 1f-b · time the Earth's own shadow
        Turn your back on the sunset and photograph the east — a phone, a wall to rest it on, twenty minutes

        Ten minutes after sunset there is a dark blue-grey band along the eastern horizon with a pink one above it: the planet's own shadow, cast on its own air, with the Belt of Venus along its top edge.[6] Rest a phone on a wall, frame the eastern horizon with something vertical of known height in shot — a lamp post, a door frame, a distant mast — and shoot one fixed-exposure frame every minute from sunset until the band has climbed out of frame. Afterwards, convert the band's top edge into an angle using the object of known height and its distance. You will have the shadow's altitude against the clock, and the clock converts to the Sun's depression.

        Independent variable
        What you change: the time since sunset, and therefore the Sun's depression θ, which an almanac gives you for your position to the minute.[1] Nothing else moves. If you can repeat it from a very different latitude, or six months later, do — that is where the sharper version lives.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the altitude of the shadow's upper edge, in degrees, frame by frame. One angle per photograph, read off against a foreground object whose height and distance you know.

        Hold constant: the camera position, the focal length and the exposure — an automatic exposure will chase the fading sky and move the very edge you are trying to follow. Pick one criterion for the top edge, the colour boundary rather than the brightness one, and keep it. Face the antisolar azimuth, not simply east: ten minutes after sunset the two differ by several degrees.
        Kit: a phone, a wall, and a foreground object. If you want the angle without trigonometry, hold a ruler at arm's length — a centimetre at 57 cm subtends one degree, near enough for a two-degree effect.
        The tells, stated in advance: the shadow's top is never below the antisolar point, at any moment, which the derivation above gives with no adjustable quantity; it accelerates, the ratio in the last column growing from about 1.1 to beyond 5 within twenty minutes; and the sky is fully shadowed at a depression of three to four and a half degrees — the same angle in Quito and in Reykjavík, though one takes a quarter of the time the other does.

        What this experiment cannot do, said plainly. It does not measure R. The single free quantity H is degenerate with the radius here — a bigger planet with a shallower atmosphere gives a similar curve — so anyone claiming a radius from a sunset photograph is claiming too much, and this page will not. Nor is the top edge sharp: air thins gradually, so two careful observers will disagree by something like half a degree, which is a few kilometres of H. What the experiment does settle is shape, and shape is what the two models disagree about.
        The verdict rule, symmetric. The sphere fails if the shadow's top is ever measured at or below the antisolar point, if it climbs at a constant ratio rather than an accelerating one, or if the depression at which it reaches the zenith turns out to depend on where you stand or on the season. The flat model fails if a boundary it must explain as distance and haze instead behaves as a shadow does: an arc curved about the antisolar point, rising at an accelerating angular rate, closing over the sky at one fixed solar depression that is the same for every observer on the planet while the clock time is not.

        Caveats this page owes you. Four, and the first is the one that matters. The heights in the first table are the geometric ceiling of the shadow; they are not a brightness model. Real twilight brightness involves multiple scattering, ozone absorption in the Chappuis band and aerosol loading, and the classical treatments are Hulburt's and Rozenberg's, not a one-line formula.[3][4][5] Second, the durations here use the mean Sun and a spherical Earth, with sunrise at the conventional −0°50′; published almanacs will differ from them by a minute or two, and a mountain horizon by rather more. Third, the measured 108 day-to-night ratio is downwelling irradiance at one dark rural site, and the same study measures a factor of 100 between that site and a city — the number is a scale, not a constant. Fourth, the anti-twilight figure is a schematic, and its colours are drawn rather than computed. None of the four moves an argument that turns on eight orders of magnitude against fewer than two, and on a stage length that goes to infinity at a latitude you can point to on a map.

        The through-line. The dip tab measures how far the horizon falls below level; this tab measures how far the shadow rises above it, which is the same geometry read upwards instead of downwards, and it arrives at the same R. Then the duration section drops R entirely and constrains the shape on its own, the way the magnetism tab does. And the inverse-square section is the page's method in miniature: take the flat model's own physics, divide out its free parameters until nothing adjustable is left, and see what it is then obliged to predict. Here it is obliged to predict that the night is seventy times darker than the day. Go outside and see whether it is.
