        Azimuth · the bearing that forgets how far away the Sun is

        Point at the Sun. You are pointing at a place on Earth.

        Every other solar panel on this page argues from a time — when the Sun rises, how long twilight lasts, where the shadow falls. This one argues from a direction, and directions are cheaper to measure than times: a stick, its shadow, and a way of finding true north. The claim being tested is not that the Sun is far away, or near, or large, or small. It is that the compass bearing you turn to when you face the Sun is the bearing of a particular place — the place that has the Sun straight overhead at that instant — and that this is true whatever the Sun's distance turns out to be.

        The result the whole tab rests on. The azimuth of any celestial body, measured from true north, is exactly the initial great-circle bearing to its sub-body point: the point on Earth that has the body at the zenith. Not approximately, and with no dependence whatever on how far away the body is. Two lines of proof: the sub-body point, the Earth's centre and the body are collinear, by the definition of the sub-body point. The observer's vertical also passes through the centre. So the vertical plane that contains the observer and the body contains the centre, therefore contains the whole line centre-to-body, therefore contains the sub-body point. Same vertical plane, same azimuth.

        Two consequences are worth stating before anything is drawn, because both of them close doors that would otherwise be argued through. First, the distance cancels completely. This is the kind of quantity rule 5 of this page's own method asks for: the Sun at 150 million kilometres and the Moon at 384,000 obey the same rule, and so would a lamp at 5,000 km. Arguing about the Sun's distance cannot touch the azimuth.

        Second, parallax moves a body along the vertical circle, toward the zenith — it changes the altitude and not the bearing. That is the objection an informed reader will make about the Moon, whose parallax reaches a whole degree, so it is answered here and not in a footnote; the numbers are further down.

        Three formulas, no free parameters

        φ_sub = δ    λ_sub = α − GMST
        The sub-body point, from an almanac and a clock. Its latitude is the body's declination; its longitude is the right ascension minus Greenwich mean sidereal time, which is the same statement as −GHA. The USNO publishes GHA and declination for the Sun, the Moon and the navigational stars for any instant you ask for[2], so this line needs nothing from this page. Both quantities here are geocentric, and that matters for the Moon: the theorem points at the geocentric sub-point, which is why parallax leaves the bearing alone.
        A = atan2( sin Δλ · cos φ₂ ,   cos φ₁ · sin φ₂ − sin φ₁ · cos φ₂ · cos Δλ )
        The sphere's prediction: the initial great-circle bearing from the observer (φ₁, λ₁) to the sub-body point (φ₂, λ₂). Standard spherical trigonometry, the same formula the distances tab uses, with nothing adjustable in it. Feed it a place, an instant and an almanac and it returns one number.
        ρ = 90° − φ    θ = λ    north = toward the centre
        The flat model's prediction, and it needs the map to be named before it can have one at all. “The flat Earth” has no azimuths; a projection does. The one used here is the north-polar azimuthal equidistant map[6] — the standard flat-Earth map, the one Gleason patented in 1892[5], and the same map the distances and seismology tabs already run the flat model on. A point sits at radius 90° − φ from the centre at polar angle λ, and an observer's local north is the direction of the map's centre. That is a complete model: given a place and a sub-solar point it returns a bearing, with no height, no lamp size and no fitted constant anywhere in it.

        A different projection would give different bearings, and that concession has to be made out loud or the tab is fighting a straw man. What it does not buy is an escape, and the reason is the thesis of the whole page rather than of this tab: a projection that repaired the bearings would have to break the distances, which the distances tab measures, or the shadow zone, which the seismology tab measures. The claim is never “no flat map gets this right”; it is that no single flat map gets two of these right at once.

        One instant, seven observatories, two predictions

        The seven places below are Global Seismographic Network stations. Their coordinates are already published[4] and this page already uses them in the seismology tab — no new list, and no place picked to flatter an answer. Three instants are offered, all fixed in advance, and nothing here is adjustable; the play button is there to show there is no favourable moment, not to find one. Every row in the table can be checked without trusting this page, against the USNO's altitude and azimuth table[1] or NOAA's solar calculator[8].

        Where the seven places and the three instants come from

        The three instants are two round solstice-week times and the moment of greatest eclipse on 12 August 2026, published to a tenth of a second[3]. At every one of them the sphere's bearing is the bearing to the sub-solar point exactly, and the flat map's is whatever its geometry forces. The play button runs the clock on from whichever instant you picked, for the same reason the magnetism tab has a latitude slider. Every frame satisfies the theorem on the sphere, and every frame leaves the flat map's lines missing each other. The Moon button does the whole thing again for the Moon, which is the interesting case.

        Instant (UTC)
        • rays arriving from the body, one per station
        • each station's great-circle bearing to the sub-point
        • the direction that station actually looks
        • the terminator, where day meets night
        • a hollow dot cannot see the body; a filled one can
        The globe from the side, rays drawn. The rays are parallel because they are computed from the body's real distance, not drawn that way. A side view shows only the near face, so a station round the limb is missing here; the strip above and the map beside carry all seven.
        Parallel to within how much

        Every ray and sight line in this panel is computed from the body's real distance — about 23,000 Earth radii for the Sun, 60 for the Moon. Across the whole planet the Sun's sight lines close on each other by at most about 18″ (0.005°), far below one pixel. The Moon's close by up to about 2°, and at the tips you can see them converge. Switch bodies and watch: that visible difference is the distance, drawn to scale.

        • the bearing at which the body really is, laid off from each station
        • beyond the rim of the map, where it has no world left to show
        • the error triangle the half-lines leave instead of meeting
        The same instant on the flat map. North-polar azimuthal equidistant, north pole at the centre, in the orientation flat maps are always printed in. Each half-line uses this map's own definition of north — the direction of its centre — at a bearing anyone can check against the USNO. On a correct map they would all run into the body. Press play: the disagreement moves, it does not resolve.

        The picture carries the whole theorem. Rays arriving from the body are parallel, and orthographic projection preserves parallelism exactly — so they are parallel on your screen for the same reason they are parallel in space, not because they were drawn that way. Follow them in. At exactly one point the ray runs straight down the radius, and the dashed line continues it through the centre: ray, sub-point and centre are one line.

        Nobody looks along a curve, and nobody is being asked to. Each coloured arc is where a station's vertical plane meets the ground; the dotted line leaving that station is the look direction inside the same plane. Every dotted line is parallel to every other, because there is one body and one direction in space. What changes from station to station is the local horizon that direction is measured against, and that alone is why one Sun hands every observer a different bearing.

        Bearing to the Sun at the selected instant: what the sphere predicts, what the flat map predicts
        StationSun's altitudeGlobeFlat mapDisagreement

        Read the last column rather than the first four. In the far north the two models very nearly agree — the flat map is least wrong near its own centre, which is exactly where its makers live and exactly where the objection “it works fine” comes from. Go south and the disagreement does not merely grow: it changes sign, and then passes 90°, and at the December instant a station on the Ross Ice Shelf is told to look almost due north for a Sun that is almost due south. That is not a three-per-cent discrepancy anyone can wave at refraction. It is the difference between turning left and turning right.

        The eclipse: a published bearing, and nobody's word for it

        Everything above is this page computing its own answers, which is worth exactly as much as your trust in this page. So here is one row this page did not compute. For the total solar eclipse of 12 August 2026, Fred Espenak publishes the instant of greatest eclipse, the place on Earth it happens, and the Sun's altitude and azimuth there — computed independently, from the JPL DE405 ephemeris[3]. The table below sets that published azimuth beside this page's own, and beside the great-circle bearing to the sub-solar point, which is the quantity the theorem says must equal it.

        Greatest eclipse, 12 August 2026, 17:45:53.3 UT1, at 65° 13.4′ N 25° 13.7′ W
        QuantityPublishedThis pageDifference

        The agreement is not the interesting part — two correct calculations of the same sphere ought to agree. The interesting part is the third row: the bearing to the sub-solar point comes out equal to the azimuth to every decimal the page prints, which is the theorem being obeyed rather than assumed.

        And the eclipse itself is the theorem at its most literal. An eclipse is the moment the Sun's sub-point and the Moon's sub-point nearly coincide; at greatest eclipse these two places are under a hundred kilometres apart on a planet forty thousand kilometres around, which is why one small patch of Iceland has the Moon exactly in front of the Sun. Two bodies, one at 384,000 km and one at 150 million, produce the same bearing from the same spot because their sub-points are in the same place. Distance does not enter.

        One honest note on the arithmetic: this page's own ΔT model gives 75.5 s where the eclipse prediction uses 72.4 s, a three-second disagreement about the Earth's rotation rate that moves the Sun by well under an arcsecond and the Moon by under two.

        The Moon, and why being close does not rescue anything

        The Moon is the one body where a reader can reasonably expect the distance to matter, because its parallax is not a rounding error: seen from the surface rather than from the centre of the Earth, the Moon shifts by up to a degree — twice its own diameter. The shift is radial, along the line from the zenith through the body, so it takes the Moon down the vertical circle it is already on. Altitude changes. Bearing does not. The table puts numbers on both, at the same instant and at the same seven stations.

        The Moon at the selected instant: what parallax does to the altitude, and what it does to the bearing
        StationAltitude shiftBearing shiftBearing to sub-lunar point

        The bearing shifts are arcseconds against a degree of altitude shift, and this page owes you an account of why they are not exactly zero. On a sphere they would be. They are not zero here because the topocentric correction used for the Moon is the standard one[9], which places the observer on an ellipsoid: the local vertical of a geodetic latitude does not quite pass through the centre, missing it by up to about 11.5′ of latitude, and the theorem's one hypothesis fails by exactly that much.

        So the residue in the third column is the Earth's flattening, not the Moon's proximity — which is a strange thing to have to admit on a page that elsewhere declares the ellipsoid out of scope, and it is admitted rather than rounded away.

        Now stop dodging it: parallax as a ruler

        Up to here parallax has been a reason to look away: it is radial, so it slides the Moon along the vertical circle it is already on, so the bearing does not care and this tab may set it aside. All of that is true, and it throws away the best thing in the section. The altitude that parallax shifts is the oldest measurement of the Moon's distance there is. So the same two observations yield two independent results, and they are not in competition: the bearing is the quantity the distance vanishes from, and the difference in altitude is the quantity that is nothing but the distance.

        What parallax measures, and what it does not. Two observers a known distance apart see the Moon in front of different stars. The angle between their two sight lines gives the Moon's distance in Earth radii, and in nothing else. Turning that into kilometres needs R, and R does not come from the sky: it comes from the surveying, distances and horizon-dip tabs, and from every other radius measurement on this page. This is the thesis of the whole page applied to a single body — the measurement constrains d/R, never d on its own.
        sin π = R / d    d / R = 1 / sin π
        The classical form. π is the horizontal parallax: the angle the Earth's radius subtends as seen from the body, which is the same thing as how far the body shifts between being seen overhead and being seen on the horizon. It is published for the Moon every day[2]. One published number, and the distance in Earth radii follows with no other input whatever. The symbol is the astronomer's, not the circle constant: here π is the name of an angle — about 57′ (0.95°) for the Moon — so sin π ≈ 0.0166, and d ≈ 60 R.
        d / R = b / (R · sin θ)
        The two-observer form, which is the one you could actually carry out. b is the part of the line joining the two observers that lies across the direction of the Moon, and θ is the angle between their two sight lines — which is exactly how far the Moon appears to move against the background stars between the two places. Nothing else enters it: no horizon, no height above sea level, no clock beyond agreeing on the instant.
        Measuring the Moon's distance from two of the stations above, at the selected instant
        QuantityAt this instantWhere the number comes from

        Two things in that table are better said out loud than left for a careful reader to catch. The two reconstructions do not agree exactly, and they are not meant to. Part of the gap is fixed and exactly known: horizontal parallax is defined against the Earth's equatorial radius of 6,378.14 km, while the row below it is quoted in mean radii of 6,371 km, so those two lines differ by that ratio — 0.112 per cent — before anything else has happened.

        The rest of the gap moves with the geometry, and it is the flattening again, exactly as in the bearing column further up: it is smallest when the two stations lie squarely across the line of sight, and largest when the baseline is badly foreshortened or the Moon is low in one of the two skies. On a sphere both parts would be zero. Watch it change as the clock runs, because a page that had quietly fitted something would not let you.

        And the same measurement fails on the Sun, which is why the last row is there. Across the whole width of the planet the Sun shifts by some sixteen arcseconds — under a hundredth of the Moon's shift, and far below anything the equipment this experiment asks for could see. That failure is what shows the method is not manufacturing its answer: an instrument that returned a distance for everything you pointed it at would be measuring itself.

        The flat model given its best chance: a lamp at a fixed height above the disc, and the altitudes it would require
        StationLamp 3,000 km up5,000 km up8,000 km upThe Moon, really

        The lamp's height is the flat model's one free parameter here, and rule 2 of this page's method says to spend it in the flat model's favour rather than to caricature it — so the table sweeps it instead of picking one. Choose whichever column comes closest at one station and it is wrong at the next; there is no height, inside that range or outside it, that produces the last column.

        Then notice what happens at the places where the Moon has set. A lamp hanging over a plane is above the horizon from everywhere on that plane, always, at every height — its altitude is the arctangent of a positive number and cannot be anything else. The Moon is below the horizon at several of these places at the same moment. That is not a disagreement of a few degrees to be haggled over: it is a change of sign, and no choice of height touches it.

        Who did this before you

        None of this is a modern measurement, and pretending otherwise would sell it short. Hipparchus, in the second century BC, got the Moon's distance out of a solar eclipse that was total at the Hellespont and about four fifths covered at Alexandria — two places, one instant, one angle. The figure usually reconstructed for him is around 67 Earth radii, with a spread of roughly 62 to 73[10], and the eclipse is most probably the one astronomers label −189, which is 190 BC[11]. Those are reconstructions from later summaries and they differ between scholars, so a range is the only honest form to give them in.

        Ptolemy, three centuries after that, measured the parallax directly, with an instrument built for the purpose, in Book V of the Almagest[12] — a different geometry from the eclipse method, and the two are routinely run together by people retelling the story. His lunar model was also badly wrong about how much the distance varies, implying a swing from about 34 to 64 Earth radii[10] where the truth is about 56 to 64: a useful reminder that having the right order of magnitude is not the same as being right.

        And in 1751 the thing was finally done properly. Lacaille observed the Moon from the Cape of Good Hope while Lalande, nineteen years old and sent in his teacher's place, observed it from Berlin on very nearly the same meridian[13]: two people ten thousand kilometres apart, agreeing on a minute. What the young Lalande then argued about with that teacher, in front of a commission of the Paris Academy, was how much to allow for the Earth not being a perfect sphere — which is the same correction that puts the tenth of a per cent into the table above.

        What could spoil your measurement

        Magnetic north is not north. This is the one that will ruin the experiment if it is not taken seriously, because the error is the same size as the effect: the declination runs to 10–20° across western Europe and much more elsewhere, and it drifts. Either correct it with the official model[7] or, better, avoid the compass entirely — at true solar noon the shadow of a vertical stick is at its shortest and lies exactly along the north–south line, so one observation removes magnetic declination from the problem altogether.

        The clock matters more than it looks. The sub-solar point travels 15° of longitude per hour; an hour of error is an hour of wrong answer, and everything on this tab is stated in UTC for that reason.

        Refraction is almost innocent here, and that is not luck: like parallax, atmospheric refraction lifts a body along its vertical circle, so in a spherically stratified atmosphere it changes the altitude by up to 34′ near the horizon and the azimuth by nothing at all. Only a horizontally structured atmosphere bends a bearing, and by arcminutes.

        And the projection is a choice, restated once more because it is the honest weak point: the numbers in the flat column are the azimuthal equidistant map's numbers, not a proof about every conceivable flat map.

        Experiment 9 · where is the Sun for you?
        A stick, its shadow, and one agreed minute — with a friend far away, if you can

        Stand a stick vertically on level ground. At an agreed UTC minute, mark the shadow. The Sun's azimuth is the shadow's direction plus 180°. Measure that angle from true north — see above for why the compass will not do — with a printed protractor and a piece of string, or by taking a second mark at local solar noon to establish the north–south line first.

        Independent variable
        What you change: your place. The sharp version needs two observers far apart in latitude, ideally one in each hemisphere, at the same UTC minute; the weaker but still decisive version is one observer and the published bearing for their own coordinates.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the Sun's azimuth in degrees from true north. One angle. Not a duration, not a brightness, not a horizon.

        Hold constant: the instant, and the north reference. The tells, stated in advance: north of about 45° N the two models differ by only a few degrees and your protractor may not separate them — say so rather than claiming a win. South of the equator they differ by tens of degrees with opposite signs, and near the Antarctic coast the flat map points the other way round the horizon. Verdict rule. The globe fails if a measured azimuth departs from the great-circle bearing to the published sub-solar point by more than your sighting error, or if three simultaneous bearings do not concur at the point the almanac publishes. The flat map fails if three simultaneous bearings do concur at a single point, when its own geometry requires the error triangle whose size is computed above before you go outside.

        Experiment 9b · the Moon against the stars
        One photograph each, two places, one agreed second — and the sky is the ruler

        Agree an instant, to the second, with someone far away from you in latitude. At that instant each of you photographs the Moon with a star close beside it in the same frame. Then measure how far the Moon sits from that star, in arcminutes, in each photograph, and take the difference. That difference is the parallax. You are deliberately not measuring a height above a horizon: an angle inside a single frame needs no level, no horizon and no calibration, and refraction lifts the Moon and the star beside it by almost the same amount, so most of it cancels instead of having to be modelled.

        Independent variable
        What you change: your place, at a fixed instant. Two observers as far apart in latitude as you can arrange; a few thousand kilometres is already plenty. Without a second observer, the published topocentric position for your own coordinates does the same job rather less convincingly.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: the Moon's angular distance from a nearby star, in arcminutes. One angle inside one photograph. Not an altitude, not a time, not a horizon.

        Hold constant: the instant, to the second, and the reference star. The tells, stated in advance: over a baseline of some ten thousand kilometres the Moon moves by rather more than a degree, which is over twice its own diameter and impossible to miss. The Sun moves by about eighteen arcseconds over the same baseline, which is why this experiment does not work on the Sun — and that failure is part of the result rather than a flaw in it. Verdict rule. The globe fails if the measured shift does not give a d/R consistent with the almanac's to within your uncertainty, or if it comes out different when the baseline is turned to a different orientation. The flat model fails if no single lamp height accounts for both observers' altitudes at once — the table above computes what each height would demand before you go outside — and it fails outright at any place where the Moon is below the horizon while a lamp over a plane must be above it.

Cited here for the date and for nothing else.

The theorem on this tab is, in navigator's language, the statement that the azimuth of a body equals the bearing of its geographical position — a working tool for two centuries before it was an argument about anything.
        Geodetic surveying · how professionals measure a planet

        Surveyors don't assume the curve — their instruments keep finding it

        The correction, and what it would be on a plane. The line of sight is level in both. On a plane the ground stays under it and the staff needs no correction at all; on a globe the ground falls away by d²/2R and every sight does. Curvature is exaggerated.

        Professional surveying is two centuries of procedures that exist only because raw measurements kept disagreeing with flat geometry by exactly the amount a sphere predicts. No knobs to turn here: every number below is a documented case — a wager, a survey, a tunnel, an accelerator — with the source linked at the bottom.

        01 · Levelling: the correction applied a thousand times a day

        A surveyor's level defines a horizontal line of sight — tangent to the level surface at the instrument. But "level" (equal height, equal gravity potential) curves with the planet: the tangent climbs away from the level surface[3] as the square of the distance. Three documented situations, three scales:

        drop = d²/2R ≈ 7.85 cm × d²[km]
        mid-span bulge of a chord: d²/8R
        with refraction (k = 0.13): × 0.87
        Field procedure encodes the first formula twice over: sights are kept short and balanced — equal back-sight and fore-sight — precisely so the curvature term cancels between the two staff readings. A correction that cancels by symmetry is still a correction: on a flat earth the whole ritual would be pointless.
        The Bedford Level wager, 1870 — surveying settles a betRowbotham sighted eight inches above the water, deep in the refraction layer; Wallace raised the line to about 4 m, set a marker mid-way, and won — and the numbers in the table above are his, documented, not computed here
        Flat-earth author Samuel Rowbotham had sighted along the Old Bedford River with a telescope eight inches above the water — deep in the strong-refraction layer — and declared the six-mile stretch flat. When his follower John Hampden staked £500 that no scientist could show curvature there, the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace — a trained surveyor — accepted, raised the sight line to ~4 m to escape the worst refraction, and set a marker mid-way between two end markers at equal height. Through the telescope the middle marker stood clearly proud of the line joining the ends — the ~1.6 m the sphere predicts (1.85 m before refraction) — and the referee, editor of The Field, awarded Wallace the wager[4]. Hampden's response was years of libel and lawsuits, but the measurement has been repeated on that canal ever since, always with the same result. The design — three markers, one sight line — is the cleanest curvature experiment ever devised, and it needs no input from you: the numbers above are the documented ones.

        02 · Triangulation: the angles confess

        Historic mapping was built from chains of triangles between hilltop stations — theodolite angles plus one measured baseline. On a plane, every triangle's angles sum to exactly 180°. On a sphere they sum to more, by the spherical excess, proportional to the triangle's area — and surveyors do not debate this, they budget for it, triangle by triangle. Pick a documented network:

        ε = Area / R²  ⇒  ε″ ≈ Area[km²] / 197
        flat prediction: ε = 0, always
        The benchmark case: Gauss's great triangle Brocken–Hohehagen–Inselsberg (sides 69, 85 and 107 km), measured in his 1820s Hanover survey with an excess of about 14.85″ — dozens of times the resolution of his theodolite. The equal-area triangle drawn below carries the same excess; the area-law and the measurement agree to a hundredth of an arcsecond.
        Documented networks and the excess their theodolites had to swallow
        NetworkSidesExcess ε per triangle

        Snellius' pioneering 1615 chain (Alkmaar–Bergen op Zoom, the first triangulation) carried ~2″ per triangle — below his instruments'[11] precision, which is why the excess only emerged as networks and theodolites grew. From Gauss onward it was measured routinely; the Struve chain's 258 triangles, Britain's 6,500-pillar retriangulation and India's Great Trigonometrical Survey all closed only because ε was carried in the books. No flat arrangement of the same stations can close at all.

        03 · The great arcs: surveying the size — and the flattening

        Measure a long north–south chain of triangles, fix its ends astronomically, and you get the length of one degree of latitude. Do it at different latitudes and you get not just the size of the planet but its shape: a degree is longer near the poles — the signature of the oblate spheroid Newton predicted from rotation.

        The classic arc measurements (simplified) · one degree of meridian: 110.57 km at the equator → 111.69 km at the poles
        YearsArcWhat it established
        1615Snellius, Alkmaar–Bergen op Zoom — the first triangulation chainThe method itself: a degree from 33 triangles and one baseline
        1669–70Picard's Paris arcThe degree Newton used to check universal gravitation
        1736–44Lapland (Maupertuis) & Peru (La Condamine) — Paris Academy expeditionsA polar degree is longer: Earth is flattened, settling Newton vs Cassini[12]
        1792–98Dunkirk–Barcelona (Delambre & Méchain), through revolutionary FranceThe quarter-meridian whose ten-millionth part defined the metre
        1816–55Struve Geodetic Arc — 2,820 km, Hammerfest to the Black Sea, 258 triangles, 10 modern countriesFirst accurate long meridian segment; UNESCO World Heritage since 2005[8]
        1802–71Great Trigonometrical Survey of India (Lambton, then Everest) — ~2,400 km arcSub-continental network; incidentally measured the Himalaya, including Peak XV
        1936–62Retriangulation of Great Britain — 6,500+ concrete trig pillars[9]A national datum (OSGB36); every triangle carrying its excess
        The metre in your ruler is a piece of the curve. The 1791 definition — one ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator meridian[10] through Paris — means the original metre is a surveyed measurement of Earth's curvature, fought for over seven years of triangulation through a revolution. Every later redefinition (prototype bar, krypton wavelength, light-second fraction) was chosen to preserve that length.

        04 · Curvature as an engineering constraint

        When the stakes are measured in billions, nobody gets to "assume" a shape. Three projects that had to build against R:

        Engineering projects where Earth's curvature entered the blueprints
        ProjectScaleThe curvature fact
        Peak XV (Everest), 1852
        Great Trigonometrical Survey        		 stations 160–240 km away Vertical angles from six distant stations, corrected for curvature, refraction (minutes of arc!) and plumb-line deflection, computed by Radhanath Sikdar's team to 29,002 ft — within 0.1% of today's 29,032 ft, without anyone climbing anything
        SLAC linear accelerator, 1962
        Stanford / U.S. DOE        		 3.2 km, dead straight Laser-aligned straight to ~0.5 mm over two miles — while a straight 3.2 km line departs from the level surface by ~20 cm end-to-middle. "Straight" and "level" split apart at accelerator tolerances; the builders had to choose straight, on purpose[5]
        LIGO gravitational-wave detectors, 1990s
        Caltech / MIT / NSF        		 two 4 km straight arms LIGO's own fact sheet: over each 4 km arm "the Earth curves away by nearly a meter", so the slab was earth-moved[2] and precision-poured to keep the laser straight while the level ground fell away; the published alignment paper computed every design height on the WGS-84 ellipsoid — a straight line varies ~1.25 m in ellipsoidal height over the 4 km baseline
        Gotthard Base Tunnel, 1999–2016
        AlpTransit / ETH Zürich        		 57 km through the Alps GPS fixed the portals; gyrotheodolites (north to 0.001°) steered underground; gravity anomalies and deflections of the vertical were corrected explicitly. Final breakthrough error: 8 cm horizontal, 1 cm vertical[6] — impossible arithmetic on any flat model

        And the professional version of this page's first tab: in trigonometric levelling, two stations observe each other's zenith angle simultaneously. On a plane the two angles must sum to exactly 180°; on the sphere they sum to 180° + the arc between the stations — for 30 km, an excess of 16.2′, enormous by theodolite standards, measured in every reciprocal campaign since the 1800s and the standard way refraction itself is calibrated (Gauss's k ≈ 0.13 comes from exactly such data[7] in his Hanover network). The Elevation-angles tab computes this same number from the amateur side.

        05 · A field guide to the methods — written for the skeptical reader

        If you doubt the globe, the best reading list is not debate videos — it is the training manuals. They are not persuasion documents; they are instructions for getting jobs done by people who are liable when heights and boundaries come out wrong, and every one of them contains steps that exist only because of R. Here is the map of where to look. For each method: what the manual instructs, and whether the step accounts for the curvature (builds it in) or outright measures it. The test is always the same — delete the curve from the procedure and the numbers stop closing.

        Professional methods, and exactly where the curve enters — every source is a training or reference document
        MethodWhat the manual instructsAccounts / measures
        Differential levelling,
        balanced sights        		 NOAA Manual NOS NGS 3 (Geodetic Leveling), Figure 3-8, states it verbatim: curvature error c "cancels if sB = sF[1]" — keep back-sight equal to fore-sight and the curve subtracts itself out of every setup Accounts — by designed cancellation, thousands of times per line
        River & valley crossings
        (unbalanced sights)        		 When sights can't be balanced, NGS's supplement to the same manual prescribes an observing routine that corrects "atmospheric refraction, Earth's curvature, pointing and collimation" explicitly — the correction that usually cancels is applied by formula instead Accounts — explicit c&r correction
        Reciprocal zenith angles
        (trigonometric levelling)        		 Two stations observe each other simultaneously; the angle sum exceeds 180° by the arc between them (16.2′ per 30 km) and the leftover scatter calibrates the refraction coefficient k ≈ 0.13 — Gauss did exactly this in Hanover Measures — the excess IS the curvature
        Triangulation adjustment
        (spherical excess)        		 Every large triangle's angles are checked against 180° + Area/R²; Legendre's classical rule — subtract one third of the excess from each measured angle, then solve as a plane triangle — has been the standard workflow since the 1800s Both — measured per triangle, then budgeted out
        Distance reduction:
        "grid vs ground"        		 Every EDM or GNSS distance is multiplied by an elevation factor R/(R+h) — reducing the measurement down to the ellipsoid — and a grid scale factor onto the map projection; open surveying course texts and provincial technical bulletins walk licensure candidates through the arithmetic, with R = 6,371,000 m sitting in the denominator of every job Accounts — R is in the formula on every project
        Map projections &
        State Plane zones        		 Snyder's USGS Map Projections — A Working Manual (PP 1395) is the standard reference: a curved surface cannot be flattened without distortion, so projections manage it and zones are sized to cap the error — the very existence of projection zones is curvature bookkeeping Accounts — the whole discipline exists because of it
        GNSS heights:
        ellipsoid vs geoid        		 Every GPS fix returns height above the WGS-84 ellipsoid; NGS procedure requires applying a geoid model to obtain the orthometric height a level would give — two different "heights" that only both exist on a curved, rotating planet with a gravity field Measures — in every RTK fix, everywhere, daily

        A fair challenge for any flat model: reproduce one row. Write the flat-earth levelling manual in which balancing sight distances buys nothing, the flat reduction formula with no R in it that still matches every EDM baseline, or the flat projection with no distortion to manage — and explain why the actual manuals, written by people with no stake in cosmology, all contain the curve.

        06 · Modern practice, same curve

        Today the National Geodetic Survey and its counterparts maintain the reference frame with GNSS networks, and heights still come from geodetic levelling tied to the geoid — the level surface itself. Datums are defined on an ellipsoid because centimetre-level measurements leave no other option; "ellipsoid height" vs "orthometric height" is a distinction that only exists on a curved, rotating planet with a gravity field. Surveyors are, in a precise sense, the profession that measures the flat-earth question every working day — and files the answer as routine paperwork.

        Experiment 7 · levelling across water
        Rent an auto level, find a calm lake or canal, and re-run Wallace yourself

        Set a levelled instrument at the shore, sight a graduated staff (or a marked board on a boat) at increasing distances across the water. Water is the level surface; your sightline is the tangent. Record the reading vs distance — or use Wallace's stronger design: three equal-height markers and one sight line.

        Independent variable
        What you change: the sight distance d — 200 m, 500 m, 1 km, 2 km, as far as optics allow.
        Dependent variable
        What you measure: how far the staff reading sits above the instrument's height — the drop of the level surface below the tangent line (or the mid-marker's rise above the end-to-end line).

        Hold constant: instrument height (well above the water — Rowbotham's 8-inch sight line is the canonical example of measuring refraction and calling it flatness), calm conditions, morning hours; read both directions if possible — reciprocal sights cancel refraction from the height difference, though not from the angle sum.
        The tell: the drop must grow as d² with coefficient ~6.8 cm/km² (refracted). A flat surface predicts zero at every distance, and no weather can manufacture a stable, season-independent d² law with precisely the coefficient 1/2R.

        The laser, considered as an instrument

        A laser fails on beam width before it fails on refraction, and that part is arithmetic. A hand-held pointer diverges by one to two milliradians; a surveyor's rotary laser, an order of magnitude better. At divergence θ the beam is θd wide at range d, so the reading is uncertain by half of that either way — while the quantity being looked for, the drop of the surface, is d²/2R. Divide one by the other and the ratio is d / θR: it does not depend on the beam's width at the muzzle, only on how far you go. With a 1 mrad pointer the drop does not even equal the beam's half-width until 6.4 km, and at 10 km, where the drop is 7.9 m, the beam is still 10 m across. The instrument's own blur is the size of the effect.

        And the spreading is not symmetric in its consequences. A beam aimed level from 1.5 m above water is 5 m tall at 5 km, so its lower edge is skimming the surface — the one layer where the temperature gradient is steepest and where ducting occurs. Whatever the centre of the beam does, some ray in it always takes the most strongly bent path available, and that is the ray that arrives. The Brighton test over the sea is the documented case: its own operators logged air half a degree cooler at 0.5 m than at 1.0 m and still read the beam's arrival as geometry[13].

        The remedy is not a better laser. The question these tests ask — does a horizontal line of sight stay the same height above the surface — needs no beam at all. Three marks at equal height above still water answer it, which is Wallace's 1870 design, and Rainy Lake answered it again in 2018 with targets on ice and a licensed surveyor's differential GPS. A target has no divergence, sits where it is put, and can be measured by someone else afterwards. Adding a laser adds two failure modes and no information[14].
        The correction is not a historical curiosity; it is a checkbox in the firmware of every instrument sold. Sokkia, Topcon, Leica, Nikon and Trimble all ship total stations whose manuals carry the same pair of terms and the same switch to enable them: subtract d²/2R for the curve, add back k·d²/2R for refraction[15]. A surveyor turning that setting on is not endorsing a cosmology. They are stopping their instrument from being wrong by 8 cm at a kilometre, which is the whole of the argument on this page, sold as a menu item.

        And the reciprocal-angle measurement has been made at ninety kilometres, by a federal agency, on purpose. In 1977 a crew surveyed seven lines radiating from station BALDY on Mount Livermore in Texas — the shortest 70 km, the longest 92.8 km — measuring distances by EDM while observing simultaneous reciprocal zenith distances at both ends, day and night. The sum of a reciprocal pair is a direct measure of how far the two plumb lines have splayed apart, which is γ and nothing else. The scheme is published as a NOAA technical report; the crew's own account of the fortnight, helicopter and whisky included, was put online by the surveyor Jesse Kozlowski[16]. It is the same quantity the celestial-theodolite tab reads from a star, measured forty years earlier with a Wild T-3.

        A worked case, with both ends read at the same instant. In 1977 the National Geodetic Survey observed seven lines around the McDonald Observatory in Texas, 32 to 93 km long, with the two theodolites reading simultaneously and the line of sight everywhere more than 30 m above the ground — out of the layer where refraction goes wild. On a plane the two verticals are parallel, so the two zenith angles must sum to exactly 180°, with no parameter to adjust. They do not. The sum exceeds 180° in every line, by 16′ at 32 km and by 45′ at 93 km, and it grows with distance.

        The published zenith angles are the only input; every column after the second is recomputed here and agrees to the third decimal with Walter Bislin's independent evaluation[17]. Globe k is the refraction coefficient needed to explain the excess if the verticals diverge by s/R; plane k is what it takes if they do not, and the last column is the temperature gradient that plane k demands.
        Read the last two columns together. On a globe the excess is the divergence of the verticals minus a small refraction term, and solving for that term gives k between 0.084 and 0.115 — ordinary standard refraction, the same value the refraction tab derives from a lapse rate of a few degrees per kilometre. On a plane the whole excess has to be refraction, and refraction of the wrong sign: light bending upward, k ≈ −0.89, which needs air that gets denser with height. The temperature gradient required is about −205 °C per kilometre. Starting from 15 °C at the ground, that reaches absolute zero 1.4 km up, and it would have to hold at every altitude and over every one of the seven lines at once.

        Every reciprocal pair returns a radius, so ask all of them at once. The relation needs no extra assumption: ζ₁ + ζ₂ − 180° = (1 − k)·d/R. Divide the distance by the excess and you have the apparent radius, the one an instrument reads before any correction; multiply by 1 − k and you have the geometric one. Thirty-two pairs are on file here — the seven NGS lines above and twenty-five from the transcontinental triangulation of 1900, spanning 18 to 157 km[18]. A plane predicts no radius at all: it needs the sum to be 180° exactly, which puts R at infinity.

        The same thirty-two pairs, read twice. Uncorrected they cluster near 7,150 km, about 12 % high — and that excess is not noise, it is refraction: R/(1 − k) is the effective radius the refraction tab derives from a temperature gradient, arrived at here from theodolites instead. Apply the page's one standard coefficient and the median lands within a few per cent of 6,371 km. Neither box goes anywhere near infinity, which is the only value a plane allows.

The modern answer to “your telescope was miscalibrated”.
        • Suez Canal Authority — canal characteristics — the lock-free length routinely cited as proof of a flat sea. It is the opposite: a canal is dug to a level, and a level surface is an equipotential, not a plane. A straight chord between the ends would run hundreds of metres below the water at the midpoint.

The French equivalents of the NOAA and Ordnance Survey references above: a national horizontal datum computed on an ellipsoid, and a national height system referred to a geoid. For a French reader, the nearest place to check that their own country's survey works the way this tab says surveys work.
        • NOAA NGS — CORS data and products. Continuously operating reference stations, with the raw observation files public. The modern successor to the triangulation networks in the table above, and still solving the same geometry.
        Celestial theodolite · someone else's experiment, taken seriously

        They swapped the theodolite for a clock. That part works.

        The instant that makes the measurement. The observer, the crest and the star lie on one straight line, so the star's altitude at that second is also the elevation angle of the crest. Nothing is measured with an instrument: the clock says when, and an almanac turns the when into an angle. The two angles marked at the ends of that one line are what the method turns on — on a plane they are equal. Elevation enlarged.

        A flat-earth project called the Celestial Theodolite films a star being occulted by a mountain. The occultation puts the observer, the crest and the star on one straight line, and the claim is that on a plane, where every horizontal is parallel to every other, that one line must make the same angle at both ends. The clock supplies the angle: a star's altitude at a stated second is known to arcseconds. The published target list runs from 8.8 to 130.7 km and pays a bounty for recordings[1]; the method is argued in a recorded debate[2] and, as of the last check, in no methodology paper[3].

        The idea is a good one, and this page has a rule about saying so. Every reciprocal-angle test here levels an instrument with a bubble, and a bubble is gravity — the very thing under dispute. A star has no bubble. At 45° a star setting due west drops 10.6″ every second, so a GPS-synchronised phone reads an angle to better than 0.2′. That is an order of magnitude finer than the difference between the two models over these distances. The timing is not the weak part of this experiment.

        1 · What the clock buys

        dα/dt = 15.041″/s × cos φ × sin A
        How fast a star loses altitude. φ is your latitude, A is the star's azimuth counted from north, and the rate is fastest due east and due west and zero due north and due south. The sidereal rate 15.041° per hour is 15.041 arcseconds per second of clock[5], which is the coincidence that makes this method cheap: one second of clock error is a tenth of the effect at the shortest range on that list, and under a hundredth of it at the longest.
        Seconds of clock worth one arcminute of altitude. Read it as the timing precision you need: anywhere below about 60° of latitude, and on a star setting anywhere near west, a clock good to one second is already ten times better than the angle in dispute.

        2 · What the two models predict

        Take the two ends of that one line: the observer, and the crest the star is grazing. Ask each of them for the star's altitude at the same second. On a plane the two horizontals are parallel, so the answer is the same at both ends and the difference is 0.000°, with no free parameter at all. On a globe the two local verticals are not parallel — they diverge by the central angle γ — so the same straight line makes two different angles, and the difference is γ. This is the reciprocal-angle test of the surveying tab, arrived at from the other direction — and the same quantity was observed over lines of 70 to 93 km by a federal survey crew in 1977, though the report is a scan and its readings could not be recovered here[9], and it is the strongest kind of comparison on this page: a prediction of exactly zero against one that grows with distance.

        θ₂ − θ₁ = 0 (plane, exactly)
        θ₂ − θ₁ = γ = s / R (globe)
        θ₁ is the star's altitude above the observer's horizontal, θ₂ its altitude above the crest's horizontal at the same instant, s the distance between them and R the radius. Neither height appears: the two heights cancel out of the difference, which is what makes this worth measuring. With refraction the globe's figure becomes γ(1 − k)[7]; the plane's stays exactly zero, because a plane has nothing to correct.
        Distances are the ones published on the project's target list[1]; γ is computed here, and the last column says how many seconds of star motion that angle is worth at latitude 45° due west. At 50.8 km γ is 27.4′ — the same 0°27′ the project's spreadsheet prints as the globe's slant, so this is not a disputed number. There is no measured column because no recording has been checked on this page, and a column headed measured stays empty until it can be filled from something published.
        How the clock column is worked outThree lines of arithmetic, so the table above can be recomputed by hand for any peak and any latitude

        Take γ from the column beside it, in arcminutes, and multiply by 60 to get arcseconds. Divide by the rate at which the star is losing altitude, 15.041 cos φ sin A arcseconds per second of clock — 10.635 at latitude 45° on a star setting due west, which is what the column assumes. The result is how much clock time that angle is worth: the size of the timing error that would be needed to fake it. Nothing else enters, and in particular no height, since the heights cancel out of a difference between two vantages.

        3 · Where the execution decides the result

        The star is occulted by the skyline, not by the summit. It comes down at an angle and vanishes wherever its path crosses the silhouette, which is a point on the ridge with its own height and its own distance. The instructions say to aim for the summit where possible and to send daytime reference photographs[1], so this is a worry the method states itself, not an outside objection. It is worth a number: at 50 km, getting the crest height wrong by 30 m moves the angle by 2.1′, about a thirteenth of the 27′ at stake there — not fatal, but it is the reason the crest has to be identified before the arithmetic starts rather than after.

        The refraction correction is switched off, and that is presented as the answer to refraction. The method's own diagrams specify Stellarium with the refraction correction function off at both vantages[2]. But a checkbox in a program does not reach the air. Turning the correction off does not remove the bending; it removes it from the number, and leaves the observation uncorrected rather than unaffected. At the altitude in the worked case, 2°31′, astronomical refraction is 15.1′[6] — which is the 15 arcminutes printed in the same spreadsheet, so the size of the thing being switched off is not in dispute either.

        A switch with two positions and two places to apply it is a free parameter. Off at both ends, off at one, on at one: those are four settings, and they move the answer by up to 15′ against a disagreement of 27′. This page allows itself exactly one refraction coefficient, announced in advance, applied to the globe only, with the uncorrected value printed beside the corrected one — and the reason for that rule is visible here. Whichever setting is chosen, it has to be chosen before the two angles are compared, and stated.

        And refraction lifts a distant object; it does not lower it. A ray through the lower atmosphere bends downward, toward the surface, so a summit is seen higher than bare geometry puts it and less of it is hidden — that is exactly what R_eff = R/(1 − k) means, an effective radius larger than the real one, curvature partly cancelled[7]. Any argument that reads the refraction literature as showing that summits sit lower has the sign backwards, and it matters: with the sign the right way round, refraction is a term that helps the flat model's numbers look closer, not a defect of the globe.

        And the second vantage is often not there at all. The call for recordings asks for a single video from a single place[1]. With one end only, there is no pair of angles to difference, and the zero the plane predicts has nothing to be tested against: what remains is one measured altitude compared with a number the same software computed, which is where the next section starts.

        4 · The simplest objection, and it is built from the method's own instrument

        Figure 1 — the rule. One line of sight, three stations lying on it. On a plane every horizontal is parallel to every other, so the one line makes the same angle a at each of them.
        Figure 2 — the same rule, one direction later. Same construction, one change: the line of sight is horizontal. That is the fixed point of the sky as an observer on the equator sees it, on the horizon, at 0°.
        The method carries an angle from one station to the next, and figure 1 is that rule. So carry it — and pick the direction whose angle is already known somewhere: the fixed point of the sky, which an observer on the equator sees at 0°. A direction horizontal at one station is horizontal at the next, because the horizontals are parallel. Apply it again and again — figure 2 — and the fixed point sits at 0° everywhere on Earth. From Paris it is at 48.9°, half way up, and Polaris marks it to 0.6°. No instrument, no second observer, no clock, no software; and the 2,930′ to explain is 86 times the biggest nuisance term the horizon has to offer.
        The two ways out, and there is no third: the instrument that supplies the measured angle assumes the very thing the conclusion has to deny.
        If they keepThen they lose
        The distant sky of the ephemeris software — stars far enough away that their rays arrive parallel, which is what lets an altitude be tabulated at all. The premise that horizontals are parallel, refuted by any observation of the pole from a mid-latitude.
        A near sky — a dome a few thousand kilometres up, whose rays are not parallel, so the same direction can make different angles in different places. The software, which computes altitudes on a globe with the stars at infinity. Without it there is no measured angle at all, and the method has nothing left to read.
        What this objection does not do. It does not show that any recording is wrong, or that a timing is sloppy. It shows that the number the method calls the measured angle is defined by the globe, so a result cannot be read as evidence for a plane until someone publishes a flat star ephemeris — a dome height and a ground track per star — and recomputes the same occultations in it. That would be a real test, and this page would have to take it seriously. Nobody has published one.

        5 · Which model fits the published readings

        One number is measured: the second at which the star is cut by the crest. Everything else is computed. From that second an almanac gives the star's altitude; from the published coordinates, trigonometry gives the crest's elevation angle — a different one for each model. Subtract, and the leftover is the residual. This answers the obvious worry that the comparison must be circular: the star's altitude comes from the clock and does not know which model you hold, while the two crest angles differ by s/2R, which is 35′ at 131 km. The star altitude cannot sit on both.

        Δ = θ_star(T) − θ_crest
        θ_flat = arctan((H − h) / s)
        θ_globe = arctan((H − h) / s) − s / 2R
        θ_flat − θ_globe = s / 2R = γ / 2
        Why the half, when section 2 used the whole γ. The chord joining observer and crest makes an angle γ/2 with the local horizontal at each end — that is the angle between a chord and the tangent. One end taken alone therefore sees half the central angle, and the pair sees all of it: γ/2 separates the two models at one vantage, γ separates the two vantages along one line. The calculator prints both under those names, Central Angle (γ) and θGeo,Terrestrial,Drop (γ/2), in a ratio of exactly two[8]. H and h are the crest and observer heights, s the ground distance, R the radius, T the occultation second; θ_star(T) is the almanac's altitude, geometric when the software's refraction correction is off and apparent when it is on, and the crest angle must be taken the same way.
        One worked case from the project's published calculator, the North Peak sheet[8]. The heights, the distance and the four star altitudes are read from it; every angle below them is recomputed here and agrees with its cells to the arcsecond. The last three rows are the two-vantage test of section 2, run on those numbers.
          The same case asked four ways: each model, with and without the almanac's refraction correction, and in each the crest angle reduced the same way as the star altitude. The bars are absolute residuals, so shorter is better, and the arithmetic is entirely from the sheet — only the subtraction is done here.
          What the dataset returns. Two questions can be put to it. The first compares the crest angle, worked out from maps and heights, against the almanac's star altitude — and that is the one that carries weight, because only one of its two terms comes from the software. The second is the two-vantage test the method itself advertises, where the plane predicts exactly zero. The figures below run both over every case, and the table under them gives the numbers. The caveat travels with the result: those star altitudes are Stellarium's, computed on a globe, so the second question is close to a check on the transcription rather than a measurement.
          Why the sheet reports the plane as the closer of the two, and it is worth following carefully. The comparison it prints puts the star's altitude at the crest beside the flat crest angle seen from the observer — two different vantages. The gap comes out small, and on the North Peak case it is the +13′35″ the sheet shows. But look at what that subtraction contains: it is the plane's residual at a single vantage, −56.5′, plus the measured difference between the two vantages, +70.1′. That second term is γ — the quantity the flat model says is exactly zero. The plane only comes close because it is handed the globe's own curvature, measured, as a credit. Hold the flat premise honestly — the star at the same altitude from both ends — and the flat residual is its worst score of the four, not its best.
          • 1 — lowest value within reach
          • 2 — first quartile
          • 3 — the median
          • 4 — the mean
          • 5 — third quartile
          • 6 — highest value within reach
          • 7 — a case beyond it
          Both studies over every case on file: the one-vantage residual at the top, the two-vantage residual below, each split between the models and each with refraction applied at both ends. The dots beyond the whiskers matter — they are the cases where both models miss together, which is the signature of a misidentified crest rather than of a curved or a flat Earth.

          The same four series as numbers. Residuals are absolute, so smaller is closer to what was measured, and the median is the column to read first — one badly identified crest moves a mean and leaves a median alone.

          Which rows are in: every row of the data_table sheet that carries the seven numbers, less four kinds set aside before the residuals were looked at — rows the sheet itself labels Test, rows where the occulted body is the Moon, the four rows whose target is an aircraft, and one row whose apparent altitude sits below its true altitude, which cannot happen. Nothing else is dropped. In particular the cases where both models miss together stay in: at 1 and 7 km the two predictions are indistinguishable, so a joint miss is a misidentified crest and not a verdict on either model. Removing them would flatter both distributions at once. Including the four aircraft rows would not change the direction either — the globe wins all four, and by more.

          The short version. Of the four ways of putting the question to the dataset, the globe with refraction applied at both ends sits closest to the recorded second, and the gap to the next best is not marginal. No arrangement of the flat model gets nearer. That is worth stating plainly — and worth stating alongside the limit that has followed this section from the start: the star altitudes come from software that computes on a globe, so this is the method's arithmetic checked against itself, not an independent measurement. The independent version is old: Canigou has been photographed from Allauch, 263 km off, cut out against the setting Sun since 1808, and the hidden-height tab shows what each model puts on the disc there — a black mass taller than the Sun, or a notch an eighth of its width.

          6 · The radius, recovered from the same data

          Every case can be run backwards. Instead of asking whether a radius of 6,371 km fits, solve for the radius each observation implies and see where they land. This is the page's unifying claim put to the other side's own numbers: one R has to satisfy everything, and here it is being asked to emerge from a flat-earth dataset. Only cases beyond 20 km are used, and the threshold is geometric rather than chosen after the fact: below it the two models differ by under 5′, the denominator is the size of the crest error, and the division returns noise or a negative radius.

          R_γ = s / (θ_crest − θ_obs)
          R_raw = s / 2(G − θ_obs)
          R_red = (1 − k) s / 2(G − θ_obs,app)
          Every symbol is a row of the case table above. s is ground distance s; Δh is the difference of the two heights on the crest and observer heights row; G is crest angle, plane — arctan(Δh/s), the only quantity here that comes from maps rather than from software. θ_obs is star altitude at the observer, geometric and θ_obs,app the apparent row beneath it; θ_crest is star altitude at the crest. Angles go in radians, so R comes out in the units of s. k is the terrestrial refraction coefficient implied by the sheet, 0.148 — that correction is written s/1,500,000 in degrees[8], which is that k and not the 0.13 the rest of this page uses. The three lines produce the three rows of the table below, in the same order.

          Three reductions, three answers. Same box plot as before — box between the quartiles, bar the median, whiskers to 1.5 interquartile ranges, dots past them — with the accepted radius drawn as a vertical line so the deviation is the distance to it.
          The same three as numbers, with the median's departure from 6,371 km in the last column.
          Read the three lines in order, because only the third one means anything. The first solves R from γ, and γ is the difference between two altitudes the software computed on a globe of 6,371 km — it lands on 6,371 by construction, and counts only as a check that the numbers were transcribed correctly. The second uses the crest angle from maps and heights, which is genuinely independent of the software, but pairs it with a geometric star altitude while the occultation happened in the apparent direction; that mismatch is the method's default setting, and it returns a radius near 3,000 km — not a plane and not the Earth, but a globe of the wrong size. The third fixes the mismatch and nothing else. It is the one to argue with.

          7 · What this page is doing about it

          Criticising somebody else's observation is cheap unless you are willing to make one. The observation tab of this page is an attempt at the same experiment, pre-registered here before the fact, and it changes three things. The Sun stands in for the star, so the frame carries its own angular scale — the disc is 32.4′ wide and the ridge is read against it — and no software has to convert a time into an angle. There are two ridges, not one: a near crest at 16 km where the two models barely differ, and a far one at 54 km where they differ in sign, so the near ridge is a control on the method rather than a second result. And the prediction sits at 0° — eye level — which is the one angle you can check without knowing where level is: the far ridge is either above the Sun's centre or below it, and the photograph says which.

          The shot can be placed on these axes before it is taken, and that is worth doing because it uses a different instrument: a solar disc as the ruler, no clock, no star altitude read out of software. Beyond 20 km the plane's miss tracks (1 − k)s/2R — the curvature term itself, not a fitted line — with a correlation of 0.97, while the globe's misses stay flat with no trend at all. So the two boxes below are not just a summary: they are a prediction. The 24 November geometry, 208 m of height over 54.1 km, says where one more point has to fall on each of them, and arithmetic alone fixes it

          The same two boxes as section 6, restricted to the 28 cases beyond 20 km, with the 24 November shot marked on each. The mark on the orange box is the 12.4′ the plane will have to be out by; the mark on the teal box is the zero the globe will have to show. If the plane is right instead, the two marks swap places — that is the whole prediction, and the photograph puts the point on one row or the other.
          What a dense solar filter will show, minute by minute, from the viewpoint on 24 November — the disc, and the terrain only where it cuts into it, at true angular scale. The blue band is the extra ridge the plane requires; the black is the globe's silhouette. The profile is sampled every 0.1° of azimuth, which is the resolution of the terrain read and not a smoothing, so the facets are the data. Each frame is centred on the disc: it is the ridge that climbs through it.
          Stated before the shot, which is the whole point. Le Grand Mourre, 54.1 km away and 208 m taller than the viewpoint, must sit 13.2′ above eye level on a plane, 1.4′ below on a sphere with straight rays, and 0.5′ above with k = 0.13. The spread is 12.7′, 39 % of the solar disc, and the Sun crosses that window on 24 November 2026 between 16:54:57 and 16:59:04 CET. Those numbers are computed, not observed: at the time of writing no photograph exists, and if it comes out against the globe this tab will say so — a verdict rule announced in advance binds whoever announced it.

          Experiment 11 · time a star onto a ridge

          Independent variable: the distance to the peak — the same summit recorded from several places, or several peaks at different ranges. Dependent: the second at which the star is cut by the skyline. Held constant: one clock discipline (GPS-synchronised), one star, the summit itself as the target rather than a shoulder. Kit: a camera that records a timestamp, published coordinates for both ends, and a published altitude for the star[4].

          Verdict rule, announced in advance and symmetric. The globe fails if the two ends of the same line of sight return the same altitude — difference zero within your error, repeatably, at 9 km and at 131 km alike. The flat model fails if the difference grows in proportion to s, returning one radius near 6,371 km from peaks at three different ranges at once. Either way the refraction setting is stated before the recording and applied the same way at both ends, because a switch worth 15′ cannot be chosen after seeing a 27′ disagreement.

          Deliberately left out: any claim about what the recordings show, since none has been checked here; the ellipsoid, which is orders of magnitude below the effect; and terrain models, since the argument is about the angle to a named point, not about a silhouette.
