          GPS · the arithmetic inside every fix

          Your phone solves a globe equation several times a second

          • each satellite's measured range is a full sphere of possible positions, drawn as a wireframe shell with its far half faded
          • the Earth is the small solid globe sitting inside all three
          • where two shells cut each other: a violet circle
          • the point on the surface where all three circles meet: you
          Three range spheres, drawn at true scale. Drag to orbit: the handshake holds from every angle.

          GPS does not measure position — it measures time. A receiver listens to at least four satellites, notes how long each signal took to arrive, multiplies by the speed of light, and solves four equations for four unknowns: where you are (x, y, z) and what time it really is. Every symbol in that math is globe-shaped: the satellite positions are broadcast as coordinates on a rotating ellipsoid, the orbits repeat with the stars rather than the sun, and the clocks are built fast-or-slow on purpose to survive curved spacetime above a round planet.

          The equation your phone actually solves

          ρᵢ = | x − sᵢ(t) | + c·δt
          four unknowns (x, y, z, δt) ⇒ four satellites
          1 μs of clock error = 300 m of position error
          The satellite positions sᵢ(t) come from the broadcast ephemeris — orbital elements[4] the receiver evaluates in Earth-centred WGS-84 coordinates, the same ellipsoid the surveying tab runs on. Note what the receiver does not carry: an accurate clock. The fourth satellite buys the time δt, which is why a $10 receiver chip can use atomic-clock timing. The solution point where the four ranges close exists because the geometry is what the ephemeris says it is; feed the same signals into any other geometry and the ranges simply fail to meet.
          ρᵢ = √((x−xᵢ)² + (y−yᵢ)² + (z−zᵢ)²) + c·δt ,   i = 1…4
          Written out, each measurement says: you lie on a sphere of radius rᵢ = ρᵢ − c·δt centred on satellite i. One sphere pins you to a surface; two intersect in a circle; three meet in exactly two points — and the second point lands thousands of kilometres out in space, so it is rejected (or resolved automatically once the fourth satellite fixes δt). The receiver solves this by Newton iteration in milliseconds; the model below draws it.

          The three circles are not independent. They all pass through the same two points: you, on the surface, and a mirror point in deep space on the far side of the satellite plane. That second point is rejected as a receiver location, and eliminated outright once the fourth satellite fixes δt. There is no third place the ranges could put you.

          The constellation, to scale. 24 baseline satellites in six orbital planes[1] inclined 55°, at 4.17 Earth radii from the centre (20,200 km up), each circling twice a day. From any point on the sphere, 8–12 are above your horizon at once — highlighted, with sight lines — and the set constantly changes as satellites rise and set, exactly as the satellite-status screen of any phone GPS app shows. Drag to orbit; the count updates live as the constellation wheels.
          Why four satellites. With a perfect clock, three ranges (solid) intersect at your position. A cheap receiver's clock is off by some unknown δt, inflating every measured range by the same c·δt (dashed) — the circles miss. Solving for δt alongside position shrinks them back until they close: the fix and the time fall out together. This closure is a strict geometric test, passed millions of times a second, everywhere on Earth, only by the broadcast globe geometry.
          T = 2π√(a³ / GM) = 2π√(26,560³ / 398,600) s = 11 h 58 min
          A bonus equation with nowhere to hide: Kepler's third law, with the broadcast semi-major axis a = 26,560 km and the Earth's measured gravitational parameter GM, reproduces the broadcast orbital period to the minute[3]. The constellation's timetable is the equation of motion around a spherical mass — there is no version of this arithmetic over a plane.

          Three globe fingerprints inside the signal

          How long a satellite can stay up, exactly. A satellite at a = 26,560 km is above a true horizon while the angle at the Earth's centre between it and you is less than arccos(R/a) = 76.12°. That is 152.2° of an 11 h 58 min orbit, so no GPS satellite is ever visible for more than 5 h 04 min — and above the 5° elevation mask most receivers apply, no more than 4 h 44 min. One radius, one orbit, nothing fitted. Fixed emitters on a plane have no such ceiling: once up, they never set.

          ① The sidereal repeat. The orbital period is 11 h 58 min — half a[2] sidereal day, not half a solar day. Each satellite's ground track repeats not every 24 hours but every 23 h 56 min: the constellation keeps time with the stars, and the ground slides 4 minutes eastward beneath it daily. That 4-minute slip is the rotation of the Earth, written into the almanac your phone downloads.

          ② The relativity ledger. Orbital speed (3.9 km/s)[3] makes the satellite clocks run slow by ~7 μs/day; sitting higher in Earth's gravity well makes them run fast by ~45 μs/day. Net: +38 μs/day[5], which at 300 m/μs would smear positions by ~11 km per day. So the clocks are manufactured deliberately slow — offset before launch so they tick correctly once in orbit. The hardware is pre-distorted for curved spacetime around a spherical mass; the fact that the fix stays put is a daily test of both relativity and the geometry it was computed for.

          ③ The relativity ledger, as an equation.

          Δf / f = ΔU/c² − v²/2c²  ⇒  +45.7 − 7.1 ≈ +38.6 μs/day  ⇒  × c ≈ 11.6 km/day of drift if ignored
          Gravitational blueshift from sitting higher in the potential of a spherical mass, minus time dilation from the 3.9 km/s orbit — both terms are functions of GM and r around a globe, and the satellites' clocks are factory-offset by exactly this amount[5]. The fix holding steady for decades is a daily audit of the arithmetic.

          ④ The range window. Every pseudorange your receiver logs falls between ~20,200 km (satellite overhead) and ~25,800 km (satellite on the horizon) — precisely √((R+h)² − R²) for a sphere of radius R. That narrow window, identical for receivers on every continent, is the sphere's signature in raw data anyone can record.

          Now try to build it on a flat plane

          Steel-man the disc: forget that nothing orbits a plane (orbits are free fall around a central mass) and simply mount the 31 transmitters on towers or hovering platforms, at any heights you like, anywhere over the disc. The public, decodable signal itself now convicts the model:

          What receivers measure vs what fixed flat-plane emitters must produce
          Measured (log it yourself)GlobeFlat emitters
          Satellites rise and set; the in-view set turns over completely in hourspredictedimpossible — anything above the plane stays above every horizon forever, alt = atan(h/d) > 0
          8–12 in view, roughly the same count everywhere — Alaska, Ecuador, New Zealandpredictedcount collapses with distance from the array; the far side of the disc sees a low cluster near one horizon
          Pseudoranges confined to 20,200–25,800 km predictedranges to never-setting distant emitters run to 40,000 km and beyond — never observed
          Southern receivers watch satellites wheel around the southern sky predictedno south to wheel around on a pole-centred disc
          One broadcast ephemeris closes the four-range equation for every receiver at oncepredictedno emitter arrangement over a plane reproduces sphere-consistent ranges at all receivers simultaneously
          Clocks pre-offset by +38 μs/day hold the fix steady for decades predictedno account — the offset is computed from orbital speed and gravitational potential around a spherical mass
          The deepest point is the simplest. GPS is not a picture of the Earth that could be faked; it is a live geometry proof re-run by billions of independent receivers, using public equations, public ephemerides, and raw observables anyone can log. The four ranges close on a point — your point — only if the transmitters are where the globe math says they are. A navigation system is the one kind of evidence that cannot humor a wrong shape and keep working: get the geometry wrong by a kilometre and every landing, harvest and package delivery drifts with it.
          Experiment 8 · read the sky with a free app
          Any GNSS status app shows the raw constellation — no account, no cost

          Install a satellite-status app (most phones expose GPS, Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou). The sky plot shows each satellite's azimuth and elevation, live.

          Independent variable
          What you change: the time — screenshot the sky plot now and again in 1–2 hours; and if you can, compare with a friend at a different latitude at the same moment.
          Dependent variable
          What you measure: each satellite's elevation over time (rising or setting?), the count in view, and where the tracks wheel (north or south).

          Hold constant: the same open-sky spot, the same app. The tells, stated in advance: a globe constellation turns over completely — satellites climb from one horizon and sink below another within hours, ~8–12 in view throughout, and tomorrow's pattern arrives 4 minutes earlier by your clock (the sidereal slip). Fixed flat-plane emitters can never set, never change count, and know nothing of sidereal time.

          Verdict rule, symmetric. The globe fails if one satellite is tracked continuously above the horizon for more than 5 h 04 min, or if the constellation repeats on a 24 h period rather than 23 h 56 min. The flat model fails on any satellite setting at all, and on the sidereal repeat: fixed emitters over a plane never set, and would repeat on the solar day. A phone GNSS status app and a clock; the four-minute daily drift is unmistakable within a week.

          Sources for this tab
          • [1]GPS.gov — the Space Segment: the official constellation description — 24 baseline slots, six equally-spaced orbital planes, ~20,200 km altitude, two orbits per day, at least four satellites in view from virtually any point on the planet.
          • [2]U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center — GPS overview: six circular orbits at 55° inclination with an 11 h 58 min period, and a minimum of six satellites in view worldwide.
          • [3]ESA Navipedia — GPS Space Segment: semi-major axis 26,560 km, orbital speed 3.9 km/s, and the nominal 12-hour sidereal period that repeats the geometry each sidereal day.
          • [4]Penn State GEOG 862, "GPS and GNSS for Geospatial Professionals" — an actual training course for the people who use this for a living: constellation design, ephemerides, and the coordinate systems the fixes land in.
          • [5]Neil Ashby, "Relativity in the Global Positioning System", Living Reviews in Relativity (2003) — the standard reference for the relativistic clock corrections; a readable walk-through of the +45/−7 = +38 μs/day ledger is Prof. R. Pogge's Ohio State lecture, "Real-World Relativity".
          Further reading
          Not cited above, and no claim on this tab rests on it — listed because it is what you would read next, or because it lets you redo the measurement on data this page did not choose.
          • IS-GPS-200, Navstar GPS Space Segment / Navigation User Interfaces — the interface specification itself, published by the U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center. This is the strongest document on the tab. Ashby's review, cited above, explains why the relativistic correction is needed; IS-GPS-200 is where it is written into the standard, as the term −2√(μa)·e·sin E / c² that every receiver is required to apply, alongside the broadcast Keplerian elements. Not an argument about the Earth — a signal specification that will not work unless the Earth is the shape and size stated here.
          • International GNSS Service — formats and standards (RINEX), with the guide to using IGS products. Over 300 permanent tracking stations in more than 80 countries, publishing precise orbits and clocks free of charge. Download a day of broadcast ephemerides and do the four-satellite closure yourself, on real data.
          • B. Hofmann-Wellenhof, H. Lichtenegger & E. Wasle, GNSS — Global Navigation Satellite Systems: GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, and more (Springer, 2008). The standard graduate text, for the reader who wants the trilateration worked through completely rather than sketched.
          • BIPM — Circular T. International atomic time is maintained by comparing clocks in dozens of national laboratories, largely over GPS links. The same relativistic corrections appear there, in metrology rather than navigation, and disagreements would show up as nanoseconds of mismatch between laboratories.
          Work in progress. This tab is a working prototype and is the only one on the page that is not translated — it stays in English in every language. Its ephemeris is validated (Sun and Moon to better than 35″ against libastro over 42 dates in 2026–27)[2], but the interface, the viewpoint picker and the Moon's phase drawing are unfinished, and the flat model here covers azimuth only. Treat its numbers as sound and its edges as rough.
          Observation · predict first, photograph second

          Point a camera at a ridge at the right minute

          What this tab is made of The refracted rays drawn here use the same single k = 0.13, and the same Reff = R / (1 − k), that is derived from scratch on that tab. There is one k in this whole page and this is it — a page arguing that refraction is not a free parameter cannot keep two of them. The elevation angle of every summit in the skyline is the same quantity that tab computes, α = Δh/d − d/(2R) for small angles. Here it is drawn as a horizon line instead of printed as a number. A ridge that a sphere hides and a plane does not is the hidden-height argument, turned into something a camera can settle. Same geometry, different output. Visibility is judged against the depression of the horizon, not against zero — the quantity that tab measures directly. The 32.4′ solar disc used as the on-frame ruler, and the position it is drawn at, come from the ephemeris that tab explains. Why the useful window is the minutes around sunset, and how bright the sky still is when the ridge goes dark.

          Every other tab on this page argues from measurements someone else published. This one hands you the instrument. Pick a date and a time, and it draws the Sun or the Moon at its true angular size against a skyline computed two ways from the same terrain — once on a plane, once on a sphere. The two curves separate by a measurable amount at certain azimuths. Go and photograph one of those azimuths at the stated minute, and the photograph decides.

          The Sun makes this cheap. Its disc is 32.4′ across, known to a fraction of an arcsecond, so a photograph containing both the disc and a ridge calibrates itself: the disc supplies the angular scale inside the frame. No theodolite, no known focal length, no assumption about where eye level was. And azimuth is immune to refraction, which is vertical — so the one prediction the flat map cannot rescue with weather is the one about direction.

          The panel

          View Camera — solid = globe, dashed = flat

          This has been done before, and for two centuries. Canigou is photographed from Allauch, 263 km away, silhouetted on the setting Sun around 9 February and 1 November — the dates the sunset azimuth lines up with the peak, exactly as 24 November lines up here. The hidden-height tab carries that case with its filtered view: on a plane the mountain would be a black mass taller than the solar disc, and what is photographed is a notch an eighth of its width. The shoot below is the same measurement, on a shorter line, with the crossing of two crests instead of one summit.

          What the disc will actually be cut by, on 24 November, is the corner where the two ridges meet. That is a stronger tell than either ridge alone, and it needs no eye level at all. The far ridge is nearly horizontal across this window and the near one climbs at about 20′ per degree of azimuth, so raising the far ridge slides the intersection along the steep branch: the corner sits at a different azimuth in each model, and at a different height. The band above reads both off the same terrain profile the panel draws — about half a degree of azimuth apart, and about 13′ of altitude, a third of a solar diameter sideways and two fifths of one vertically. The panel’s solar-filter view draws exactly what a dense filter shows and nothing else: the disc, and the terrain only where it cuts into it. The plane’s extra ridge is the blue band, the globe’s silhouette the black one, and the two predictions cannot both be where the notch falls.

          True scale, no exaggeration. The bar at the right is the object's own diameter — the only honest ruler in a panel meant to be held against a photograph. The refraction switch is the page's single k, shared with every other tab; the object itself is refracted by Bennett's formula,[3] which is the same physics integrated over the whole atmosphere rather than one layer.
          Map The flat model's own map, seen from above
          • the bearing a compass reads at that instant
          • the line to the point the Sun stands over, which is what a direction means on a flat world
          • the true great-circle path, for context only — do not measure an angle off it
          This is the Gleason azimuthal-equidistant disc — the map flat-earth sources publish, not one invented here to be knocked down. North pole at the centre, Antarctica as the rim, updating with the panel above second for second. Both rays are bearings measured off local north, which on this map is the direction to the centre, so they can be compared. The projection is equidistant from the centre but not conformal — it stretches east–west by about 12 % at this latitude — which is why the great-circle curve is context and not a protractor. The comparison that means something is between the two straight rays and the numbers above them: it needs no instrument beyond a compass, and refraction cannot touch it, being vertical.
          Data Targets from this viewpoint
          SummitDistanceAbove eyeFlatGlobeGap
          Distance and azimuth are derived, not copied. Each row carries only what a source publishes — name, coordinates, summit height — and the page computes the rest by great circle, so a rounded readout from an app can never enter the arithmetic. Sphere, not ellipsoid: the WGS-84 geodesic differs by 0.3 %, which moves the Grand Mourre answer by 0.08′ out of a 12.7′ effect.[4]

          The crossing: one point that has to be in two places

          The strongest thing at this viewpoint is not a summit. It is the place where two ridges touch. Sweep left from Mourre Frey[5] and the near ridge at 16 km sinks; sweep right from Le Grand Mourre and the far ridge at 54 km rises to meet it. At azimuth 241.36° the two silhouettes cross. Photograph that spot and you have measured nothing — you have only observed that two ridges touch — and yet the flat model is already finished.

          The two points that meet are on opposite sides of the observer. The near side of the crossing is the summit listed as C in the table above — PeakFinder publishes it at 1,677 m, thirteen metres below the viewpoint, and the elevation model reads 1,669 m at the same spot, twenty-two metres away, well inside one 3″ cell (93 m north–south at this latitude). The far side is at 1,759 m, sixty-nine metres above the viewpoint. On a plane, anything lower than you is below eye level and anything higher than you is above it, at every distance, with no exception and no free parameter: only height enters the formula. So those two points cannot appear at the same height. They do. The same pixel in the photograph would have to be above and below eye level at once.

          On a sphere there is nothing to reconcile: curvature takes 200 m from the far ridge and 18 m from the near one, the 90 m difference in altitude is exactly absorbed, and both land at about −8′, which is where the crossing is observed. Put the other way round — solve a plane for the observer height that would make the two coincide, and it returns 1,642 m using the published near height, or 1,631 m using the model's. The viewpoint is at 1,690 m. The flat model is wrong about your own altitude by 48 to 59 m, and no value of k can repair it, because a plane has no curvature for k to correct.

          This is the cheapest test on the page: no instrument, no clock, no angle, not even a level. Two published altitudes, your own altitude, and a photograph in which two ridges touch. Its limit, stated plainly: it works only because the viewpoint sits between 1,677 m and 1,759 m, and the lower margin is just thirteen metres — smaller than the elevation model's own bias on a sharp peak, which is why the near point is quoted from a published height rather than from the model. Know your altitude to better than about ten metres, from a map or a published spot height and not from a phone's GPS, which is rarely that good vertically, or the argument does not close. Standing 13 m lower would end it. The far margin is safer than it looks: 1,759 m is a model value, and the model reads low by around 20 m on high ground, so the real far point is higher still and that error runs in the argument's favour rather than against it.

          Why this viewpoint

          The viewpoint is a documented spot at 44.09388° N, 6.92856° E, 1,690 m in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence.[1] Its interest is one summit: Le Grand Mourre, 1,898 m, 54.1 km away on a bearing of 241.2°. It stands 208 m higher than the observer — and on a plane, a summit higher than you is above eye level at every distance, because on a plane only height counts. A sphere of R = 6,371 km costs it 231 m of curvature drop over that range, which is more than its 208 m of extra height, so it must sit below eye level. Refraction at k = 0.13 lifts it back to roughly level, and no further.

          A 2.4°-wide window where the models disagree about the sign. Ray-marching a 90 m elevation model out to 200 km from this spot, the far ridge is the skyline between azimuth 239.1° and 241.4°, and across that whole window it is above eye level on a plane and below it on a globe. The Sun's disc rides that window on 24 November 2026: first contact with Le Grand Mourre at 16:54:57 CET, last of the upper limb at 16:59:04. Four minutes, and the evenings either side are nearly as good — one filtered video takes it.

          Two things the panel deliberately refuses to do. It does not treat the drawn skyline as evidence: both curves come from an elevation model, and a terrain model cannot test the geometry that built it — the curves are there to show where to point the camera. And it does not use the model's heights for the named summits, because 90 m sampling shaves about 22 m off a sharp peak, which is 1.4′ at 54 km, eleven per cent of the effect. Named summits use published heights.

          Experiment · photograph the sign change
          One filtered camera, one synchronised clock, six minutes

          Stand at the published viewpoint. Point a solar-filtered camera at azimuth 241°, start recording before 16:53 CET and stop after 17:00. Film a network-synchronised clock in shot, or note the timestamps. That is the entire apparatus.

          Independent variable
          What you change: the instant, and nothing else. The viewpoint, the azimuth and the target summit are all fixed and published in advance — you only choose when to read the frame.
          Dependent variable
          What you measure: the ridge's height above or below the Sun's centre, in units of the solar disc, read straight off that frame. The disc is 32.4′ wide, so the frame carries its own scale — you do not get to choose this, the photograph tells you.

          Hold constant: one tripod, one clock synchronised to network time and filmed in shot. The tells, stated in advance: a plane requires Le Grand Mourre to stand 13.2′ above eye level, a sphere with straight rays 1.4′ below, a sphere with k = 0.13, 0.5′ above. The spread between plane and sphere is 12.7′, or 39 % of the solar disc, and it converts to about 83 seconds of sunset timing at this latitude. Read the limb, not the blaze: a Sun photographed near the horizon is overexposed, and the white blob is wider than the real disc, so judging "half hidden" by eye runs early. Stop the exposure down until the disc has an edge before you time anything.

          What would settle it for the plane. If the ridge photographs 13′ above the Sun's centre at the stated minute — two fifths of a disc high, unmistakable at any zoom — the flat prediction is right and this page is wrong. If it photographs level with the Sun or below it, no value of k on a plane can produce that, because a plane has no curvature to correct for. The measurement is the same either way; only the answer differs.

          The arithmetic, in full

          Everything on this tab comes out of three formulas, and the argument is entirely about which symbols appear in them. Here they are, with nothing hidden.

          Plane  ·  tan α = Δh / d
          Δh is the target's height above the observer's eye, d the distance between them. That is the complete formula. Notice what is absent: any length to compare d against. Double d and double Δh and α is unchanged, because a plane has no size. This is not a simplification of the flat model — it is the flat model, and it has no free parameter left to tune.
          Sphere  ·  tan α = (r₂ cos γ − r₁) / (r₂ sin γ)   with   γ = d / R
          r₁ = R + h₁ and r₂ = R + h₂ are the two distances from the planet's centre, and γ is the angle the two radii open between them. γ = d/R is where the whole disagreement lives. The observer's horizontal is perpendicular to his own radius, and the target's vertical has swung away by γ, so the target has to be found lower than a plane would put it — by an amount that depends on distance alone. This is the exact form the page computes; it is not expanded or approximated.
          Small γ  ·  α ≈ Δh/d − d/(2R)   →   with refraction, d(1−k)/(2R)
          Expand the sphere formula and the plane's answer falls out first, followed by a correction of d/(2R). Everything this page argues is contained in that one term. Set R = ∞ and it vanishes and you are back on a plane — so a plane is not a rival model here, it is the R → ∞ limit of the same formula. Refraction does not remove the term, it only replaces R with R/(1−k), shrinking it by a factor (1−k). At the standard k = 0.13 that is a 13 % reduction. To cancel it outright you need k = 1, which makes the effective radius infinite — that is, k = 1 is the plane, and it would take a temperature rising 12.9 °C per hundred metres held over the whole sight line.

          Diagram: where d/R enters

          Panel B's curvature is exaggerated ×90 by drawing a smaller planet and scaling the heights to match, then rendering both axes at one scale. Stretching the vertical axis instead would turn the globe into an ellipse and reduce the tilt between the two verticals, which is the very effect being shown. Panel C is at true scale and needs no exaggeration. This figure is generated by make_fig_curvature.py, shipped beside the page — edit the generator, never these coordinates.
          And the flat model's own object. The dashed outline in the panel is where a lamp circling above the disc would have to be. Its azimuth is simply the direction, across the azimuthal-equidistant map, from the viewpoint to the point the Sun stands over — a direction that does not depend on the lamp's height at all, so there is no parameter to adjust and no refraction to appeal to, refraction being vertical. Its altitude does depend on the height, which is why the slider is there: run it from 500 to 20,000 km and watch the dashed disc refuse to reach the horizon at any setting. Even at 500 km it still stands 2.5° up while the real Sun is touching the ridge.

          Its size is fixed, not fitted. The lamp is given the one physical diameter the flat model would itself choose — the diameter that subtends the observed 32.4′ when it is straight overhead, which at 5,000 km makes it 47 km across. Nothing after that is adjustable. At sunset the lamp has retreated to 11,578 km across the map, so the same object must appear 12.8′ wide, 40 % of what the camera records. Move the height slider and the diameter moves with it, because the overhead calibration is held; the shrink toward the horizon never goes away.

          You will usually not see it in frame. At the moment of the 24 November sunset the dashed object sits 40° away from the real one, so at any useful zoom it is off the edge — an arrow at the border points to it and states the separation. Choose Frame both in the camera menu to pull back far enough to hold the two at once, and the disc becomes a ringed dot with a leader. That the two cannot share a normal photograph is the finding.

          The mirror of the front page

          What would change our mind

          Every tab on this page ends with a number you can go and check. This one collects the other half of each of them: the result that would sink the globe. Not a rhetorical concession — a stated threshold, decided before the measurement, with the precision your instrument has to reach for the answer to mean anything. If one of these is produced, this page is wrong, and it says so in advance rather than afterwards.

          Building this page found a gap in it. Nine tabs state what would refute them. Six did not: celestial navigation, horizon dip, gravity, the pendulum, magnetism and GPS carried the measurement and the numbers but never the threshold. Those six rules are written here for the first time, and they still have to be carried back into their own tabs. A page that asks to be checked owes that line everywhere, not in most places.
          Read a row from the middle out. The centre column is what a flat-earth measurement would have to show to end this page; the right column is what a globe measurement would have to show to end the flat model. Both are stated with the same care on purpose — a threshold that only ever fires one way is not a threshold.

          What would not settle anything, and why

          A horizon that looks flat. At two metres above the sea the horizon is 5 km away and drops 0.04° below eye level — forty times finer than the width of a pencil held at arm's length. Both models predict you see a straight line. A photograph of one is not evidence for either.

          An oval star trail. As soon as the camera is not aimed at the celestial pole, the image of a circle in the sky is a conic, and a real lens adds its own distortion. Both models produce ovals. The star tab measures angles instead, for exactly this reason.

          A laser that crossed a lake. Without a documented eye height, a measured distance, a stated time of day and a temperature profile, a laser shot over water is not a measurement of anything. Refraction over a cold surface on a warm afternoon routinely reaches several times the standard coefficient. This cuts both ways: it is also why laser shots are not counted here when they did show curvature.

          Anything an official body says. Not one row of the table above needs you to trust an agency. Every threshold is reachable with a phone, a stopwatch, a protractor or a pendulum, and the two rows that use published data — earthquake arrival times and the star catalogue — name archives that are open, are maintained by rival institutions in different countries, and would have to be falsified in concert.

          The one that keeps the page honest. Any single test can be met with “your instrument was off”, and often fairly. That is why the page's real claim is not any one row: it is that one radius, R ≈ 6,371 km, satisfies every row at once. To refute that you do not need to beat one threshold — you need a flat arrangement that beats two of them with the same parameters. None has ever been shown, and the page would print it if one were.
